evidence.snippet: Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome (BRRS) is a rare genetic disorder caused by germline mutations in the phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) gene.
evidence.explanation: Directly assigns germline PTEN variants as the cause of BRRS.

evidence.snippet: Mutations were identified in 26 of 43 (60%) BRR cases.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the approximately 60% germline PTEN detection rate in a dedicated BRRS cohort.

evidence.snippet: Among CS, BRR and BRR/CS overlap families that are PTEN mutation positive, the mutation spectra appear similar.
evidence.explanation: Supports the claim that the BRRS mutation spectrum is not distinguishable from that of Cowden syndrome.

evidence.snippet: We have identified a germline mutation, R335X, in PTEN in a family consisting of two female members with the phenotypic findings of CS and two male members with the phenotypic findings of BZS.
evidence.explanation: A single PTEN nonsense variant segregating with both Cowden and BRRS phenotypes in one family, the key intrafamilial evidence for allelism.

evidence.snippet: Germline pathogenic variants have been found throughout PTEN and include missense, nonsense, and splice site variants, small deletions, insertions, and large deletions.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews molecular-genetics section describes the spectrum, including sequence and structural variants.

evidence.snippet: Thus 3 (11%) of 27 patients with BRRS or BRRS/CS-overlap had PTEN deletions.
evidence.explanation: This additional yield is in a selected subgroup without previously PCR-detected intragenic variants, not 11% of all BRRS. The promoter-variant cases in this study had Cowden syndrome.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous germline pathogenic PTEN variants establish PHTS and cause PTEN-positive BRRS. Sequence variants and deletions occur, and the spectrum overlaps Cowden syndrome. The classic clinically ascertained BRRS study identified variants in 26 of 43 cases (60%). Detection rates depend on ascertainment and assay coverage; a negative test does not exclude the clinical BRRS phenotype. The spectrum includes nonsense, missense, splice, small insertion/deletion, and larger copy-number variants. In selected BRRS/overlap cases without a previously identified intragenic variant, deletion analysis found additional diagnoses.

evidence.snippet: We exome-sequenced 35 unrelated PTEN-wildtype patients with classic presentation of BRRS and identified TTN germline missense variants in 12/35 (34%) patients.
evidence.explanation: The primary human genetic observation: rare TTN missense variants in about a third of PTEN-wildtype classic BRRS patients.

evidence.snippet: suggested lack of contact inhibition in mutant cells
evidence.explanation: Cell-based functional support for one TTN variant. Limited to the cell assay, with evidence_source IN_VITRO because it is an edited-cell phenotype, not a demonstration of the human disease mechanism.

evidence.snippet: our observations suggest TTN as a candidate predisposing gene in classic PTEN-wildtype BRRS patients, perhaps suggesting this syndrome join the growing list of Titinopathies
evidence.explanation: The authors' own framing as a candidate gene, which is why this is curated as SUSCEPTIBILITY rather than CAUSATIVE.

genes/1.notes: TTN is a candidate predisposing locus in PTEN-wildtype BRRS. The discovery study identified germline missense variants in 12 of 35 unrelated classic BRRS probands. Functional study of one edited variant suggested impaired contact inhibition, but does not establish pathogenicity of all variants or a validated disease-gene relationship. This susceptibility annotation denotes a research candidate and is not a basis for predictive clinical testing or treatment selection.

evidence.snippet: Thus, PTEN mutation-positive CS and BRR may be different presentations of a single syndrome and, hence, both should receive equal attention with respect to cancer surveillance.
evidence.explanation: The primary justification for applying full Cowden-equivalent surveillance to PTEN-positive BRRS.

evidence.snippet: As targeted treatment is still lacking, symptom relief and long-term surveillance remain the main management strategies.
evidence.explanation: BRRS-specific systematic review confirming that surveillance plus symptom-directed care, rather than any disease-modifying therapy, is the management mainstay.

evidence.snippet: at this time, it is not felt that genotype-specific recommendations could be made for individuals with PHTS
evidence.explanation: The consensus explicitly rejects genotype-specific surveillance recommendations at present.

evidence.snippet: Regardless of clinical phenotype, individuals with a germline PTEN pathogenic variant are thought to have the same cancer risks.
evidence.explanation: The updated GeneReviews chapter bases shared PHTS risk management on a germline pathogenic PTEN variant.

treatments/0.description: Individuals with a germline pathogenic PTEN variant and a BRRS phenotype require long-term PHTS cancer-risk management. Recent guidelines differ in starting ages, intervals, and the evidence for renal and endometrial surveillance. The 2025 international consensus and 2026 ERN GENTURIS recommendations are therefore described separately below. Personal and family history, prior lesions, local guidance, and shared decision-making inform the plan. Molecularly negative clinical BRRS requires individualized assessment; the same cancer risk is not established. Genotype-based surveillance stratification is not supported by current evidence.

evidence.snippet: Women with PHTS should undergo annual breast MRI (with contrast) from age 25 years and additional surveillance with breast mammography (with digital breast tomosynthesis) starting at age 40 years until 75 to 80 years of age.
evidence.explanation: The consensus breast imaging recommendation is stated with its age thresholds.

evidence.snippet: From age 12 years, individuals with PHTS should undergo baseline thyroid ultrasound.
evidence.explanation: The 2025 consensus begins thyroid ultrasound at 12 years.

evidence.snippet: We recommend surveillance with thyroid ultrasound every 3 to 5 years for individuals with PHTS and without nodules seen on initial thyroid ultrasound and every 2 to 3 years for individuals with clinically nonactionable nodules seen on initial thyroid ultrasound.
evidence.explanation: Intervals depend on the initial ultrasound findings.

evidence.snippet: We recommend that all individuals with PHTS undergo a baseline colonoscopy at 35–40 years.
evidence.explanation: This is routine baseline surveillance, distinct from earlier symptom-directed evaluation.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with PHTS and a high colon polyp burden (five or more tubular adenomas), or polyps greater than or equal to 1 cm in diameter or with high-grade dysplasia, should undergo colonoscopy at a 1- to 3-year interval, as directed by their gastroenterologist.
evidence.explanation: The shorter interval is conditional on polyp burden, size, or dysplasia.

evidence.snippet: If the decision to offer surveillance for endometrial cancer is made, this should be part of a clinical trial.
evidence.explanation: The 2025 recommendation reflects limited evidence for routine endometrial surveillance.

evidence.snippet: Starting at the age of 35–40 years, a surveillance ultrasound every 2 years for renal cell carcinoma may be considered in individuals with PHTS.
evidence.explanation: This is explicitly an expert-opinion recommendation with limited evidence.

treatments/1.description: The 2025 international consensus recommends annual breast MRI from age 25 and annual mammography from age 40. Thyroid ultrasound begins at age 12, then every 3-5 years when normal or every 2-3 years for clinically nonactionable nodules. Baseline colonoscopy is recommended at 35-40 years, with 1-3-year follow-up for a high adenoma burden, large polyps, or high-grade dysplasia. Routine endometrial surveillance, if offered, should be within a clinical trial; abnormal uterine bleeding requires evaluation. Renal ultrasound every two years from 35-40 may be considered as expert opinion. These recommendations concern PTEN-confirmed PHTS, not BRRS-specific trial evidence.

evidence.snippet: Surveillance for breast cancer with MRI should probably start at age 25.
evidence.explanation: Recommendation 3 gives the MRI starting age.

evidence.snippet: In addition, mammography every 1–2 years can be considered, preferably from the age of 40 years
evidence.explanation: The full guideline text describes mammography in addition to annual MRI and allows alignment with national surveillance guidance.

evidence.snippet: Surveillance for thyroid cancer should probably start between 10 and 18 years of age.
evidence.explanation: Recommendation 8 gives an age range, rather than a universal starting age.

evidence.snippet: Individuals should be offered surveillance for thyroid cancer annually initially. Individuals with two ultrasound examinations with no suspicious findings should probably be re-scanned at an increased interval of two to three years as clinically indicated.
evidence.explanation: Recommendation 9 distinguishes initial annual imaging from longer intervals after normal scans.

evidence.snippet: If surveillance for endometrial cancer is offered, it should probably start at 35-40 years.
evidence.explanation: The European guideline differs from the 2025 international consensus on endometrial surveillance.

evidence.snippet: If surveillance for endometrial cancer is offered, it should probably be via transvaginal ultrasonography done at least annually. Endometrial biopsy can be considered.
evidence.explanation: Recommendation 12 identifies the proposed modality and interval.

evidence.snippet: Individuals should be offered a baseline imaging exam at age 35–40 years for renal cell carcinoma (RCC).
evidence.explanation: Recommendation 14 specifies baseline renal imaging.

evidence.snippet: Where renal baseline imaging is normal, further regular surveillance is not recommended, just follow-up based on signs and symptoms.
evidence.explanation: The renal footnote differs materially from the 2025 consensus suggestion of repeated imaging.

evidence.snippet: Baseline colonoscopy should be undertaken at 35–40 years to assess polyp load, preferably in an expert centre. Interval of monitoring is guided by the number, size and pathology of resected polyps.
evidence.explanation: Recommendation 15 bases subsequent colonoscopy on the findings.

evidence.snippet: In individuals with only hamartomas or no polyps at baseline colonoscopy, colorectal cancer surveillance may follow general population guidelines. However, a repeat colonoscopy after 5 to 10 years can be considered.
evidence.explanation: Recommendation 16 distinguishes hamartomas from higher-risk polyp findings.

evidence.snippet: Individuals probably should have a baseline skin examination performed by a doctor with expertise in this condition at age 30, further surveillance as required
evidence.explanation: Recommendation 17 gives baseline skin assessment without assuming annual lifelong dermatologic screening.

treatments/2.description: The 2026 ERN GENTURIS guideline recommends breast MRI surveillance from age 25, with mammography every 1-2 years considered from age 40 or according to national guidance. Thyroid ultrasound starts between 10 and 18 years, annually initially, then every 2-3 years after two examinations without suspicious findings. Endometrial surveillance is probably appropriate from 35-40 years using at least annual transvaginal ultrasonography, with biopsy considered. Renal baseline imaging is offered at 35-40; when normal, further regular renal screening is not recommended. Baseline colonoscopy at 35-40 determines follow-up by polyp number, size, and pathology; only hamartomas or no polyps may permit general-population screening or repeat colonoscopy after 5-10 years. A baseline skin examination is suggested at 30, with further assessment according to findings or symptoms.

evidence.snippet: Polypectomies of hamartomatous polyps were also frequent, with two cases of proctocolectomy and subtotal colectomy due to severe symptom burden and recurrence
evidence.explanation: The BRRS review records endoscopic polyp removal and surgery for severe recurrent disease.

evidence.snippet: BRRS patients with polyps may present with abdominal pain, hematochezia, anemia, invagination, constipation, or diarrhea
evidence.explanation: These complications motivate symptom-directed care independently of routine screening ages.

treatments/3.description: Symptomatic gastrointestinal polyps require evaluation and endoscopic management according to size, histology, and complications. Childhood bleeding, anemia, obstruction, or intussusception may warrant assessment before routine adult cancer-screening ages. Severe or recurrent disease can require surgery.

evidence.snippet: Treatment for the benign and malignant manifestations of PHTS is the same as for their sporadic counterparts.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews establishes the principle of treating manifestations as for sporadic disease.

evidence.snippet: cutaneous lesions should be excised only if malignancy is suspected or symptoms (e.g., pain, deformity, increased scarring) are significant.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports restricting excision to symptomatic or suspicious lesions.

treatments/4.description: Lipomas, vascular lesions, and other benign manifestations are treated the same way as their sporadic counterparts, with excision reserved for lesions causing pain, functional impairment, deformity, or diagnostic uncertainty rather than performed prophylactically.

evidence.snippet: Early paediatric diagnosis is important for institution of medical and developmental surveillance as well as for testing other at- risk family members.
evidence.explanation: Supports developmental surveillance and support as an explicit goal of early pediatric diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: Referral to an early intervention program is recommended for access to occupational, physical, speech, and feeding therapy as well as infant mental health services, special educators, and sensory impairment specialists.
evidence.explanation: The updated GeneReviews chapter specifies multidisciplinary early intervention for developmental difficulties.

treatments/5.description: Because developmental delay, intellectual disability, and autism spectrum characteristics are core to the BRRS presentation, early developmental assessment and intervention (speech, motor, and educational support) is a management priority independent of the cancer-surveillance agenda.

evidence.snippet: PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (PHTS) is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) overactivity.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the mechanistic rationale for mTOR inhibition in PHTS.

evidence.snippet: Changes in the primary endpoint between groups from baseline to Month 6 were not apparent
evidence.explanation: Recorded as REFUTE for the claim of neurocognitive efficacy. The randomized trial's primary endpoint was null, which is why this treatment is curated as investigational rather than established.

evidence.snippet: Gastrointestinal adverse events were more common in the everolimus group
evidence.explanation: Documents the principal treatment-emergent toxicity signal in the trial.

treatments/6.description: Everolimus targets the mTOR overactivity that follows PTEN loss, giving a direct mechanistic rationale. A 6-month phase II randomized placebo-controlled trial in 46 individuals with PHTS (eligible ages 5 to 45 years) found the drug tolerable but did not meet its primary neurocognitive endpoint, with gastrointestinal adverse events more common on treatment. mTOR inhibition therefore remains investigational for the neurodevelopmental features of BRRS and is not routine care.

treatments/6/targets/0.description: Pharmacologic inhibition of mTOR is the molecular target; clinical benefit for each indication requires separate evidence.

evidence.snippet: mTOR inhibitors have been investigated in patients with vascular anomalies when previous treatments were ineffective
evidence.explanation: Establishes the lesion-directed indication. This evidence is limited because it describes an investigational, salvage-setting use rather than established efficacy.

evidence.snippet: only one study reported the use of rapamycin
evidence.explanation: Quantifies how thin the BRRS-specific evidence is: a single report among 33 reviewed articles, which is why this is curated as anecdotal rather than standard care.

evidence.snippet: There is no established standard treatment for PHTS patients
evidence.explanation: Confirms the absence of an established standard therapy in PHTS, the framing under which any mTOR-inhibitor use in BRRS should be read.

treatments/7.description: Sirolimus (rapamycin) is the lesion-directed mTOR-inhibitor use in BRRS, distinct from the neurocognitive indication that the everolimus trial tested and missed. It is used off-label for symptomatic vascular anomalies when other treatments have failed, and the BRRS-specific published experience is a single pediatric case in the 2024 systematic review. Evidence is therefore anecdotal, and this is curated as an off-label option under investigation rather than standard care.

treatments/7/targets/0.description: Pharmacologic inhibition of mTOR is the molecular target; clinical benefit for each indication requires separate evidence.

evidence.snippet: When a PTEN pathogenic variant has been identified in a proband, molecular genetic testing of asymptomatic at-risk relatives can identify those who have the family-specific pathogenic variant and warrant ongoing surveillance.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports cascade testing of at-risk relatives to direct surveillance.

evidence.snippet: To our knowledge, this is the first report that shows the presence of separate subjects with CS and with BZS in a single family associated with a single germline PTEN mutation.
evidence.explanation: Supports counseling about intrafamilial variable expressivity: the same variant can produce either BRRS or Cowden syndrome in different relatives.

evidence.snippet: Once the PTEN pathogenic variant has been identified in an affected family member, prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports reproductive counseling after the familial molecular diagnosis is established.

treatments/8.description: Genetic counseling covers the autosomal dominant 50% transmission risk, the variable expressivity that lets one PTEN variant produce BRRS in one relative and Cowden syndrome in another, and the value of predictive testing in at-risk relatives so that carriers can enter surveillance.

evidence.snippet: Five participants were enrolled, with 2 completing the planned study course.
evidence.explanation: The published completion count limits interpretation of efficacy.

evidence.snippet: For the patients completing the study, polyp numbers decreased
evidence.explanation: A within-person observation in two completers is not controlled evidence of benefit.

evidence.snippet: there was not a change in polyposis staging despite the reduction in total colorectal polyp burden.
evidence.explanation: The trial did not establish a reduction in colonoscopy or colectomy requirements.

evidence.snippet: Withdrawals were due to side effects likely related to sirolimus for 2 subjects (pneumonitis after 6 weeks requiring withdrawal and recurrent vaginal candidiasis leading to withdrawal after 3 months)
evidence.explanation: Two likely treatment-related withdrawals limit tolerability in the small pilot study.

treatments/9.description: A small adult PHTS trial found fewer colorectal polyps in the two participants completing a year of sirolimus, without a change in polyposis stage. Drug-related pneumonitis and recurrent vaginal candidiasis caused withdrawals. This remains investigational and does not establish colorectal cancer prevention or a pediatric BRRS indication.

treatments/9/targets/0.description: Pharmacologic inhibition of mTOR is the molecular target; clinical benefit for each indication requires separate evidence.

evidence.snippet: Physical therapy is recommended to maximize mobility and to reduce the risk for later-onset orthopedic complications (e.g., contractures, scoliosis, hip dislocation).
evidence.explanation: The updated GeneReviews chapter describes management of gross motor dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: Occupational therapy is recommended for difficulty with fine motor skills that affect adaptive function such as feeding, grooming, dressing, and writing.
evidence.explanation: The chapter distinguishes fine-motor and adaptive support from gross motor therapy.

treatments/10.description: Physical therapy supports mobility and addresses hypotonia and orthopedic complications. Occupational therapy targets fine-motor and adaptive difficulties, with equipment and support tailored to individual function.

evidence.snippet: Given the high lifetime risk of female breast cancer and second primary breast cancer in individuals with PHTS and pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in PTEN, we recommend discussing the options of surveillance versus RRM with an experienced high-risk breast clinic team.
evidence.explanation: The guideline recommends a discussion of alternatives rather than universal preventive surgery.

evidence.snippet: Generally, RRM should only be considered in individuals older than 25 years of age, unless otherwise clinically indicated
evidence.explanation: The usual age threshold is explicitly qualified.

evidence.snippet: We do not recommend routine hysterectomy for endometrial cancer risk reduction in PHTS individuals with a uterus.
evidence.explanation: The consensus opposes routine hysterectomy and recommends individualized assessment.

treatments/11.description: For PTEN-confirmed PHTS, risk-reducing mastectomy may be discussed as an alternative to breast surveillance with an experienced high-risk breast team, generally after age 25. Counseling considers individual risk, surgical complications, reconstruction, and preferences. Routine hysterectomy is not recommended by the 2025 international consensus; decisions are individualized, including uterine pathology and reproductive plans. These are adult risk-management options, not routine interventions for children with BRRS.

evidence.snippet: Purified recombinant PTEN catalyzed dephosphorylation of PtdIns(3,4,5)P3, specifically at position 3 on the inositol ring.
evidence.explanation: Biochemical assays establish the direct PIP3 3-phosphatase activity of PTEN.

evidence.snippet: In PHTS, loss of PTEN function leads to disinhibition of the PI3K (phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate 3-kinase)-AKT–mTOR pathway
evidence.explanation: The trial introduction summarizes established PHTS signaling biology; the clinical trial did not itself measure this molecular chain.

hypotheses/0.description: PTEN lipid-phosphatase loss increases PIP3-dependent AKT signaling and downstream mTOR activity, contributing to abnormal growth. This is a central mechanism in PTEN-positive BRRS, but does not establish a single causal route for every clinical feature or explain all PTEN-negative presentations.

evidence.snippet: The homozygous Pten(m3m4) mice have decreased total Pten levels including a specific drop in nuclear Pten and exhibit region-specific increases in brain weight.
evidence.explanation: The model combines reduced Pten abundance with altered localization and shows regional brain enlargement.

evidence.snippet: It is important to note that although we observe decreased nuclear Pten in the brain of the Ptenm3m4 mouse, we also observe decreased cytoplasmic Pten
evidence.explanation: The authors explicitly acknowledge the abundance/localization confound in interpreting the model.

hypotheses/1.description: The cytoplasmic-predominant Ptenm3m4 mouse supports a contribution of PTEN localization and dosage to neuronal growth, glial proliferation, and microglial function. Both nuclear and cytoplasmic Pten are reduced, so it does not isolate localization from protein abundance. Its behavioral and cellular findings do not establish an autism-versus-cancer division in patients or a basis for changing cancer surveillance.

evidence.snippet: suggested lack of contact inhibition in mutant cells
evidence.explanation: Edited HEK293T cells continued proliferating after confluence; one TTN variant was tested.

evidence.snippet: we note paradoxical downstream readouts of decreased phosphorylation of AKT and ERK1/2
evidence.explanation: The measured signaling direction differs from canonical PTEN-loss hyperactivation.

hypotheses/2.description: An edited TTN p.Cys5096Arg HEK293T model showed impaired contact inhibition and altered focal adhesion kinase readouts. AKT and ERK phosphorylation decreased, despite lower PTEN protein, so the observations do not support canonical AKT hyperactivation in these cells. The proposed TTN-dependent growth mechanism remains a candidate based on one functionally tested variant; neither human disease causality nor response to mTOR inhibitors was established.

evidence.snippet: Although these estimates provide guidance for clinical care, discrepancies between studies, sample sizes, retrospective designs, strongly ascertained cases, and lack of pediatric research emphasizes that data should be interpreted with great caution.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly identifies the absence of pediatric data and ascertainment bias as the gap.

evidence.snippet: We acknowledge the limited understanding of the natural history of childhood-onset PHTS as a cancer predisposition syndrome and present a summary of important management considerations.
evidence.explanation: A pediatric-focused review stating directly that the natural history of childhood-onset PHTS as a cancer predisposition syndrome is poorly understood.

open_questions/0.rationale: The cancer surveillance imposed on children diagnosed with BRRS rests on allelism with Cowden syndrome rather than on direct BRRS-cohort incidence data. The original BRRS delineation explicitly noted that malignancy had not been formally documented in BRRS, and contemporary reviews flag that existing PHTS risk estimates come from strongly ascertained, mostly adult cohorts with an acknowledged absence of pediatric research. If BRRS-ascertained carriers have materially different risk, current pediatric surveillance may be either over- or under-calibrated.

evidence.snippet: Mutations were identified in 26 of 43 (60%) BRR cases.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the incomplete molecular yield that defines this gap.

evidence.snippet: Comparisons between BRR and a previously studied group of 37 CS families suggested an increased likelihood of identifying a germline PTEN mutation in families with either CS alone or both CS and BRR when compared with BRR alone
evidence.explanation: Documents that BRRS-alone families have a lower PTEN detection rate, sharpening the question of what underlies mutation-negative BRRS.

evidence.snippet: The remaining cases are of unknown genetic etiology.
evidence.explanation: The TTN study frames the remaining genetic etiology as unknown; its candidate findings do not resolve this clinical group.

open_questions/1.rationale: The classic BRRS series identified PTEN variants in 26 of 43 cases. This historical yield depends on ascertainment and testing methods and is not a current universal residual fraction. Structural and promoter variants warrant appropriate testing. A TTN study reported a candidate association and an edited-cell phenotype, but did not establish TTN as a BRRS disease gene. KLLN methylation was studied in Cowden/Cowden-like patients and is not an established explanation for BRRS. Cancer-risk estimates for PTEN-confirmed PHTS cannot automatically be applied to this unresolved group.

evidence.snippet: Herpes simplex virus type 1 genomes were detected in 11 of 14 patients (79%) with Bell palsy but not in patients with the Ramsay-Hunt syndrome or in other controls.
evidence.explanation: This human molecular observation is evidence for a viral hypothesis, not proof that all Bell's palsy is infectious.

steps/0.description: Reactivation of latent HSV-1 is one proposed initiating event, not an established cause in every idiopathic case. A small prospective study detected HSV-1 DNA in endoneurial fluid or posterior auricular muscle from 11 of 14 Bell's palsy patients, compared with none of nine Ramsay Hunt patients and twelve other controls. Detection in selected clinical samples supports the hypothesis but does not establish timing, causal sufficiency or population prevalence.

evidence.snippet: While the pathogenesis remains unknown, previous studies have implicated post-viral inflammation and resulting compression of the facial nerve.
evidence.explanation: The GWAS introduction summarizes the inflammatory model rather than experimentally demonstrating it.

steps/1.description: Local inflammation around the facial nerve is a leading explanatory process. The initiating event and relative contributions of viral reactivation, immune responses and vascular factors remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: The pathophysiology of Bell’s palsy includes edematous swelling of the facial nerve within the Fallopian canal, which causes a conduction block and subsequent dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: The surgical study's background summarizes the anatomical model; its operative comparison is separate evidence.

steps/2.description: Swelling of the facial nerve within the narrow bony facial canal limits its ability to expand. This is the proposed anatomical substrate for secondary compression.

evidence.snippet: As a result of this viral infection, the facial nerve swells and is compressed in its canal as it courses through the temporal bone.
evidence.explanation: The guideline describes compression in a proposed viral-inflammatory model; the viral antecedent is not independently proven by this review.

steps/3.description: The rigid intratemporal canal constrains a swollen facial nerve, producing local compression, particularly at narrow segments. Anatomical compression is distinct from the resulting conduction failure and from axonal degeneration.

evidence.snippet: Many patients with Bell's palsy fortunately only develop neurapraxia, i.e., a transient blockage of facial nerve conduction without axonal damage
evidence.explanation: This explicitly distinguishes reversible conduction block from axonal injury.

steps/4.description: Reduced conduction through affected facial nerve fibers produces lower motor neuron facial weakness and can disturb facial-nerve-associated taste, stapedius function and tear secretion. In neurapraxia, conduction block occurs without axonal disruption and can recover without the regeneration required for synkinesis.

evidence.snippet: Only those patients with Bell's palsy and axonal damage can develop facial synkinesis.
evidence.explanation: The synkinesis review identifies axonal damage as a prerequisite, not a universal feature of Bell's palsy.

steps/5.description: More severe lesions include axonal degeneration rather than isolated neurapraxia. Wallerian degeneration reaches distal segments after a delay, explaining why early distal electrical responses may remain intact. Axonal injury increases the possibility of incomplete recovery and creates the substrate for abnormal reinnervation.

evidence.snippet: The synkinesis is a result of misguided nerve regeneration following axonal damage.
evidence.explanation: This supports aberrant regeneration as the principal explanatory process for synkinesis.

evidence.snippet: Facial synkinesis occurs when one axon sends sprouts to muscle fibers of two different muscles, i.e., the original target muscle and any other muscle.
evidence.explanation: The full text describes the specific branching error rather than inferring regeneration from a drug trial.

steps/6.description: Regenerating motor axons may send collateral sprouts into inappropriate facial nerve branches, coupling muscles that should move independently. This established regeneration model explains post-paralytic synkinesis; ephaptic transmission and central remodeling are additional proposed contributors with different levels of evidence.

evidence.snippet: Another rare symptom is gustatory hyperlacrimation (crocodile tears) induced by misdirected reinnervation of gustatory fibers through the greater superficial petrosal nerve to reach the lacrimal gland. This results in tearing when the patient eats (38).
evidence.explanation: The review describes gustatory tearing as an autonomic sequela of misdirected reinnervation.

steps/7.description: Aberrant reinnervation can redirect meal-associated secretomotor output to the lacrimal gland through the greater superficial petrosal nerve. This autonomic miswiring produces gustatory tearing and is distinct from motor-axon branching into facial muscles.

evidence.snippet: Bell's palsy, also known as "acute facial palsy of unknown cause", is a common cranial neuropathy leading to facial muscle paresis or complete paralysis characteristically on one side, occurring suddenly and may progress over 48 hours.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports acute unilateral peripheral facial weakness as the core phenotype of Bell's palsy.

steps/8.description: Acute unilateral lower motor neuron weakness of the muscles of facial expression is the defining phenotype of Bell's palsy.

evidence.snippet: Symptoms of Bell's palsy include the inability to blink or close the eye, ruck up the lips or raise the mouth corner
evidence.explanation: The review describes motor manifestations of peripheral facial nerve dysfunction.

steps/9.description: Incomplete eyelid closure can accompany acute peripheral facial weakness and increases ocular surface exposure risk.

evidence.snippet: Failure to protect the cornea among patients who are unable to blink adequately may result in corneal ulceration and permanent visual impairment.
evidence.explanation: The guideline directly links inadequate protection in impaired blinking with corneal complications.

steps/10.description: Impaired blinking and eyelid closure expose the cornea; inadequate lubrication can result in epithelial injury, exposure keratitis and corneal ulceration. This is a secondary complication of facial dysfunction, not a primary cause of the neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: Other symptoms include hyperacusis caused by nerve fiber breakdown in the stapedius muscle, alterations in taste, and dry eyes caused by parasympathetic affliction.
evidence.explanation: Review-level support for associated facial nerve functions; no phenotype frequency is estimated.

steps/11.description: Bell's palsy can impair taste sensation over the anterior tongue because facial nerve dysfunction affects the chorda tympani pathway.

evidence.snippet: Other symptoms include hyperacusis caused by nerve fiber breakdown in the stapedius muscle, alterations in taste, and dry eyes caused by parasympathetic affliction.

steps/13.description: Some patients develop persistent involuntary linked facial movements as a sequela of incomplete recovery and aberrant facial motor reinnervation.

steps/14.description: Reduced tear secretion and exposure from incomplete blinking can cause ocular dryness.

steps/15.description: A potentially serious secondary complication when impaired blinking or closure leaves the ocular surface inadequately protected; it is not present in every patient.

evidence.explanation: The phrase 'believed' denotes an etiologic model; the small PCR study supports, but does not settle, that model.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report findings from a meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies uncovering the first unequivocal association with Bell's palsy (rs9357446-A; P = 6.79 × 10-23, OR = 1.23; Ncases = 4714, Ncontrols = 1,011,520).
evidence.explanation: This supports a reproducible common-genetic susceptibility signal for Bell's palsy.

evidence.snippet: The variant is not correlated (r2 < 0.2) with any known coding or structural variants.
evidence.explanation: This restricts the associated locus to an unresolved noncoding signal.

evidence.snippet: We examined cis-eQTL in blood and adipose tissue in Iceland and did not find an association between rs9357446 and expression of nearby genes (Supplementary Note).
evidence.explanation: Negative expression analyses do not support naming a regulatory target gene.

genes/0.notes: The common intergenic rs9357446-A allele at 6p21.1 was associated with Bell's palsy in 4,714 cases and 1,011,520 controls from Iceland, the UK, Denmark and Finland (OR 1.23). The risk allele was common, not a high-penetrance Mendelian cause. Linked variants were noncoding; no correlated coding or structural variant was identified. Blood/adipose and 18 other expression datasets did not nominate an expression target, and 4,792 plasma-protein measurements did not establish a protein effect. Nearby CDC5L and SLC35B2 remain speculative candidates, not proven causal genes. Noncoding location alone does not establish enhancer disruption or a regulatory target.

evidence.snippet: clinicians should prescribe oral steroids within 72 hours of symptom onset for Bell's palsy patients 16 years and older

evidence.snippet: In patients with Bell's palsy, early treatment with prednisolone significantly improves the chances of complete recovery at 3 and 9 months.
evidence.explanation: The 551-participant randomized factorial trial supports adult steroid benefit.

evidence.snippet: Prednisolone shortened the time to complete recovery in patients with Bell's palsy, whereas valaciclovir did not affect facial recovery.
evidence.explanation: An independent multicenter trial randomized 839 adults and analyzed 829, corroborating prednisolone benefit.

treatments/0.description: Oral corticosteroids improve recovery in adults when started within 72 hours; the AAO-HNSF recommendation applies to patients aged 16 years and older. Two large placebo-controlled factorial trials support prednisolone. In the 2007 study, complete recovery at three months was 83.0% with prednisolone versus 63.6% without it, and at nine months 94.4% versus 81.6%. These are factorial comparisons, not a comparison of combination therapy with double placebo. Contraindications and individual risks still require clinical assessment.

evidence.snippet: Prednisone and other oral corticosteroids reduce nerve swelling and may speed up the recovery of facial actions and expressions.
evidence.explanation: Review-level mechanistic rationale for corticosteroid treatment.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Anti-inflammatory therapy is intended to reduce swelling; efficacy trials establish recovery benefit, not direct measurement of local nerve edema.

evidence.snippet: The combination of antivirals and corticosteroids may have little or no effect on rates of incomplete recovery in comparison to corticosteroids alone in Bell's palsy of various degrees of severity, or in people with severe Bell's palsy, but the results were very imprecise.
evidence.explanation: The synthesis separates uncertain facial recovery benefit from sequelae reduction.

evidence.snippet: The combination of antivirals and corticosteroids probably reduced the late sequelae of Bell's palsy compared with corticosteroids alone.
evidence.explanation: The pooled composite of motor synkinesis or crocodile tears favored combination therapy (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.36-0.87, two trials with 469 participants); it is not a separate estimate for each component.

evidence.snippet: At the end of the 3rd month, 17 patients (68%) had good recovery and 8 patients (32%) had poor recovery in the steroid group compared with 23 patients (92%) and 2 (8%) respectively in the steroid and antiviral group
evidence.explanation: The small trial reports a positive comparison that must be considered alongside larger studies and risk-of-bias-sensitive synthesis.

evidence.snippet: clinicians should not prescribe oral antiviral therapy alone for patients with new-onset Bell's palsy
evidence.explanation: Antivirals alone are not a recommended substitute for corticosteroids.

treatments/1.description: Acyclovir or valacyclovir may be offered with corticosteroids within 72 hours, with discussion of uncertain additional recovery benefit; antiviral monotherapy is not recommended. The 2019 Cochrane analysis restricted to trials at lower risk of bias found no clear improvement in incomplete recovery (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.38-1.74), including an imprecise severe-palsy subgroup. Combination treatment probably reduces the composite late outcome of synkinesis or crocodile tears. A small 50-patient trial reported better recovery with add-on acyclovir, but this does not override the larger trials or pooled uncertainty.

evidence.snippet: Facial training is the basis of synkinesis therapy.

evidence.snippet: Outcomes of studies with physical therapy varied, regarding recovery rate and time to recovery, although most studies showed better outcomes for physical therapy, compared to usual care.

treatments/2.description: Specialist facial neuromuscular retraining, with feedback where available, is first-line management for established synkinesis and can help persistent weakness. The aim in synkinesis is selective control of intended movements and relaxation of unintended contractions. Evidence and goals differ from acute-phase exercises; studies vary in timing, method and quality.

evidence.explanation: This supports botulinum toxin treatment for persistent Bell's palsy sequelae such as synkinesis and asymmetry.

evidence.snippet: Botulinum toxin injections are an established and effective but off-label use therapy for patients with facial synkinesis worldwide
evidence.explanation: Consensus supports symptomatic treatment of synkinesis, not treatment of the acute neuropathy.

treatments/3.description: Specialist botulinum toxin type A injections can reduce troublesome synkinetic contractions after incomplete recovery, often alongside retraining. This is symptomatic, off-label management of established synkinesis; unintended weakness can occur through excessive dose or diffusion to adjacent muscles. It does not restore an injured facial nerve.

evidence.snippet: clinicians should implement eye protection for Bell's palsy patients with impaired eye closure.

evidence.snippet: Patients with incomplete eye closure should be given eye protection, with lubricating drops and ointments, to prevent corneal damage.
evidence.explanation: This supports concrete protective measures.

treatments/4.description: Protect the cornea whenever eye closure or blinking is incomplete. Lubricating drops during the day and lubricating ointment with assisted eyelid closure at night reduce exposure. Eye pain, redness or visual symptoms require reassessment. Eye care remains necessary regardless of whether corticosteroids or antivirals are used.

treatments/5.description: Adult corticosteroid efficacy should not be assumed in younger children. BellPIC randomized 187 children aged six months to under 18 years within 72 hours, rather than the planned 540. Ten days of prednisolone did not improve complete recovery at one month (49% versus 57% with placebo); the study was underpowered and cannot exclude important benefit or harm. Most children recovered by six months. Pediatric guidance therefore describes insufficient evidence for routine early prednisolone.

treatments/6.description: Decompression has been studied for severe paralysis with substantial electrophysiologic degeneration but is not routine care. It does not establish whether other surgical timing or approaches benefit selected patients.

The table reports low shared-variant posterior probabilities for CCL19, VCAM1, IL27RA and OSM (approximately 0.007-0.022), despite stronger claims in the discussion. open_questions/1.rationale: A 2025 study combined Bell's palsy genetic associations with single-cell profiling and SLIT2 immunofluorescence in rat facial motor nuclei after mechanical nerve crush. Nominal plasma-protein MR associations and altered expression generate a repair hypothesis. Its PPH3+PPH4 threshold combines distinct-variant and shared-variant hypotheses and therefore does not by itself prove colocalization. CellChat and pseudotime are computational inferences; no SLIT2 perturbation or therapeutic rescue was performed. The rat lesion and central nuclear response do not reproduce the unknown initiating cause of human Bell's palsy.

evidence.explanation: Review interpretation of variable clinical severity.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic pathogenic variants are causal. The 2025 review lists missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice-site and an intragenic inverted-duplication allele. Some observed variants remain uncertain; p.Arg500His and the co-occurring p.Gln145Pro should not be treated as definitively pathogenic merely because they were found in affected individuals. Clinical severity is not reliably predicted by residual activity or broad variant class.

evidence.explanation: Supports the assessment strategy when cooperation affects behavioral thresholds.

treatments/2.description: Hearing aids may improve communication. Combine behavioral and objective audiological assessment when cooperation limits threshold measurement, and reassess hearing annually. Disease-specific cochlear-implant outcomes are not established by the cited sources.

evidence.explanation: Supports the described care, with indication and limitations stated in the description.

evidence.explanation: Supports the described care, with indication and limitations stated in the description.

evidence.snippet: If the MANBA pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: Supports the described care, with indication and limitations stated in the description.

evidence.snippet: If both parents are known to be heterozygous for a MANBA pathogenic variant, each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being an asymptomatic carrier, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier.
evidence.explanation: Mendelian recurrence risks, conditional on both parents being carriers.

treatments/9.description: Autosomal recessive counseling includes the 25% recurrence risk when both parents carry a pathogenic allele. Offer appropriate testing of at-risk relatives and discuss reproductive testing once familial variants are known.

evidence.snippet: Our findings suggest that hematopoietic cell transplant can correct the biochemical defect in β-mannosidosis, although preservation of the neurocognitive trajectory may be a challenge.
evidence.explanation: Single treated patient, without an untreated comparator.

evidence.snippet: At 10 years of age, he developed progressive regression in gross motor skills, urinary incontinence, low muscle bulk, axial hypotonia, end point dysmetria, and dysarthria
evidence.explanation: Later follow-up of the same transplant recipient, not an independent treatment case.

treatments/10.description: An HLA-matched cord-blood transplant in one boy at approximately 4.5 years normalized leukocyte enzyme activity and reduced urinary oligosaccharides. Early neurological worsening partly improved, but the developmental gap persisted and memory declined by two years. Follow-up of the same patient in 2025 documented renewed motor regression and worsening spasticity/ataxia. This does not establish durable neurological efficacy or routine use; biochemical correction is not a validated surrogate for clinical benefit.

evidence.snippet: We show restoration of leukocyte β-mannosidase activity which remained normal at 2 years posttransplant
evidence.explanation: Observed biochemical response in one patient.

treatments/10/targets/0.description: Restored leukocyte beta-mannosidase activity after donor-cell engraftment; correction in brain cells and durable clinical benefit were not established.

evidence.snippet: additional studies should be developed to determine whether CTBS (Di-N-Acetyl-Chitobiase) acts as a modifier gene in severe cases.
evidence.explanation: The authors pose a question; they do not demonstrate a CTBS modifier effect.

open_questions/0.rationale: Additional urinary glycans in two severely affected patients and species differences motivate a CTBS hypothesis. No causal human modifier allele or functional epistasis experiment has established that link. Background-dependent mouse pathology indicates modifier effects without identifying the responsible gene.

evidence.snippet: Neuropathology between 1 and 9 months of age included selective, variable neuronal vacuolation with no hypomyelination.
evidence.explanation: Explicit lack of the human myelin phenotype in the reported mouse analysis.

evidence.snippet: Degeneration staining did not occur in areas of vacuolation or adjacent regions, suggesting that vacuolation does not lead to substantial cell body or axon loss.
evidence.explanation: Experimental pathology limits a simple vacuolation-to-cell-death chain.

open_questions/1.rationale: Human MRI, severe ruminant myelin deficiency and mouse vacuolation are distinct observations. Storage substrate composition, cell susceptibility and developmental timing may differ. Neuronal degeneration in mice is spatially separate from major vacuolated populations; vacuolation does not automatically imply neuronal death.

evidence.snippet: Exposures occurred with higher frequency in warm-weather states and during summer months.
evidence.explanation: The geographic and seasonal distribution of the exposure, across 15,299 reported cases.

evidence.snippet: This 130 kDa toxin binds to receptors at presynaptic nerve terminals and triggers a massive release of neurotransmitters.
evidence.explanation: The target and the outcome in one sentence. BACKGROUND because it is the structural paper's framing of established biology rather than its own cryo-EM result.

evidence.snippet: A surprising finding was the biochemical description of two distinct cell surface proteins that bind alpha-latrotoxin with nanomolar affinities; Neurexin I alpha binds alpha-latrotoxin in a Ca(2+)-dependent manner, and CIRL/latrophilin binds in a Ca(2+)-independent manner.
evidence.explanation: Both receptor families and the binding property that distinguishes them, which is the claim this node makes.

evidence.snippet: Neurexins are single transmembrane proteins which bind to alpha-latrotoxin in a calcium-dependent manner and also interact with the synaptic vesicle protein, synaptotagmin. On the other hand, latrophilin is a seven-transmembrane protein and belongs to the family of G-protein-coupled receptors.
evidence.explanation: The two receptor families and the property that distinguishes them, which is why the calcium-free experiments discriminate between the hypotheses.

steps/1.description: Alpha-latrotoxin binds two structurally unrelated families of presynaptic receptor - neurexin-1alpha, which binds calcium-dependently, and latrophilin/CIRL, a G-protein-coupled receptor that binds without calcium. Their shared and best-evidenced function is tethering: holding the toxin at the membrane so that it can insert. The evidence for that is unusually clean, because a chimera carrying only the extracellular domain of CIRL-1 on an unrelated viral transmembrane anchor produced the same channels as the wild-type receptor.

evidence.snippet: We discovered that alpha-latrotoxin exists in two oligomeric forms: it is dimeric in EDTA but forms tetramers in the presence of Ca2+ or Mg2+.
evidence.explanation: The divalent-cation dependence of tetramerization, which is the first step of this node.

evidence.snippet: The C4-symmetric tetramers represent the active form of alpha-latrotoxin; they have an axial channel and can insert into lipid bilayers with their hydrophobic base, providing the first model of alpha-latrotoxin pore formation.
evidence.explanation: The tetramer as the active, membrane-inserting form.

evidence.snippet: Four distinct helical bundles rearrange and together form a highly stable, 15 nm long, cation-impermeable coiled-coil stalk. This stalk, in turn, positions an N-terminal pair of helices within the membrane, thereby enabling the assembly of a cation-permeable channel.
evidence.explanation: The prepore-to-pore transition in structural detail, and the source of the two resolutions quoted elsewhere in this entry.

steps/2.description: In the presence of calcium or magnesium the toxin assembles into a C4-symmetric tetramer, then undergoes a large conformational change: four N-terminal helical bundles refold into a rigid coiled-coil stalk that drives a pair of helices into the bilayer, opening a cation-permeable channel. The prepore and pore states have both been resolved by cryo-EM, so this is a structurally described event rather than an inferred one.

evidence.snippet: An analysis of CIRL-1 mutants indicated that channel formation in HEK293 cells is unlikely to be transduced by a G-protein-dependent mechanism.
evidence.explanation: REFUTE, and narrowly: what it excludes is a G-protein-dependent route to *channel formation*, in HEK293 cells overexpressing CIRL-1. This node claims a G-protein route to *secretion*, which is a different claim in a different system, and PMID:42121922 has since demonstrated exactly that route at the neuromuscular junction. Kept because it is a real negative result about a neighbouring claim and a reader should see it; it is not evidence that this arm does not exist.

steps/3.description: The alternative arm, and no longer a black box. Engagement of latrophilin-1 couples to Gaq and phospholipase C, generating IP3 that releases calcium from intracellular stores through IP3 receptors; the resulting store depletion opens store-operated calcium entry, which supplies the sustained calcium that exocytosis needs. The cascade was delineated at the mouse neuromuscular junction using a pore-deficient toxin mutant, so the pore is excluded by construction rather than by argument. What this does not establish is how much of a human envenomation runs through it.

evidence.snippet: we demonstrate that the interaction of alpha-latrotoxin with CIRL-1 produces a high conductance channel that permits increases in cytosolic Ca(2+)
evidence.explanation: States what this node claims - the channel admits calcium into the cytosol - rather than only reporting a conductance.

evidence.snippet: alpha-Latrotoxin interaction with CIRL-1 transiently expressed in bovine chromaffin cells produced a 400-pS channel, which rarely closed under Ca(2+)-free conditions.
evidence.explanation: The measured conductance. INDIRECT because it was measured in CIRL-1-overexpressing bovine chromaffin cells, not at a presynaptic terminal, which is what this node is about.

steps/4.description: Calcium enters the terminal through the toxin's own channel, a high conductance pore measured at around 400 pS, bypassing the voltage-gated calcium channels that normally gate release.

evidence.snippet: The major component of black widow spider venom, alpha-latrotoxin, triggers massive exocytosis in a variety of neurosecretory cells.
evidence.explanation: The node's central claim, and that it is not restricted to one cell type.

steps/5.description: The convergence point of both hypothesis arms, and the event that produces the whole clinical syndrome. Vesicular acetylcholine and catecholamines are discharged continuously rather than in response to action potentials.

evidence.snippet: In nerve-muscle preparations treated for 1 h with a low dose of alpha-latrotoxin in the absence of extracellular Ca2+ (a condition under which nerve terminals are depleted of both quanta of neurotransmitter and synaptic vesicles), the immunolabeling for both proteins was distributed along the axolemma.
evidence.explanation: Depletion of both quanta and vesicles, with vesicle membrane proteins redistributed to the axolemma. INDIRECT because the condition is calcium-free and an envenomated patient is not - see the refuting item below, which is the same paper's own control.

evidence.snippet: When the same dose of alpha-latrotoxin was applied in the presence of extracellular Ca2+, the immunoreactivity patterns resembled those obtained in resting preparations
evidence.explanation: The same paper's calcium-present control, which is the condition that applies in a patient, and in which retrieval kept pace. REFUTE against reading this node as an established step of the human syndrome. Recorded rather than omitted because the supporting quote alone would misrepresent the paper.

steps/6.description: Sustained exocytosis outrunning endocytic retrieval empties the terminal of both transmitter quanta and the vesicles themselves, with vesicle membrane left incorporated into the axolemma. Read the limitation, because it is load-bearing: the experiment showing this was run in the *absence* of extracellular calcium, and the same paper's calcium-present control found active recycling of both quanta and vesicles with no depletion at all. Calcium is present in an envenomated patient, so this node describes a demonstrated capability of the toxin rather than an established step of the human syndrome. No source cited here establishes that vesicle depletion is what makes latrodectism self-limited.

evidence.snippet: Black widow species (Latrodectus species) envenomation can produce a syndrome characterized by painful muscle rigidity and autonomic disturbances.
evidence.explanation: The two clinical arms this node and the next one split into. BACKGROUND because it is the study's framing rather than its own result.

steps/7.description: Continuous acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction holds skeletal muscle in involuntary contraction. The cramping spreads contiguously from the bitten limb to the trunk, which is the feature that most often distinguishes latrodectism from an acute abdomen at the bedside.

evidence.snippet: The widow venom, a powerful neurotoxin known as a-latrotoxin, causes muscle pain, diaphoresis, tachycardia, flushing, and hypertension.
evidence.explanation: Names four of the autonomic features wired downstream of this node, and attributes them to the toxin rather than to pain alone.

evidence.snippet: Latrodectism results from bites by widow spiders (Latrodectus spp) and causes local, regional, or generalised pain associated with non-specific symptoms and autonomic effects.
evidence.explanation: The authoritative review's statement of the syndrome, including its autonomic component.

steps/8.description: The same unregulated release at autonomic terminals - acetylcholine at ganglia and exocrine glands, catecholamines at postganglionic sympathetic terminals - produces a mixed autonomic picture rather than a purely sympathetic one. Hypertension, tachycardia and diaphoresis sit alongside nausea, vomiting and lacrimation.

evidence.snippet: Latrodectism is a severe systemic manifestation of the envenomation that includes severe abdominal pain mimicking acute surgical abdomen and, in rare cases, could lead to acute myocarditis and rhabdomyolysis.
evidence.explanation: Places myocarditis and rhabdomyolysis as rare complications of the systemic syndrome, which is what this node and the rhabdomyolysis edge above assert.

steps/9.description: A rare complication: myocarditis with raised troponin and, in reported cases, echocardiographic abnormality. Deliberately named for the association rather than for a mechanism - a catecholamine-mediated route is the usual explanation and is plausible given the adrenergic excess upstream, but no source cited here demonstrates it, so the node does not assert it. Curated because it is the one route by which a self-limited envenomation becomes an intensive care problem.

evidence.snippet: Black widow spider bites cause a characteristic envenomation syndrome consisting of severe pain, muscle cramping, abdominal pain, and back pain.
evidence.explanation: Names cramping as a defining component of the syndrome.

steps/10.description: The defining feature. Severe involuntary cramping that begins near the bite and spreads to the abdomen, back and thighs.

evidence.snippet: envenomation can produce a syndrome characterized by painful muscle rigidity and autonomic disturbances
evidence.explanation: Rigidity named as a defining feature of the syndrome.

steps/11.description: Painful rigidity, classically of the abdominal wall, mimicking peritonitis.

evidence.snippet: severe abdominal pain mimicking acute surgical abdomen
evidence.explanation: The clinical mimicry that makes this phenotype diagnostically important.

steps/12.description: Severe enough to be mistaken for a surgical abdomen, and the reason latrodectism appears in differential diagnoses of acute abdomen.

evidence.snippet: causes muscle pain, diaphoresis, tachycardia, flushing, and hypertension
evidence.explanation: Hypertension named among the toxin's autonomic effects.

evidence.snippet: autonomic disturbances, such as tachycardia, hypertension, and diaphoresis
evidence.explanation: Tachycardia named among the characteristic autonomic disturbances.

evidence.snippet: autonomic disturbances, such as tachycardia, hypertension, and diaphoresis
evidence.explanation: Diaphoresis named among the characteristic autonomic disturbances.

steps/15.description: Sweating, sometimes in a localized or asymmetric distribution near the bite, which is a recognised diagnostic clue.

evidence.snippet: The effects of BWS bites ranges from local damage to systemic manifestations including paresthesia, stiffness, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, headache, anxiety, hypertension and tachycardia.
evidence.explanation: Names nausea among the systemic manifestations. BACKGROUND because it is the case report's framing of the syndrome rather than its own finding.

evidence.snippet: The effects of BWS bites ranges from local damage to systemic manifestations including paresthesia, stiffness, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, headache, anxiety, hypertension and tachycardia.
evidence.explanation: Names vomiting among the systemic manifestations.

evidence.snippet: Rhabdomyolysis after spider bite has been reported in a small number of patients, and myocarditis in even fewer.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the occurrence and the rarity, which is what this phenotype's description claims.

steps/18.description: Rare, and reported together with myocarditis and arrhythmia in severe cases.

evidence.snippet: We report the case of a 26-year-old active duty male soldier evacuated from field training with latrodectism and possible envenomation-induced myocarditis after a suspected BWS bite.
evidence.explanation: The reported case of envenomation-associated myocarditis this phenotype records.

evidence.snippet: Cases of myocarditis following a BWS bite are rare but they can be fatal on occasion.
evidence.explanation: The correction to any impression that this complication is uniformly reversible. Cited specifically so the description cannot be read as reassurance.

steps/19.description: Reversible in the reported cases cited here, with recovery of ventricular function - but not uniformly so, and the literature describes fatal cases.

evidence.snippet: "Latrodectus facies" or "facies latrodectismica" is an additional distinctive but rarely described clinical finding characterized by periorbital edema, lacrimation, and blepharospasm.
evidence.explanation: Defines the sign and names periorbital oedema as one of its three components.

steps/20.description: Part of "facies latrodectismica", a distinctive but rarely described facial appearance combining periorbital oedema, lacrimation and blepharospasm.

evidence.snippet: Latrodectism results from bites by widow spiders (Latrodectus spp) and causes local, regional, or generalised pain associated with non-specific symptoms and autonomic effects.
evidence.explanation: Names the local-to-regional-to-generalised progression, attributed to Latrodectus specifically rather than to spider bite in general.

steps/21.description: The presenting complaint, and the feature that makes latrodectism recognisable: pain begins locally and spreads regionally rather than staying at a bite that looks like almost nothing.

evidence.snippet: characterized by periorbital edema, lacrimation, and blepharospasm
evidence.explanation: Names lacrimation as the third component of the sign.

steps/22.description: The third component of facies latrodectismica, and the one attributable to cholinergic drive at the lacrimal gland rather than to muscle.

evidence.snippet: characterized by periorbital edema, lacrimation, and blepharospasm
evidence.explanation: Names blepharospasm as a component of the sign.

steps/23.description: The second component of facies latrodectismica.

evidence.snippet: We propose that alpha-latrotoxin receptors recruit toxin to facilitate its insertion across the membrane and that alpha-latrotoxin itself controls the conductance properties of the channels it produces.
evidence.explanation: States the causal role this edge asserts - recruitment for insertion - and separates it from the conductance, which is the toxin's own.

edges/0.description: Receptor tethering raises the efficiency of membrane insertion by orders of magnitude; insertion is inefficient without it.

edges/1.description: Under the alternative account the same binding event initiates receptor signalling rather than merely positioning the toxin.

edges/2.description: Pain begins where the venom is deposited, so it is drawn from the first node rather than from the systemic ones. Unknown intermediates on purpose: the entry models no local sensory-terminal node, and no cited source traces the route from toxin binding to nociception.

evidence.snippet: Upon activation, LPHN1 engages the Gαq-phospholipase C pathway to generate inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3), triggering Ca2+ release from intracellular stores via IP3 receptors.
evidence.explanation: The intermediates this edge claims, named and ordered, from electrophysiology in latrophilin-1 knockout mice with pharmacological inhibitors and calcium imaging.

edges/4.description: The intermediates are named: Gaq, phospholipase C, IP3, IP3-receptor store release, then store-operated calcium entry. INDIRECT rather than DIRECT because that is five steps, and KNOWN rather than UNKNOWN because each was tested rather than assumed.

edges/13.description: The muscular component of facies latrodectismica - sustained orbicularis oculi contraction, the same end-plate mechanism as the cramping elsewhere.

edges/19.description: Cholinergic drive at the lacrimal gland, the same exocrine mechanism as the salivation and bronchial secretion described for autonomic excess.

edges/20.description: Part of facies latrodectismica. Drawn with unknown intermediates because the source describes the sign without establishing what produces the oedema; a local autonomic vasomotor effect is the usual explanation and is not demonstrated.

evidence.snippet: The black widow spider, Latrodectus mactans, stands out as one of the most medically significant arachnids due to its extensive geographic distribution in the United States and its ability to produce a potent neurotoxin, α-latrotoxin.
evidence.explanation: Names the exposure and the toxin it delivers, which is what this link asserts.

edges/23.description: The bite is the route by which the toxin reaches presynaptic terminals; nothing in the chain happens without it.

evidence.snippet: The significant pain associated with envenomation is often refractory to traditional analgesics.
evidence.explanation: Why opioids rather than simple analgesia, stated as the clinical problem.

treatments/0.description: The mainstay, and the comparator RAVE-II measured antivenom against. Pain in latrodectism is characteristically refractory to simple analgesics, so intravenous opioids are the practical first line.

evidence.snippet: Fifty-five percent of patients initially receiving IV morphine and 70% of those initially receiving both IV morphine and benzodiazepines obtained symptomatic relief without additional medication.
evidence.explanation: INDIRECT: a therapeutic response cited in support of the node it acts on. The series is retrospective and uncontrolled, so the numbers describe practice rather than isolating the drug's effect.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Drawn at the node that generates the pain rather than upstream, and MODULATES rather than INHIBITS on purpose - opioids do nothing to the toxin or to transmitter release, they raise the threshold at which the resulting nociception is felt.

evidence.snippet: The most common therapies received were wound care (43.7%) and benzodiazepines (18.6%).
evidence.explanation: Benzodiazepines at 18.6%, second only to wound care. The abstract does not report opioid use, so this establishes frequency in practice rather than that benzodiazepines are the commonest drug given.

treatments/1.description: Given with opioids rather than instead of them. In the largest published series the combination outperformed opioid alone, and benzodiazepines are the second most frequently recorded therapy in US poison centre data.

evidence.snippet: Fifty-five percent of patients initially receiving IV morphine and 70% of those initially receiving both IV morphine and benzodiazepines obtained symptomatic relief without additional medication.
evidence.explanation: The same sentence supports both drugs, and the comparison within it - 70% versus 55% - is what justifies adding the benzodiazepine. INDIRECT, and uncontrolled.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Central muscle relaxation against the sustained contraction this node produces.

evidence.snippet: Fifty-eight patients received antivenin with complete resolution of symptoms in a mean time of 31 +/- 26.7 minutes.
evidence.explanation: The positive retrospective signal, and the one clinicians most often cite. INDIRECT and uncontrolled - there is no comparator arm inside this number, and a self-limited syndrome will resolve on its own.

evidence.snippet: The addition of antivenom to standardized analgesia in patients with latrodectism did not significantly improve pain or systemic effects.
evidence.explanation: The largest placebo-controlled trial, and it is negative. REFUTE against the claim that antivenom adds benefit on top of adequate analgesia - which is the claim that matters clinically, since analgesia is given either way.

evidence.snippet: Two hours after treatment, 26 of 112 patients (23%) from the placebo arm had a clinically significant improvement in pain versus 38 of 112 (34%) from the antivenom arm (difference in favor of antivenom 10.7%; 95% confidence interval -1.1% to 22.6%; P=.10).
evidence.explanation: The numbers behind that conclusion. Worth reading rather than summarising: the point estimate favours antivenom by 10.7 points and the interval only just crosses zero, so this is an underpowered null as much as a demonstration of no effect.

evidence.snippet: There were 15 treatment failures in the antivenom group and 24 in the placebo group (P=.019).
evidence.explanation: The second placebo-controlled trial, and it is positive on its primary endpoint. Note the endpoint differs from RAVE-II's: sustained pain reduction over 48 hours rather than improvement at 2 hours.

evidence.snippet: The rate of symptom improvement in the placebo group was higher than expected, which may be related to enrollment criteria or placebo effect.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own caveat on their positive result, quoted so the entry does not present it as cleaner than its investigators did.

evidence.snippet: Acute systemic hypersensitivity reactions occurred in 4 of 112 patients (3.6%) receiving antivenom.
evidence.explanation: The cost side of the decision. Cited as SUPPORT for the harm claim, not for efficacy.

evidence.snippet: One patient died of severe bronchospasm after receiving antivenin.
evidence.explanation: A death caused by the treatment, in the same series that supplies this entry's strongest positive signal for it. REFUTE against a favourable risk-benefit reading. Recorded here rather than left out because a treatment framed as a risk-benefit judgement cannot omit the fatal outcome in its own best source.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, antivenom may provide no benefit over placebo.
evidence.explanation: A third randomised trial, and note where this sentence comes from - RAVE-I compared intravenous with intramuscular administration, not antivenom with placebo, so this is the trialists' inference from their own null route comparison rather than a placebo-controlled result. It is the observation that motivated RAVE-II.

evidence.snippet: Antivenoms are an important treatment for spider envenomation but have been less successful than have those for snake envenomation, with concerns about their effectiveness for both latrodectism and loxoscelism.
evidence.explanation: The field's own summary of where this stands. `quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS` already records that the sentence is a review's assessment rather than a study this paper ran, so `evidence_source` grades the human clinical evidence the assessment is about.

treatments/2.description: The contested treatment. Four studies bear on it and they do not agree, which is curated here rather than resolved: a large retrospective series reporting resolution in about half an hour, a route-comparison trial whose authors concluded antivenom may add nothing over placebo, a placebo-controlled trial in 224 patients finding no benefit over standardised analgesia, and a second placebo-controlled trial in 60 patients meeting its primary endpoint. The entry records all four and the reasons they may differ.

evidence.snippet: Redback spider antivenom is effective in neutralizing the lethal effects of L. hesperus and L. mactans venoms in a mouse envenomation model.
evidence.explanation: Neutralisation is the mechanism this edge asserts. INDIRECT because it is a mouse lethality assay rather than a measurement at the receptor and the antigen was premixed with antibody, which is the condition the companion item below records.

evidence.snippet: While this study is limited by the optimized premixing of antigen with antibody
evidence.explanation: The authors' own caveat, and it is the same point this edge makes: premixing guarantees the antivenom meets the toxin before the toxin meets a receptor, which is exactly the condition a patient presenting hours after a bite does not satisfy. Quoted because it strengthens the edge's stated limitation rather than the treatment's case.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Antivenom neutralises circulating toxin, so it acts upstream of the receptor - which is also the likeliest reason the trials disagree. By the time a patient presents in severe pain the binding and insertion steps have already happened, and neutralising toxin that has not yet bound cannot undo them.

evidence.snippet: Calcium gluconate was not effective in providing symptomatic relief in this series, with 96% of the grade 2 and 3 envenomations treated initially with calcium gluconate requiring the addition of IV opioids or other analgesics for symptomatic relief.
evidence.explanation: REFUTE, and quantified: 96% of patients given calcium first needed something else anyway. No target_mechanisms edge is drawn, because on this evidence it does not act on the pathograph at all.

evidence.snippet: Although calcium gluconate usually has been considered the first-line treatment of severe envenomations by black widow spiders, we found it ineffective for pain relief compared with a combination of IV opioids and benzodiazepines.
evidence.explanation: States both the former standard and the finding against it, which is why this treatment is curated rather than omitted.

treatments/3.description: Historical, and recorded because it was standard practice rather than despite it. Intravenous calcium was for years the recommended first-line treatment for severe envenomation; the largest series tested it against opioids and found it did not work.

evidence.snippet: The stimulation of secretion by alpha-latrotoxin in neuroendocrine cells is a consequence of Ca(2+) influx through these alpha-latrotoxin-induced channels.
evidence.explanation: States the canonical account - the channel is the route, and calcium influx through it is the trigger.

hypotheses/0.description: The tetrameric toxin inserts into the presynaptic membrane and forms a cation-selective channel; calcium entering through that channel triggers the massive exocytosis. This is the structurally resolved account and the one the cryo-EM work describes in detail.

evidence.snippet: However, this mechanism fails to explain exocytosis which occurred in the complete absence of extracellular calcium.
evidence.explanation: The observation that requires a second arm at all, stated as the failure of the first. This is what makes the two accounts rival explanations rather than a single chain.

evidence.snippet: In addition to channel formation, alpha-latrotoxin enhances secretion in permeabilized cells through interaction with the plasma membrane receptor CIRL/latrophilin.
evidence.explanation: Secretion enhanced through the receptor in permeabilized cells, which is the pore-independent claim.

evidence.snippet: The action of alpha-latrotoxin may therefore be mediated by independent parallel pathways, of which the CIRL/latrophilin pathway is sufficient for neurotransmitter release, whereas the neurexin I alpha pathway contributes to the Ca(2+)-dependent action of alpha-latrotoxin.

hypotheses/1.description: A second route in which the toxin's receptors do more than tether it: engagement of latrophilin/CIRL, a G-protein-coupled receptor, stimulates secretion without requiring calcium entry through a pore. It began as an inference from a negative observation - exocytosis happens in the complete absence of extracellular calcium, which the pore account cannot explain - and has since been given a full cascade, demonstrated with a pore-deficient toxin mutant so that the pore cannot be doing the work. Recorded as ALTERNATIVE rather than CANONICAL because what has been demonstrated is spontaneous quantal release at the mouse neuromuscular junction; no work apportions the two arms in a human envenomation.
