evidence.snippet: Twelve of 14 (85.71%) steroid-resistant cases had CR or PR after alternative immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide, or mycophenolate mofetil.
evidence.explanation: Adult cohort supporting cyclophosphamide-containing salvage therapy in steroid-resistant MCD, while acknowledging that the abstract pooled outcomes with MMF.

evidence.snippet: This article provides a perspective of the Immunonephrology Working Group (IWG) of the European Renal Association (ERA) and discusses the KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases focusing on the management of MCD and primary forms of FSGS in the context of recently published evidence, with a special emphasis on the role of rituximab, cyclophosphamide, supportive treatment options and ongoing clinical trials in the field.
evidence.explanation: Contemporary ERA review supporting cyclophosphamide as a recognized adult management option in relapsing or resistant podocytopathies including MCD.

treatments/3.description: Alkylating immunosuppressive therapy used as a steroid-sparing option for frequently relapsing, steroid-dependent, or steroid-resistant adult MCD when relapse burden or steroid toxicity justifies escalation.

evidence.snippet: MF therapy was able to maintain steroid-free remission for the whole duration of therapy (12 months) in 20 (83.3%) patients.
evidence.explanation: Retrospective adult cohort supporting mycophenolate as an effective steroid-sparing maintenance therapy in frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent MCD.

evidence.snippet: Thus, in adult patients, treatment with low-dose prednisone plus enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium was not superior to a standard high-dose prednisone regimen to induce complete remission of MCNS.
evidence.explanation: Keeps the mycophenolate entry calibrated: adult randomized induction data support its use as an option, but not as a clearly superior first-line regimen.

treatments/4.description: Mycophenolate-based immunosuppression, including mycophenolate mofetil and enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium formulations, is used as a steroid-sparing option in frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent adult MCD and as salvage therapy in selected resistant cases.

evidence.snippet: The first step in Moco biosynthesis, the conversion of GTP into cPMP, is catalyzed by two proteins encoded by the MOCS1 locus
evidence.explanation: Places MOCS1 at the first step and names the product whose absence defines the block.

evidence.snippet: Moco is synthesized by a three-step biosynthetic pathway that involves the gene products of MOCS1, MOCS2, MOCS3, and GPHN
evidence.explanation: The pathway architecture that separates type A from types B and C.

steps/1.description: The initiating lesion, and its position in the pathway is what makes this subtype treatable. Molybdenum cofactor is built in three steps by the products of MOCS1, MOCS2, MOCS3 and GPHN. MOCS1 catalyzes the first of them, the conversion of GTP into cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate. A block at step one leaves every downstream step intact and starved of substrate - which is precisely the situation a substrate can be given back into.

evidence.snippet: There are two cytosolic Mo-enzymes, xanthine oxidoreductase and aldehyde oxidase, which are closely related Mo-iron-flavin enzymes catalyzing the hydroxylation reactions of purines and various heterocyclic substrates
evidence.explanation: Names the cytosolic molybdoenzymes that fail alongside sulfite oxidase.

steps/2.description: Four molybdoenzymes exist in humans, and all of them lose activity together: sulfite oxidase, xanthine oxidoreductase, aldehyde oxidase and the mitochondrial amidoxime-reducing component. The name of the disease - combined deficiency of sulfite oxidase, xanthine dehydrogenase and aldehyde oxidase - records this. What the name does not record is that the deficiencies are not clinically equal, which the next two nodes separate.

evidence.snippet: The molecular cause of the disease is the loss of sulfite oxidase (SOX) activity, one of four Moco-dependent enzymes in men
evidence.explanation: Attributes the disease specifically to the sulfite oxidase arm rather than to combined molybdoenzyme loss as such.

evidence.snippet: Accumulating toxic sulfite causes a secondary increase of metabolites such as S-sulfocysteine and thiosulfate as well as a decrease in cysteine and its oxidized form, cystine
evidence.explanation: The downstream metabolite shifts, including the fall in cysteine that the dietary restriction is aimed at.

evidence.snippet: Most of the symptoms in MoCD patients are mirrored by iSOD, which is caused by mutations in the SUOX gene
evidence.explanation: The comparative argument that the sulfite oxidase arm carries the phenotype: a disease lacking only that enzyme looks the same.

steps/3.description: Sulfite oxidase normally converts sulfite to sulfate at the end of cysteine catabolism. Without it sulfite accumulates and drives secondary chemistry: S-sulfocysteine and thiosulfate rise while cysteine and cystine fall. This is the arm that produces the clinical disease. The evidence for that is comparative rather than direct - isolated sulfite oxidase deficiency, in which only this one enzyme is lost, reproduces almost the whole phenotype.

evidence.snippet: In MoCD-A and MoCD-B, plasma and urinary xanthine and S-sulfocysteine concentrations were high; urate remained below the normal reference range
evidence.explanation: The biochemical signature measured across the natural history cohort, combining both arms - S-sulfocysteine from the sulfite arm, xanthine and urate from this one.

steps/4.description: Xanthine oxidoreductase converts hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to urate, so its loss raises xanthine and lowers urate. This arm is curated separately from the sulfite arm because it behaves differently: it produces the biochemical signature that makes the diagnosis - high xanthine with a urate below the reference range - while contributing little of the clinical disease. A patient with isolated xanthinuria has kidney stones, not a neonatal encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: SSC represents a structural analog of glutamate and has been proven to cause excitotoxicity in neurons by activating N-methyl-D-aspartate type glutamate (NMDA) receptors, causing calcium influx and downstream signaling such as calpain activation
evidence.explanation: The molecular basis of the neurotoxicity, including the receptor and the downstream effector.

evidence.snippet: The effects of these S-sulfonated species remain largely unknown except for S-sulfocysteine (SSC)
evidence.explanation: Curated PARTIAL because it qualifies the node rather than supporting it: S-sulfocysteine is the one accumulating species whose mechanism is known, and the contribution of thiosulfate and the other S-sulfonated metabolites is not established.

steps/5.description: The step that converts a metabolic block into neuronal death. S-sulfocysteine is a structural analog of glutamate, and it activates NMDA-type glutamate receptors, admitting calcium and triggering downstream signalling including calpain activation. This is why the encephalopathy is destructive rather than merely dysfunctional, and why the neonatal window is so narrow.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with early-onset MoCD typically present in the first days of life with severe encephalopathy, including refractory seizures, opisthotonos, axial and appendicular hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and apnea
evidence.explanation: The clinical syndrome of the early-onset form.

evidence.snippet: panlobar diffusion restriction throughout the forebrain and midbrain with relative sparring of the brain stem
evidence.explanation: The imaging distribution, including the brain stem sparing. The source's spelling of "sparring" is reproduced as published.

steps/6.description: Presentation in the first days of life with severe encephalopathy - refractory seizures, opisthotonos, axial and appendicular hypotonia, feeding difficulty and apnea - with imaging showing loss of grey-white differentiation, gyral swelling and panlobar diffusion restriction through the forebrain and midbrain, characteristically sparing the brain stem. The injury is largely complete by the time it is recognized, which is the central fact governing treatment.

evidence.snippet: Sequelae included profound developmental delay, truncal hypotonia, limb hypertonia that evolved to spastic quadriplegia or diplegia, dysmorphic features, and acquired microcephaly
evidence.explanation: The sequelae in survivors, from the natural history cohort.

evidence.snippet: One-year survival rates were 77.4% (overall), 71.8% (neonatal onset MoCD-A), and 76.9% (neonatal onset MoCD-B); median ages at death were 2.4, 2.4, and 2.2 years, respectively
evidence.explanation: The survival figures, with the type A neonatal-onset stratum reported separately - which is the number that applies to this entry.

evidence.snippet: The median survival for the overall population was 36 months
evidence.explanation: An independent survival estimate from the pre-treatment published-case series, close to the 2.4-year median above. This is the untreated natural history the substitution therapy is measured against; it is not type A-stratified, so it corroborates rather than replaces the stratified figure.

steps/7.description: Survivors have profound developmental delay, truncal hypotonia and limb hypertonia evolving into spastic quadriplegia or diplegia, acquired microcephaly and dysmorphic features. Mortality is high and early: about a quarter of neonatal-onset type A patients die before their first birthday, and the median age at death is 2.4 years.

edges/1.description: No cofactor means no active molybdoenzyme of any kind.

edges/2.description: Loss of sulfite oxidase is the arm that causes the disease.

edges/3.description: Loss of xanthine oxidoreductase is the arm that gives the biochemical signature.

edges/4.description: One of the accumulating metabolites is not merely a marker.

edges/5.description: Excitotoxic neuronal death across the forebrain and midbrain.

edges/6.description: Survivors of the acute injury carry its consequences.

evidence.snippet: The majority of mutations leading to MoCo deficiency have been identified in the genes MOCS1 (type A deficiency), MOCS2 (type B deficiency), with one reported in GPHN
evidence.explanation: Maps each gene to its complementation group and records that type A is the commonest, which is the assertion this entry's scope rests on.

evidence.snippet: MOCS1 expression undergoes alternative splicing, yielding two different types of transcripts, one bicistronic and one monocistronic mRNA
evidence.explanation: The unusual transcript architecture of the locus.

genes/0.notes: Scoping note that matters for this entry. The deep-research report and much of the literature discuss MOCS2 (type B) and GPHN (type C) alongside MOCS1, and the NEC preflight flagged MOCS2 as a rival gene for exactly that reason. Nothing in this entry is sourced from a type B or type C observation. In particular the mouse model in PMID:27138983 is a type B model and is deliberately not curated here, and the survival figures are quoted from the type A stratum rather than the combined cohort.

evidence.snippet: In those with MOCS1-related MoCD (MoCD type A), fosdenopterin (NULIBRY) daily infusion through an indwelling catheter (dose based on weight and age; each vial contains 9.5 mg) may be considered, but must be initiated in a very short window after symptom manifestation to achieve maximum benefit
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the type A restriction and the narrow treatment window. The quote omits the registered trademark symbol after NULIBRY as the cached record renders it.

evidence.snippet: Substitution therapy with cPMP is highly effective in reducing sulfite toxicity and restoring biochemical homeostasis, while the clinical outcome critically depends on the degree of brain injury prior to the start of treatment
evidence.explanation: Curated PARTIAL deliberately. The first clause supports the therapy; the second withholds the claim that matters most to a family, which is neurological outcome. The entry keeps both halves rather than quoting only the first.

evidence.snippet: This distinction is relevant for patient management because the metabolic block in MoCD type A can be circumvented by administering cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate (cPMP)
evidence.explanation: States why the subtype distinction is actionable rather than taxonomic.

treatments/0.description: The only disease-modifying therapy, and it exists only for type A. Fosdenopterin is synthetic cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate - the exact intermediate MOCS1 fails to make - given by daily infusion through an indwelling catheter. It works because the block is at step one: everything downstream is intact and merely starved, so supplying cPMP restores the pathway. Substitution is highly effective at reducing sulfite toxicity and restoring biochemical homeostasis, but biochemical rescue is not the same as clinical rescue, and outcome depends on how much brain injury has already occurred. Patients on fosdenopterin must avoid direct sunlight and UV phototherapy.

evidence.snippet: Affected individuals (all subtypes) are often placed on a cysteine-restricted diet, which typically includes low protein intake with restriction of whole natural protein
evidence.explanation: The dietary intervention and its explicit application to all subtypes.

evidence.snippet: Routine measurement of essential amino acids in those on a low-cysteine low-protein diet
evidence.explanation: The monitoring requirement attached to the restriction.

treatments/1.description: Low protein intake with restriction of whole natural protein, aimed at reducing the cysteine load whose catabolism generates sulfite. Unlike fosdenopterin this is applied across all subtypes. It requires monitoring of essential amino acids, since the restriction that lowers sulfite also risks deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Valproate should be avoided if possible, as sulfite intoxication impairs mitochondrial function in vitro
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews Agents/Circumstances to Avoid entry, quoted directly. Note the stated rationale is an in vitro observation, which the entry does not upgrade.

treatments/2.description: A contraindication rather than a therapy, and one that collides with the presentation: valproate is a standard choice for refractory neonatal seizures, which is exactly how these patients present. GeneReviews advises avoiding it where possible because sulfite intoxication impairs mitochondrial function in vitro, and valproate is itself mitochondrially toxic.

evidence.snippet: For at-risk newborn sibs in whom prenatal testing was not performed, metabolic treatment should be initiated immediately and continued until such a time as the diagnosis has been excluded
evidence.explanation: States the treat-first principle for at-risk newborns, which follows directly from the narrowness of the window.

treatments/3.description: Autosomal recessive counseling with a 25 percent recurrence risk, but with an unusual operational consequence: because the therapeutic window is days, an at-risk newborn sib should be started on metabolic treatment immediately and only stopped once the diagnosis is excluded. Treatment precedes diagnosis rather than following it.

open_questions/0.rationale: This is the most consequential unquantified statement in the disease. The therapy reliably corrects the biochemistry and unreliably corrects the outcome, and the difference is how much excitotoxic injury has already happened. Yet the guidance is qualitative. A neonatologist deciding whether to start empiric treatment before molecular confirmation, or a service deciding whether rapid genome sequencing is worth standing up for a disease this rare, needs a number. The excitotoxicity mechanism suggests the injury is fast, which would make hours rather than days the relevant unit and would push the decision toward treating before confirming - which is what GeneReviews already advises for at-risk sibs, but not for undiagnosed neonates. That asymmetry is itself worth resolving.

open_questions/1.rationale: The comparative argument is strong: isolated sulfite oxidase deficiency mirrors most of the phenotype, and isolated xanthinuria is a mild stone-forming condition rather than an encephalopathy. So the sulfite arm evidently dominates. But "most of the symptoms" is not all of them, and the question of what the residual difference consists of has not been answered systematically. Xanthine oxidoreductase and aldehyde oxidase are major drug-metabolizing enzymes, so their loss might matter pharmacologically rather than developmentally - a treated survivor could metabolize certain drugs abnormally for life. The amidoxime-reducing component has no reported human deficiency at all, so its contribution is entirely unknown.

open_questions/2.rationale: A Mocs1-null mouse exists and is curated in this entry, so the preclinical evidence for cPMP substitution does come from the genotype the therapy targets. The open question is narrower and concerns what the model measures. Reiss et al. explicitly excluded morphological brain damage and found instead a massive transcriptional cell-death program, whereas the human disease is radiologically defined by structural destruction. Two readings are possible and they diverge therapeutically: either the mouse dies too fast for the structural lesion to develop, in which case it models the early, treatable phase and is the right system for a treatment-window study; or the structural findings in humans arise partly by a route the mouse does not run, in which case cPMP timing data from the mouse would systematically overstate the window. Species differences in developmental timing make the first reading more likely - mouse survival is days to two weeks against a human course running into infancy - but nothing in the cited evidence settles it, and the entry's central unresolved clinical question is precisely a question about timing.

evidence.snippet: The disorders are caused by mutations in GNPTAB, which encodes two of three subunits of the heterohexameric enzyme, N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase.
evidence.explanation: The cohort directly links ML II/III alpha/beta to GNPTAB mutations and the phosphotransferase enzyme.

evidence.snippet: diseases caused by a deficiency of alpha and/or beta subunits of the enzyme N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, which is encoded by the GNPTAB gene.
evidence.explanation: The Japanese cohort independently supports GNPTAB-encoded alpha/beta subunit deficiency.

steps/1.description: Biallelic pathogenic GNPTAB variants reduce activity of the alpha/beta subunits of UDP-N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, preventing normal synthesis of mannose-6-phosphate recognition markers on lysosomal hydrolases.

evidence.snippet: Without these important recognition markers, lysosomal enzymes are not transported to the lysosomes; instead, they leak out of cells, and the serum levels of these enzymes are higher than normal.
evidence.explanation: Autopsy review directly explains lysosomal hydrolase mistargeting and extracellular leakage.

evidence.snippet: the activity of nearly all lysosomal hydrolases is up to tenfold higher in plasma and other body fluids than in normal controls because of inadequate targeting to lysosomes.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports elevated plasma and fluid hydrolases due to inadequate lysosomal targeting.

steps/2.description: Hydrolases lacking mannose-6-phosphate tags fail to localize efficiently to lysosomes, producing elevated extracellular lysosomal enzyme activities and deficient intracellular lysosomal degradation.

evidence.snippet: global deficiencies of lysosomal degradative enzymes with concomitant intracellular accumulation of both partly degraded glycosaminoglycans and sphingolipids.
evidence.explanation: The natural-history study links defective hydrolase targeting to intracellular storage products.

evidence.snippet: Accumulation of mucopolysaccharides along with lipids within lysosomes of patients with mucolipidosis is the characteristic abnormality.
evidence.explanation: Autopsy review identifies lysosomal mucopolysaccharide and lipid storage as characteristic.

steps/3.description: Incompletely degraded glycosaminoglycans, sphingolipids, and related macromolecules accumulate in lysosomes across connective tissue, cardiac, neural, cartilage, and fibroblast-rich tissues.

evidence.snippet: All patients had dysostosis multiplex and progressive secondary osteoarthritis, characterised by cartilage destruction and bone lesions in multiple joints.
evidence.explanation: Adult cohort supports progressive skeletal and joint degeneration in ML III.

evidence.snippet: Biochemical indices of bone turnover were increased, and transiliac bone biopsy demonstrated both trabecular osteopenia and marked subperiosteal bone resorption.
evidence.explanation: The pamidronate study supports osteodystrophy with high bone turnover and osteopenia.

steps/4.description: ML III skeletal disease combines dysostosis multiplex, osteodystrophy, progressive osteoarthritis, cartilage destruction, bone lesions, bone pain, joint stiffness, and entrapment neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: The most documented cardiac manifestation is the thickening and insufficiency of mitral and aortic valves, but there are very few reports about the myocardial involvement.
evidence.explanation: Cardiology case report supports valve insufficiency and rare myocardial involvement in ML III alpha/beta.

evidence.snippet: Valvular cardiac disease has also been well established in ML III.
evidence.explanation: Autopsy review supports established valvular cardiac disease.

steps/5.description: Lysosomal storage in cardiovascular tissues produces valve thickening and insufficiency, most often involving mitral and aortic valves, and can rarely involve myocardium or right ventricular function.

evidence.snippet: The external exam revealed a patient of short stature (138 cm) weighing 43 kg with slightly coarsened facial features. She appeared younger than her stated age with pale white to waxy skin.
evidence.explanation: Autopsy examination supports facial and skin involvement in ML III.

evidence.snippet: Mucolipidosis III alpha/beta (MLIII alpha/beta) is a lysosomal disorder characterized by progressive slowing of the growth rate from early childhood, stiffness and pain in joints, gradual coarsening of facial features, moderate developmental delay and mild intellectual disability in most patients.
evidence.explanation: Orphanet definition supports gradual facial coarsening as a core manifestation.

steps/6.description: Lysosomal storage in fibroblast-rich connective tissues and related Hurler-like tissue involvement produces facial coarsening, gingival overgrowth, thickened skin, abdominal wall findings, and ocular surface manifestations.

evidence.snippet: Chronic otitis media was present in 7/10 patients.
evidence.explanation: Natural-history cohort supports frequent middle-ear involvement.

evidence.snippet: The lungs revealed patchy fibrosis and prominent chronic inflammation with increased intra-alveolar macrophages and lymphocytes as well as evidence of resolving aspiration pneumonia.
evidence.explanation: Autopsy supports clinically important respiratory involvement.

steps/7.description: ML III alpha/beta affects airway cartilage and recurrent middle-ear disease, producing otitis media, hearing impairment, hoarse voice, and recurrent respiratory infections.

evidence.snippet: By electron microscopy there were scattered, diffuse vesicular cytoplasmic granules in neurons and glia and an increase in lysosomal structures with fine electron lucent granularity in the above tissue types.
evidence.explanation: Autopsy documents neuronal and glial lysosomal storage in ML III alpha/beta.

evidence.snippet: gradual mild coarsening of facial features; and normal to mildly impaired cognitive development.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports mild cognitive involvement in some patients.

steps/8.description: Attenuated neuronal and glial lysosomal storage in ML III alpha/beta can accompany mild developmental or cognitive impairment.

evidence.snippet: a slowly progressive disorder with clinical onset at approximately age three years, is characterized by slow growth rate and subnormal stature
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports slow growth rate and subnormal stature in ML III alpha/beta.

evidence.snippet: ML III retains a low level of phosphotransferase activity because of at least one missense or splice site mutation. The phenotype is milder, with minimal delays in milestones, the appearance of facial coarsening by early school age, and slowing of growth after the age of 4 years.
evidence.explanation: Large cohort supports growth slowing in the attenuated ML III phenotype.

steps/9.description: Childhood-onset ML III alpha/beta causes slowing of growth after early childhood and produces persistent short stature.

steps/4.description: NOG mutations reduce noggin's ability to antagonize BMPs (particularly BMP2, BMP4, and GDF5), leading to excessive BMP signaling in developing joints. This causes progressive ossification and fusion of joints that would normally remain separate. GDF5 mutations cause gain-of-function changes that similarly enhance BMP pathway activity in joint development, and the SYNS4 GDF6 p.Y444N variant raises BMP signaling by the same route, resisting noggin-mediated antagonism.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, the binding of FGF9(S99N) to its receptor is severely impaired although the dimerization ability of mutant FGF9 itself or with wild-type FGF9 is not detectably affected, providing a basis for the defective FGFR signaling.
evidence.explanation: Identifies impaired receptor binding, not impaired dimerization or secretion, as the molecular defect behind reduced FGF signaling in SYNS3.

evidence.snippet: Further study reveals that the S99N mutation in Fgf9 disrupts joint interzone formation by affecting the chondrogenic differentiation of mesenchymal cells at the early stage of joint development.
evidence.explanation: Places the SYNS3 lesion at interzone formation in a mouse carrying the human allele, which is the step this node names.

evidence.snippet: We also show that Fgf9 is required for normal expression of Gdf5 in the prospective elbow and knee joints through its activation of Gdf5 promoter activity.
evidence.explanation: Links the FGF9 lesion to the same GDF5-dependent joint program that the BMP-side subtypes disturb, supporting convergence on one cavitation defect.

steps/5.description: SYNS3 is caused by the FGF9 p.S99N substitution, which is secreted normally but binds FGFR poorly, so FGF signaling in the developing joint is reduced rather than increased. FGF9 normally restrains mesenchymal cells from differentiating into chondrocytes at the prospective joint site and sustains Gdf5 expression there; the mutant protein does neither, and the interzone fails to form. This is a separate route to the same synostoses from the BMP-side lesions in SYNS1, SYNS2 and SYNS4, and it converges on the same failure of joint separation.

evidence.snippet: Nog-/- mice die at birth from multiple defects that include bony fusion of the appendicular skeleton.

evidence.snippet: noggin has both species-specific and joint-specific dosage-dependent roles during joint formation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that noggin dosage is critical for joint formation and that haploinsufficiency causes joint-specific pathology.

steps/6.description: Normal joint formation requires interzone specification and subsequent cavitation. Both routes above disrupt this process: excess BMP signaling from loss of noggin antagonism (SYNS1) or from noggin-resistant GDF5/GDF6 ligands (SYNS2, SYNS4), and loss of FGF9 receptor signaling at the prospective joint (SYNS3). Either way joint space formation fails and synostosis is progressive.

steps/5.description: Larvae breach the epidermis or mucosa and burrow into the dermis, subcutis, or submucosa, creating the cavity in which they will feed. steps/11.description: Necrotic tissue, exudate, and a breached epithelial barrier permit bacterial colonization and invasive soft-tissue infection. This is the principal mechanism by which myiasis becomes life-threatening. Most isolates are the ordinary wound flora - Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes - but the larvae also carry their own: Wohlfahrtiimonas chitiniclastica is a chitinolytic gram-negative rod associated with the larvae themselves rather than with the host's skin, first isolated from Wohlfahrtia magnifica, and it is reported almost exclusively in myiasis. That makes it a myiasis-specific superinfection risk rather than generic wound contamination, and it is easily missed without MALDI-TOF or 16S sequencing.

open_questions/0.rationale: The molecular arm of this entry rests entirely on non-human evidence: the serine-protease characterization comes from Oestrus ovis larvae harvested from slaughtered sheep and goats, the transcriptomic parasitism profile from Wohlfahrtia magnifica larvae taken from Bactrian camel wounds, and the immunosuppression data from Lucilia cuprina in sheep. No study quantifies larval protease activity, complement or immunoglobulin cleavage, or lymphocyte suppression in human tissue. The mismatch is mechanistically meaningful rather than merely notational, because the species that dominate human disease differ from those studied: Dermatobia hominis produces a closed furuncular cavity with a single larva, whereas the characterized species feed as aggregating masses in open ruminant wounds, so both the enzyme dose and the host response could differ substantially.

steps/2.description: DHX16 is the human Prp2 orthologue and acts after the pre-catalytic B complex has assembled, converting it to a catalytically competent spliceosome. A defective DHX16 therefore does not block spliceosome assembly - the B complex still forms - it blocks the transition to catalysis. This is a precise step-level lesion, and it is why the disease is a spliceosomopathy of activation rather than of assembly.

steps/4.description:
A node for the fact that a universal splicing defect produces a selective phenotype. Retina, cochlea, skeletal muscle and the developing CNS are consistently affected; most other tissues are not. This is not an oddity of this disease alone - it is the central puzzle of the spliceosomopathies as a class, where core spliceosome components produce retinitis pigmentosa or craniofacial disease rather than global collapse.
Nothing curated here explains it, and the node exists to hold the gap rather than to assert a mechanism. Candidate explanations in the wider field - tissue differences in splicing-factor abundance, in transcript intron burden, or in the reserve capacity of the spliceosome - are not tested in DHX16 and are not asserted.

genes/0.notes:
Two things about the variant spectrum are worth a curator's attention and are easy to lose in prose. First, it is missense-only: no truncating allele has been reported in an affected individual, across a series now in double figures. For a gene this constrained that is unlikely to be chance, and it is the strongest argument that the mechanism is dominant-negative rather than haploinsufficiency. Second, codon 454 recurs with two different substitutions in unrelated patients - p.Arg454Trp (PMID:37574199, and again in PMID:41052356) and p.Arg454Gly (PMID:42562406). Distinct substitutions at one residue in unrelated people is the signature of a specific functional site rather than of a tolerant one.
A caution on variant interpretation here: PMID:40326698 reports in-silico pathogenicity predictors positive for its allele while Missense3D shows no structural damage. For a helicase whose disease mechanism is probably an interaction defect rather than a folding defect, structural-damage prediction may be the wrong instrument, and a negative one should not be read as reassurance.

open_questions/0.rationale:
This is the entry's principal gap and the reason the pathograph has a node that asserts a selectivity it cannot explain. DHX16 is the human Prp2 orthologue, needed for the catalytic activation of every spliceosome, and the dominant-negative work shows intron retention across many genes. Yet the phenotype is a fairly reproducible three-tissue syndrome.
The question is not specific to DHX16 - the spliceosomopathies as a class have it, with core PRPF components causing isolated retinitis pigmentosa and others causing craniofacial disease - which is an argument for looking at it as a class rather than one gene at a time. The candidate explanations in the wider field (tissue differences in splicing factor abundance, in intron burden, or in spliceosome reserve capacity) are untested in DHX16 and are deliberately not curated as edges.

open_questions/1.rationale:
The entry records `functional_impact_category: DOMINANT_NEGATIVE`, and the grounds for that are worth stating openly because they are circumstantial. The allele spectrum is missense-only with no truncating variant reported; one residue recurs with two substitutions; and mutant DHX16 added to competent nuclear extract actively inhibits splicing. But the direct-inhibition experiments used engineered constructs (G724N, S552L), not patient alleles, and the one patient-allele assay (p.Arg454Gly) measured intron retention in a transfected cell line without testing whether the mutant interferes with wild-type DHX16.
Pushing against it: PMID:37574199 found DHX16 expression *decreased* in patient fibroblasts and muscle, which is what a destabilising loss-of-function allele would do, and is not what a stable interfering protein predicts. Those two observations have not been reconciled.

open_questions/2.rationale:
`kb/modules/` was grepped for `splic`, `spliceosom`, `RNA`, `helicase`, `transcript` and `mRNA`, and `just list-modules` read in full: nothing covers spliceosomal dysfunction, so `conforms_to` is unset here. But the family is real and recurrent - DHX16, DHX37, DDX54 and DHX34 came out of one paper, and EFTUD2, SNRPB and the PRPF retinitis-pigmentosa genes sit alongside them - and it shares the tissue-selectivity puzzle above as a defining feature rather than as an incidental one.
Not created here, because a module built from a single disease encodes that disease rather than the mechanism. Recorded so the next spliceosomopathy curated has somewhere to find the argument.
The peers already exist in the KB and each models the pathway locally in its own `pathophysiology` block rather than through `conforms_to`, which is the duplication a module would remove: `PRPF31-Related_Retinopathy` (a tri-snRNP assembly factor, and the closest structural analogue - one gene, dominant, one MONDO term, no subtypes), `Burn-McKeown_Syndrome`, `Mandibulofacial_Dysostosis_with_Microcephaly` and `Cerebrocostomandibular_Syndrome`. All four were verified present in `kb/disorders/` while writing this note. Note what that list already shows: a tri-snRNP assembly factor gives isolated retinal disease, an EFTUD2-family defect gives craniofacial disease, and a catalytic-activation helicase gives this neuromuscular-sensory syndrome. Five entries, five different tissues, one machine - which is the argument for a module and simultaneously the reason a module would have to be built around the selectivity question rather than around the splicing step.
Surfaced by the automated second-opinion comment on the claim issue (dismech#12391), which named the four peers and independently reached the same conclusion that no core-spliceosome module exists.

evidence.snippet: CRTAP, P3H1, and cyclophilin B (CyPB) form an intracellular collagen-modifying complex that 3-hydroxylates proline at position 986 (P986) in the alpha1 chains of collagen type I.

evidence.snippet: CyPB is ubiquitously expressed and its stability is independent of CRTAP/P3H1. PPIB-null cells, however, have moderately reduced CRTAP and P3H1 protein levels, suggesting CyPB provides some support to the complex

steps/1.description: PPIB encodes cyclophilin B (CyPB), a peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase that, with cartilage-associated protein (CRTAP) and prolyl 3-hydroxylase 1 (P3H1), forms the 1:1:1 endoplasmic-reticulum complex that 3-hydroxylates alpha1(I)Pro986 of type I collagen, isomerizes prolyl peptide bonds, and chaperones collagen folding. Biallelic loss-of-function PPIB variants eliminate CyPB. Unlike CRTAP and P3H1 (which mutually stabilize each other), CyPB stability is independent of the other two subunits, although PPIB-null cells show moderately reduced CRTAP and P3H1 levels. The same complex underlies the closely related recessive OI types VII (CRTAP) and VIII (P3H1).

evidence.snippet: Proα1(I) chains are slow to assemble into trimers, and abnormal procollagen molecules concentrate in the RER, and bind to protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) and prolyl 4-hydroxylase 1 (P4H1).
evidence.explanation: Documents delayed procollagen chain assembly and ER accumulation in PPIB-deficient patient fibroblasts, implicating CyPB in chain association and folding.

evidence.snippet: These findings suggest that prolyl cis-trans isomerase may be required to effectively fold the proline-rich regions of the C-terminal propeptide to allow proα chain association
evidence.explanation: Identifies a role for CyPB beyond helix isomerization — in C-propeptide folding required for chain association.

evidence.snippet: The proband's collagen had normal collagen folding and normal prolyl 3-hydroxylation, suggesting that CyPB is not the exclusive peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase that catalyzes the rate-limiting step in collagen folding, as is currently thought.
evidence.explanation: Documents the contrasting biochemical phenotype (normal folding and 3-hydroxylation) in a moderate CyPB-deficient case, showing the consequences of CyPB loss are heterogeneous.

steps/2.description: CyPB has been considered the major PPIase catalyzing the rate-limiting cis-trans isomerization step of collagen triple-helix folding, but its loss also impairs folding of the C-terminal propeptide and proalpha chain association into trimers. In severely affected PPIB-deficient cells, proalpha1(I) chains assemble slowly into trimers and abnormal procollagen accumulates in the rough ER, binding protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) and prolyl 4-hydroxylase 1 (P4H1), with collagen overmodification. The biochemical consequences are heterogeneous across patients, however: some cases retain normal alpha1(I)Pro986 3-hydroxylation and normal helical modification, indicating that another PPIase can partly substitute for CyPB and that the primary lesion is loss of CyPB folding/chaperone function rather than loss of 3-hydroxylation.

evidence.snippet: Knock-out (KO) mice are small, with reduced femoral areal bone mineral density (aBMD), bone volume per total volume (BV/TV) and mechanical properties, as well as increased femoral brittleness.
evidence.explanation: The Ppib-/- mouse recapitulates the reduced bone mass, impaired mechanics, and brittleness of OI type IX.

evidence.snippet: The altered crosslink pattern was associated with decreased collagen deposition into matrix in culture, altered fibril structure in tissue, and reduced bone strength.
evidence.explanation: Links the CyPB-dependent collagen crosslinking/modification defect to a defective bone matrix and reduced bone strength.

steps/3.description: Loss of CyPB alters collagen lysyl hydroxylation, glycosylation, and crosslinking and impairs collagen deposition and fibril structure, producing a defective bone extracellular matrix with reduced bone mass and mechanical strength. Clinically this manifests as low bone mineral density, recurrent fractures, growth deficiency, and long-bone bowing/deformity, ranging from perinatally lethal to moderately severe disease. A cyclophilin B knockout (Ppib-/-) mouse recapitulates the OI phenotype.

open_questions/0.rationale: CyPB was long considered the unique PPIase catalyzing the rate-limiting step of collagen folding, but human PPIB-null cases are biochemically discordant: lethal cases show reduced alpha1(I)Pro986 3-hydroxylation with overmodification, while moderate cases retain normal 3-hydroxylation and helical modification. A Ppib-/- mouse shows slower folding (consistent with a rate-limiting role) yet cyclosporine A causes further delay, implying an additional collagen PPIase. The true rate-limiting determinant and the basis of the genotype-biochemistry-phenotype heterogeneity remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Macrophage inflammation results in enhanced oxidative stress and cytokine/chemokine secretion, causing more LDL/remnant oxidation, endothelial cell activation, monocyte recruitment, and foam cell formation.
evidence.explanation: Documents the macrophage inflammatory loop that amplifies foam-cell formation.

steps/1.description: In the peripheral arterial intima, recruited monocytes become macrophages and internalize retained apoB-containing lipoproteins, forming lipid-laden foam cells. Their inflammatory feed-forward loop promotes further lipoprotein oxidation, endothelial activation, monocyte recruitment, and foam-cell formation.

evidence.snippet: vascular smooth muscle cell phenotypic switching through transdifferentiation and stem/progenitor cell activation resulting in the promotion of inflammation, calcification, and secretion of extracellular matrix, altering fibrous cap structure, and necrotic core growth.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports smooth-muscle-cell phenotypic switching and extracellular-matrix secretion in plaque assembly.

steps/2.description: In the inflamed peripheral arterial intima, vascular smooth muscle cells switch to a synthetic, migratory phenotype, proliferate, and organize extracellular matrix to build the fibrofatty plaque and its fibrous cap. This is the atomic smooth-muscle-cell and matrix assembly step.

evidence.snippet: It was observed that serum IL-6, IL-8, ICAM and VCAM levels in type II diabetes mellitus (T2DM) with PAD patients were increased significantly (85.93, 597.08, 94.80 and 80.66) as compared to T2DM patients (59.52, 231.34, 56.88 and 50.19) and healthy individuals (4.81, 16.93, 5.55 and 5.16).
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates marked elevation of endothelial activation markers (ICAM, VCAM) in PAD patients, indicating severe endothelial dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: We have previously shown that VEGF165b, an alternatively spliced anti-angiogenic VEGF-A isoform, inhibits the VEGFR-STAT3 pathway in ischemic endothelial cells (ECs) to decrease their angiogenic capacity.
evidence.explanation: Describes impaired angiogenic signaling in ischemic endothelial cells in PAD, contributing to endothelial dysfunction and inadequate collateral formation.

steps/3.description: Impaired endothelium-dependent vasodilation reduces blood flow reserve. Decreased nitric oxide production and increased endothelin contribute.

evidence.snippet: the local arterial microenvironment of a stable atheroma promotes destabilizing conditions that result in the transition to an unstable atheroma.
evidence.explanation: Human histopathology and vascular-imaging evidence supports transition of a mature stable atheroma to an unstable lesion; peripheral artery is the disease-specific location substituted here.

steps/4.description: Continued lipid accumulation, foam-cell death, and matrix remodeling produce a mature peripheral arterial atheroma with a necrotic lipid core beneath a fibrous cap. Local plaque changes can destabilize the cap and create a rupture-prone lesion.

evidence.snippet: atherosclerotic plaque rupture-related thrombosis was more common above the knee.
evidence.explanation: PAD-specific histopathology summarized by this review directly supports rupture-related thrombosis in above-knee disease and defines the qualified atherosclerotic branch represented by this node.

evidence.snippet: Continuous release of NETs in response to external stimuli leads to activation of surrounding platelets and monocytes/macrophages, resulting in damage to endothelial cells (EC) and vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMC).
evidence.explanation: Supports platelet-activating and vascular-injury context in atherosclerosis, but does not directly establish plaque rupture-related thrombosis in PAD.

evidence.snippet: NETs not only capture pathogens in innate immunity but also respond to sterile inflammatory stimuli in atherosclerosis, such as lipoproteins and inflammatory cytokines.
evidence.explanation: Supports NET responses to sterile atherosclerotic stimuli, but does not directly establish thrombosis or a PAD-specific rupture event.

steps/5.description: In the atherosclerotic PAD branch, plaque rupture-related thrombosis is reported more often above the knee. PAD also includes occlusive thrombosis without significant plaque, so this node records a qualified association rather than a universal plaque-rupture consequence or an asserted acute limb-ischemia outcome.

evidence.snippet: Peripheral artery disease (PAD), coronary artery disease (CAD), and cerebrovascular disease (CeVD) are characterized by atherosclerosis and inflammation as their underlying mechanisms.
evidence.explanation: Establishes inflammation as a core mechanism underlying PAD pathophysiology.

evidence.snippet: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are network-like structures of chromatin filaments decorated by histones, granules, and cytoplasmic-derived proteins expelled by activated neutrophils under multiple pathogenic conditions.
evidence.explanation: Describes neutrophil-driven inflammatory mechanisms involving NET formation in atherosclerosis.

evidence.snippet: Continuous release of NETs in response to external stimuli leads to activation of surrounding platelets and monocytes/macrophages, resulting in damage to endothelial cells (EC) and vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMC).
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates how neutrophil-mediated inflammation causes vascular cell damage in atherosclerotic disease.

steps/6.description: Chronic inflammation drives plaque progression and instability. Elevated CRP and inflammatory markers predict cardiovascular events.

evidence.snippet: Arterial injury causes endothelial dysfunction promoting modification of apoB containing lipoproteins and infiltration of monocytes into the subendothelial space.
evidence.explanation: Directly links endothelial injury and modified apoB lipoproteins to monocyte entry into the subendothelial space.

evidence.snippet: Macrophage inflammatory chemoattractants stimulate infiltration and proliferation of smooth muscle cells. Smooth muscle cells produce the extracellular matrix providing a stable fibrous barrier between plaque prothrombotic factors and platelets.
evidence.explanation: Connects macrophage inflammation to smooth-muscle-cell proliferation and extracellular-matrix production, the next core stage.

evidence.snippet: Unresolved inflammation results in formation of vulnerable plaques characterized by enhanced macrophage apoptosis and defective efferocytosis of apoptotic cells resulting in necrotic cell death leading to increased smooth muscle cell death, decreased extracellular matrix production, and collagen degradation by macrophage proteases.
evidence.explanation: Identifies macrophage/foam-cell death and extracellular-matrix remodeling as known intermediates in progression toward vulnerable advanced plaque.

edges/2.description: Continued lipid accumulation, foam-cell death, and matrix remodeling intervene between initial fibrofatty plaque assembly and advanced atheroma.

evidence.snippet: atherosclerotic plaque rupture-related thrombosis was more common above the knee.
evidence.explanation: PAD-specific histopathology summarized by this review directly supports plaque rupture leading to thrombosis in the above-knee atherosclerotic branch; it does not generalize to every PAD occlusion.

genes/0.notes: Same as CAD

evidence.snippet: During follow-up to 5 years, patients who quit smoking had significantly lower all-cause mortality (14% vs 31%; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% confidence interval, 0.18-0.90) and improved amputation-free survival (81% vs 60%; hazard ratio, 0.43, 95% confidence interval, 0.22-0.86) compared with patients who continued smoking
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that smoking cessation in PAD patients significantly reduces mortality and improves amputation-free survival.

treatments/0.description: Most important intervention, reduces progression.

treatments/1.description: Aspirin or clopidogrel to reduce cardiovascular events.

evidence.snippet: Higher dosing of statins confers a significant improvement in patient outcomes, especially ACM and amputations, although the quality of the evidence was variable.
evidence.explanation: Meta-analysis demonstrating statins significantly reduce mortality and amputations in PAD patients.

treatments/2.description: LDL lowering, plaque stabilization.

treatments/3.description: Cardiovascular risk reduction.

evidence.snippet: A meta-analysis of 25 randomized trials demonstrated a 180-meter increase in treadmill walking distance in response to supervised exercise interventions compared with a nonexercising control group.
evidence.explanation: Meta-analysis of 25 RCTs demonstrates supervised exercise significantly improves walking distance in PAD patients.

evidence.snippet: The update consistently emphasises supervised exercise therapy and best medical therapies as first line treatment.
evidence.explanation: The ESVS focused update emphasises supervised exercise therapy, alongside best medical therapy, as first-line treatment for intermittent claudication.

treatments/4.description: First-line for claudication, improves walking distance.

evidence.snippet: Cilostazol therapy increased maximal and pain-free walking distances by 50% and 67%, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Meta-analysis of 8 RCTs showing cilostazol significantly improves walking distances in claudication patients.

treatments/5.description: Phosphodiesterase inhibitor for claudication symptoms.

evidence.snippet: Endovascular revascularisation is recommended only for persistent lifestyle limiting symptoms despite conservative therapy.
evidence.explanation: The ESVS focused update restricts endovascular revascularisation to patients with persistent lifestyle-limiting symptoms despite conservative therapy.

treatments/6.description: Endovascular or surgical for severe disease.

evidence.snippet: Four of the patients have mutations that disrupt the translation frame and/or create an early termination codon in the PEX12 open reading frame predicted to result in truncated protein products, lacking at least the COOH-terminal zinc-binding domain. All these patients display the more severe phenotypes
evidence.explanation: Ties loss of the zinc-binding domain to the severe end of the spectrum, which is the presentation this entry curates.

evidence.snippet: Fibroblasts derived from patients with the peroxisome deficiency Zellweger syndrome of complementation group III (CG-III) were also complemented for peroxisome biogenesis with PEX12.
evidence.explanation: The complementation experiment that assigned group III to PEX12; IN_VITRO because the result is in cultured patient fibroblasts.

steps/1.description: Variants on both PEX12 alleles. Truncating alleles that remove the C-terminal zinc-binding domain are the ones associated with the severe presentation.

steps/2.description: PEX12 co-assembles with its paralogues PEX2 and PEX10 into the ubiquitin-ligase retrotranslocation channel of the peroxisomal membrane. Losing PEX12 leaves the channel unable to regulate PEX5 ubiquitination.

steps/3.description: PEX5 delivers PTS1-tagged matrix enzymes and must be ubiquitinated and exported back to the cytosol to be reused. Without a functioning channel it is not returned, so the import cycle stalls after a single round.

steps/4.description: Matrix enzymes never reach the organelle. The membrane compartment still forms - the "peroxisomal ghost" - which is the morphological signature distinguishing a biogenesis defect from a single enzyme deficiency.

steps/5.description: Ether phospholipid synthesis begins in the peroxisome, so plasmalogens - major constituents of myelin - and DHA are not made. This is the deficiency half of the signature, and the one most plausibly linked to the white-matter disease.

steps/6.description: Substrates that only peroxisomes degrade build up systemically: C26:0 and other VLCFA, phytanic and pristanic acid, and C27 bile-acid intermediates. This is the accumulation half of the biochemical signature and the basis of diagnostic testing.

steps/7.description: Neuronal precursors fail to reach their laminar destinations during fetal cortical development, producing the perisylvian polymicrogyria and heterotopia that make this a congenital malformation rather than a purely degenerative disease. Because the lesion is formed before birth, it is not reversible by any postnatal intervention.

steps/8.description: VLCFA and C27 bile-acid intermediates are directly hepatotoxic, driving cholestasis and fibrosis.

steps/9.description: VLCFA accumulation in adrenocortical cells impairs steroidogenesis. Often subclinical at first, which is why GeneReviews asks for ACTH and cortisol measurement by age one even in children who look adrenally well.

evidence.snippet: Infants with severe ZSD are significantly impaired and typically die during the first year of life, usually having made no developmental progress.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states the course of the severe end of the spectrum, which is what PBD3A denotes.

steps/10.description: Profound hypotonia, intractable neonatal seizures, and absent developmental progress. In the severe form death usually follows within the first year.

edges/8.description: Peroxisomal failure demonstrably disrupts cortical migration, but which accumulating substrate or missing lipid does it is not established.

evidence.snippet: the loss of PEX12 function leads to more-severe cellular and clinical phenotypes
evidence.explanation: States the dose-of-function relationship that separates the A and B ends of this locus.

genes/0.notes: The complementation group 3 gene. Genotype-phenotype correlation is unusually tractable here: alleles truncating the protein before the C-terminal zinc-binding domain give the severe presentation, while alleles preserving residual function shift toward the milder end of the spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Treatment of manifestations: The focus is on symptomatic therapy and may include gastrostomy to provide adequate calories, hearing aids, cataract removal, glasses to correct refractive errors, supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins, and cholic acid supplementation
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews Management states that therapy is symptomatic and lists the measures.

treatments/0.description: There is no treatment for the biogenesis defect. Management is entirely symptomatic - gastrostomy feeding, anti-seizure medication, hearing aids, cataract surgery, fat-soluble vitamin and cholic acid supplementation, adrenal replacement. None of it restores peroxisomal import, and the congenital brain malformation is fixed before birth, so no postnatal intervention can address the central lesion.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Addresses consequences - nutrition, seizures, sensory deficits - without acting on peroxisome biogenesis.

evidence.snippet: Cholic acid significantly improved urine bile acid metabolite scores (P < 0.0001) and serum aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase (P < 0.0001) in patients with SED and ZSD.
evidence.explanation: The fall in atypical urinary bile acids is the direct readout of the targeted mechanism, and the transaminase fall is the hepatic consequence.

treatments/1.description: Oral cholic acid restores feedback inhibition of endogenous bile acid synthesis, so the hepatotoxic C27 intermediates that peroxisome-deficient hepatocytes cannot process stop accumulating. It is the only FDA-approved therapy for Zellweger spectrum disease and the only intervention in this entry that acts on a curated mechanism node rather than on a consequence - which is why it is curated separately from supportive care rather than inside it.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Suppresses synthesis of the atypical C27 bile-acid intermediates that accumulate because peroxisomal side-chain shortening is blocked. It does not restore peroxisomal import, so the other accumulating substrates are unaffected.

treatments/1/targets/1.description: Removing the hepatotoxic intermediates is what improves the liver chemistry.

evidence.snippet: adrenal replacement therapy; vitamin D supplementation and consideration of bisphosphonates for osteopenia
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews Management names adrenal replacement among the interventions.

treatments/2.description: Glucocorticoid replacement once adrenal insufficiency is documented. Curated separately from general supportive care because it depends on active surveillance rather than on symptoms - the deficiency is often silent until stressed.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Replaces the missing hormone output; it does not correct the VLCFA accumulation that impaired steroidogenesis.

evidence.snippet: ACTH and cortisol levels by age one year and annually thereafter
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews Surveillance gives the adrenal monitoring interval.

treatments/3.description: Structured monitoring rather than symptom-driven follow-up, because several complications are silent until advanced - adrenal insufficiency in particular.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Detects the deficiency before it presents as crisis; it does not prevent it.

evidence.snippet: However, one patient who presented relatively mild clinical and cellular phenotypes was a compound heterozygote for two seemingly severe mutations on each PEX12 allele.
evidence.explanation: States the discrepant case that the mechanism explains.

evidence.snippet: this mutant PEX12 cDNA displayed significant PEX12 activity in a functional complementation assay
evidence.explanation: The functional result showing the supposedly null allele retains activity; IN_VITRO because it is a cell-based complementation assay.

open_questions/0.rationale:
Genotype predicts phenotype well in complementation group 3 - less PEX12 function, worse disease - with one documented exception that turns out to be informative rather than noise. A compound heterozygote carrying two seemingly null alleles was mildly affected. The explanation was that the expressed allele, a 2-bp deletion eight codons into the reading frame, still produced a functional protein because translation reinitiated at a downstream AUG.
The general lesson is that "predicted truncating" is a statement about the reading frame, not about the protein. An early frameshift can be rescued by internal initiation, so severity prediction from variant class alone will occasionally be wrong in the direction of over-calling severity. Curated here because this entry is defined by being the severe end of its locus, and the boundary between 3A and the milder presentations is exactly what such an allele blurs.

open_questions/1.rationale: Every treatment in this entry is symptomatic. Restoring import would mean restoring a membrane translocon in every affected tissue, and the two organs that determine outcome present different obstacles: the brain lesion is a completed malformation of fetal migration, so even perfect postnatal correction could not undo it, while the liver and adrenal disease is progressive and might in principle respond. No approach - gene therapy, read-through of nonsense alleles, chaperone rescue of hypomorphic alleles - has reached patients. The gap is recorded rather than left implicit because the absence of disease-modifying options is the single most important fact about managing this diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: deficiency of GIMAP5, an evolutionarily conserved GTPase selectively expressed in lymphocytes and endothelial cells
evidence.explanation: Establishes the restricted expression pattern that determines which tissues the disease affects. Graded IN_VITRO rather than HUMAN_CLINICAL because the quoted clause reports where the protein is expressed, which is an expression result, not a clinical observation about patients.

steps/1.description: Two damaged GIMAP5 alleles leave little or no functional GTPase. GIMAP5 is expressed selectively in lymphocytes and endothelial cells, which is what confines the disease to those two compartments despite the gene being lost everywhere.

evidence.snippet: GIMAP5 controls CER abundance by interacting with protein kinase CK2 (CK2), attenuating its ability to activate CER synthases
evidence.explanation: Identifies CK2 and the ceramide synthases as the immediate downstream effectors.

steps/2.description: Without GIMAP5 to attenuate it, protein kinase CK2 over-activates ceramide synthases. This is the shared upstream step proposed for both arms of the disease.

evidence.snippet: Inhibition of CK2 and CER synthase rescues GIMAP5-deficient T cells by preventing CER overaccumulation and cell deterioration
evidence.explanation: The rescue experiment establishing that the ceramide accumulation causes the cellular deterioration rather than accompanying it.

steps/3.description: Pathological accumulation of long-chain ceramides, the defining metabolic signature of GIMAP5 deficiency. That inhibiting either CK2 or ceramide synthase rescues the cells is what makes this a causal step rather than a correlate.

evidence.snippet: a new human genetic disease that causes cell senescence, liver and immune dysfunction, and early mortality
evidence.explanation: Establishes senescence as the cellular endpoint of the shared pathway.

steps/4.description: Senescence and organelle dysfunction in the GIMAP5-expressing compartments. From here the disease divides into a hepatic vascular arm and an immune arm, which proceed independently of each other.

evidence.snippet: places GIMAP5 upstream of GATA4, a transcription factor required for LSEC specification
evidence.explanation: Identifies GATA4 and its role in specifying the affected cell type.

steps/5.description: Loss of GATA4, the transcription factor required to specify liver sinusoidal endothelial cell identity. This is the step that turns a generic endothelial defect into a specifically hepatic one.

evidence.snippet: selective gene ablation of the mouse gimap5 gene impairs the final intrathymic maturation of CD8 and CD4 T cells and compromises the survival of postthymic CD4 and CD8 cells
evidence.explanation: Establishes the survival defect in T cells on Gimap5 loss.

evidence.snippet: a human patient with a GIMAP5 loss-of-function mutation has lymphopenia and impaired T cell proliferation in vitro that can be rescued with GSK3 inhibitors
evidence.explanation: Confirms the proliferation defect in a human patient and identifies a pharmacological rescue.

steps/6.description: Spontaneous T and NK cell apoptosis with impaired proliferation. GIMAP5 has long been recognized as an anti-apoptotic factor required for lymphocyte survival, and this arm of the disease was characterized in rodents well before the human portal hypertension phenotype was described.

evidence.snippet: this effect is also seen when GIMAP5 is selectively deleted in endothelial cells
evidence.explanation: The endothelial-specific deletion experiment establishing cell-intrinsic causation.

evidence.snippet: reveals replacement of LSECs with capillarized endothelial cells, a reduction of macrovascular hepatic endothelial cells
evidence.explanation: Describes the cellular composition change by single-cell sequencing.

steps/7.description: The specialized fenestrated sinusoidal endothelium is replaced by capillarized endothelium, and macrovascular hepatic endothelial cells are reduced. Critically this happens when GIMAP5 is deleted in endothelium alone, which is what establishes the lesion as endothelial-intrinsic rather than a consequence of the immune disease.

evidence.snippet: He was found to have an increased portal pressure of 14 mm Hg (normal portal venous pressure ranges between 5 and 10 mm Hg)
evidence.explanation: The one directly measured portal pressure in the cohort, establishing the haemodynamic abnormality rather than inferring it.

steps/8.description: Raised resistance to portal venous flow within a liver that is not cirrhotic. This is the defining haemodynamic abnormality, and the absence of cirrhosis, fibrosis and portal vein thrombosis is what makes the entity noncirrhotic portal hypertension rather than ordinary chronic liver disease.

evidence.snippet: four families with unexplained portal hypertension
evidence.explanation: The presenting feature in every index family.

steps/9.description: The defining feature, and noncirrhotic by definition: cirrhosis, fibrosis and portal or splanchnic vein thrombosis are explicitly excluded.

evidence.snippet: All affected subjects have splenomegaly
evidence.explanation: Gives both the finding and its frequency in the founding cohort of nine patients.

evidence.snippet: caused lymphopenia, splenomegaly, progressive liver pathology, and extramedullary hematopoiesis (EMH)
evidence.explanation: The orthologous lesion reproduces the splenomegaly in the model system, corroborating the human finding rather than standing in for it.

steps/10.description: Present in all affected subjects of the founding series, and the source of the hypersplenic thrombocytopenia.

evidence.snippet: thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases, and esophageal varices were nearly universal (Table 1)
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency directly in the founding cohort.

steps/11.description: Portosystemic collaterals, endoscopically confirmed in the founding series and the main source of life-threatening bleeding.

evidence.snippet: GIMAP5 deficiency drives a distinct vascular remodeling characterized by nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) and porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder (PSVD), frequently progressing to non-cirrhotic portal hypertension
evidence.explanation: States the histology and its progression to portal hypertension for this disease specifically.

steps/12.description: The characteristic biopsy finding, together with obliterative portal venopathy. It is what places the disorder within porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder rather than among the cirrhotic liver diseases.

evidence.snippet: a human patient with a GIMAP5 loss-of-function mutation has lymphopenia and impaired T cell proliferation in vitro
evidence.explanation: Documents lymphopenia in a human patient.

steps/13.description: T and NK lymphopenia with T-cell exhaustion, the laboratory hallmark of the immune arm.

evidence.snippet: cause a severe syndrome characterized by altered immunity, lymphoproliferation, and progressive hepatopathy
evidence.explanation: Establishes altered immunity as a core component.

steps/14.description: Consequence of the lymphopenia and T-cell exhaustion; severe viral infections are reported.

evidence.snippet: The 11-year-old proband presented with autoimmune cytopenias, severe viral infections, and early biochemical liver anomalies
evidence.explanation: Documents autoimmune cytopenias in a genetically confirmed patient.

steps/15.description: One of the autoimmune cytopenias of the immune arm. Their occurrence alongside immunodeficiency is what makes this an inborn error of immunity rather than a simple immune deficiency.

evidence.snippet: GIMAP5 controls CER abundance by interacting with protein kinase CK2 (CK2), attenuating its ability to activate CER synthases
evidence.explanation: States the direct molecular interaction and what its loss releases.

edges/1.description: GIMAP5 normally binds CK2 and attenuates its activation of ceramide synthases, so losing GIMAP5 removes that restraint.

evidence.snippet: In the absence of Gimap5, constitutive GSK3beta activity constrains c-Myc induction and NFATc1 nuclear import, thereby limiting productive CD4+ T cell proliferation
evidence.explanation: Gives the second, GSK3-beta-dependent route from GIMAP5 loss to the lymphocyte phenotype.

edges/2.description: In lymphocytes, GIMAP5 loss also leaves GSK3-beta constitutively active, which constrains c-Myc induction and NFATc1 nuclear import and limits productive proliferation independently of the ceramide route.

evidence.snippet: We show that GIMAP5 restricts the pathological accumulation of long-chain ceramides (CERs), thereby regulating longevity
evidence.explanation: States the accumulation and its consequence for cell longevity.

edges/3.description: Over-active ceramide synthases produce ceramide faster than it is cleared.

evidence.snippet: we report a new human genetic disease that causes cell senescence, liver and immune dysfunction, and early mortality that results from deficiency of GIMAP5
evidence.explanation: Names cell senescence as the consequence, together with the two organ systems affected.

edges/4.description: Ceramide overaccumulation drives the senescent phenotype in the two cell types that express GIMAP5.

evidence.snippet: places GIMAP5 upstream of GATA4, a transcription factor required for LSEC specification
evidence.explanation: Establishes the ordering without demonstrating the intervening mechanism.

edges/5.description: GIMAP5 is placed upstream of GATA4 by single-cell transcriptomics, but the steps connecting the ceramide and senescence pathway to GATA4 have not been demonstrated.

evidence.snippet: its loss in both humans and mice results in capillarization of liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs)
evidence.explanation: States the consequence in both species.

edges/6.description: Without GATA4 the sinusoidal endothelium loses its specialized identity and takes on a continuous, capillary-like phenotype.

evidence.snippet: GIMAP5 is a critical regulator of liver endothelial cell homeostasis and, when absent, produces portal hypertension
evidence.explanation: Links the endothelial lesion to the haemodynamic outcome without resolving the intervening steps.

edges/7.description: Capillarized sinusoids, with nodular regenerative hyperplasia and obliterative portal venopathy, raise resistance to portal flow. The quantitative contribution of each histological change has not been partitioned.

evidence.snippet: GIMAP5 is a critical regulator of liver endothelial cell homeostasis and, when absent, produces portal hypertension
evidence.explanation: States the causal endpoint directly.

edges/8.description: The raised resistance is the portal hypertension.

evidence.snippet: All affected subjects have splenomegaly
evidence.explanation: Establishes the splenomegaly alongside the portal hypertension in the same cohort. The step from raised portal pressure to splenic enlargement is standard portal-hypertension physiology and is the curator's inference, not a claim this paper makes.

edges/9.description: Portal congestion enlarges the spleen. The universal splenomegaly and the raised portal pressure are both reported, but no source states the causal step between them, so it is curated as an inference.

evidence.snippet: Esophageal varices, a consequence of increased portal pressure, were confirmed in seven subjects by endoscopy
evidence.explanation: States the causal relationship between raised portal pressure and varices, and confirms it endoscopically in seven patients.

edges/10.description: Portosystemic collaterals decompress the hypertensive portal system through the oesophageal veins.

evidence.snippet: GIMAP5 deficiency drives a distinct vascular remodeling characterized by nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) and porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder (PSVD), frequently progressing to non-cirrhotic portal hypertension
evidence.explanation: Ties the histological lesion to the haemodynamic outcome in this disease.

edges/11.description: The characteristic hepatic histology of the disorder, found on biopsy in the absence of cirrhosis.

evidence.snippet: Germline knockout alleles of Mfsd1, Glmp, and Gimap5 each caused lymphopenia, liver pathology, EMH, and lipid deposition in the bone marrow and liver
evidence.explanation: Reports lymphopenia on Gimap5 loss alongside the liver pathology.

edges/12.description: Failure of lymphocyte survival and proliferation manifests as lymphopenia.

evidence.snippet: cause a severe syndrome characterized by altered immunity, lymphoproliferation, and progressive hepatopathy
evidence.explanation: Names altered immunity as a defining component of the syndrome.

edges/13.description: Lymphopenia and T-cell exhaustion leave the patient susceptible to infection.

evidence.snippet: alongside an expanded atypical memory B-cell population and T-cell exhaustion
evidence.explanation: Records the immune dysregulation accompanying the cytopenias without establishing how a lymphocyte survival defect produces autoimmunity.

edges/14.description: Immune dysregulation produces autoimmune cytopenias; how a survival defect in lymphocytes gives rise to autoimmunity rather than simple immunodeficiency is not resolved.

evidence.snippet: we demonstrate homozygous damaging mutations in GIMAP5, a small organellar GTPase, in four families with unexplained portal hypertension
evidence.explanation: The gene-discovery study.

evidence.snippet: Notably, all four mutations (p.I47T, p.P109L, p.L204P, and p.L223F) lead to loss of GIMAP5 protein expression
evidence.explanation: The mechanistically important convergence. Four different missense substitutions, in four different kindreds, all produce the same consequence of absent protein, which is what makes this a clean loss of function rather than a set of allele-specific effects.

genes/0.notes: All reported disease alleles are germline and recessive, and most are missense substitutions in or near the AIG1-type G domain; at least one nonsense allele is reported. Every reported allele converges on loss of GIMAP5 protein expression, which is both the mechanism and the basis for the immunoblot as a diagnostic test. GIMAP5 is loss-of-function tolerant at the population level, which is consistent with heterozygous carriers being unaffected. Note that the stability of GIMAP5 depends on the lysosomal MFSD1-GLMP complex, so MFSD1 and GLMP are candidate biological modifiers rather than established ones.

evidence.snippet: Notably, three affected individuals in kindred 2 are deceased; two of them died from complications of portal hypertension
evidence.explanation: Establishes that portal-hypertension complications are lethal in this disease, which is what motivates prophylaxis. No GIMAP5-specific trial evidence exists.

treatments/0.description: Nonselective beta-blockade to lower portal pressure and reduce variceal bleeding risk, alongside endoscopic surveillance and band ligation. This is standard portal-hypertension care rather than anything specific to GIMAP5 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Esophageal varices, a consequence of increased portal pressure, were confirmed in seven subjects by endoscopy
evidence.explanation: Establishes the raised portal pressure and the varices that prophylaxis targets. The efficacy of beta-blockade in this disorder specifically has not been studied.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Beta-blockade reduces portal inflow and pressure; it does not act on the endothelial lesion.

evidence.snippet: the proband achieved sustained clinical remission of cytopenias through immunomodulation with the mTOR inhibitor sirolimus
evidence.explanation: Reports the observed response of the autoimmune cytopenias to sirolimus.

treatments/1.description: An mTOR inhibitor used for the immune arm, reported to achieve sustained remission of the autoimmune cytopenias in the most recently published case.

evidence.snippet: Targeted therapies, particularly mTORC1 inhibitors like sirolimus, offer a compelling strategy to reverse the metabolic and senescent defects observed in patient lymphocytes
evidence.explanation: States that the agent acts on the lymphocyte compartment, which is the arm this link targets.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Acts on the immune arm of the disease and not on the hepatic vascular arm.

evidence.snippet: GIMAP5 is a critical regulator of liver endothelial cell homeostasis and, when absent, produces portal hypertension
evidence.explanation: Establishes the hepatic-endothelial locus of disease that motivates transplantation.

treatments/2.description: Considered for end-stage hepatic disease. It is mechanistically rational here in a way it is not for many multisystem disorders, because the causal lesion for the hepatic arm is intrinsic to the liver endothelium and would be replaced along with the organ.

evidence.snippet: this effect is also seen when GIMAP5 is selectively deleted in endothelial cells
evidence.explanation: The endothelial-intrinsic nature of the lesion is what makes organ replacement a coherent strategy; no transplant outcome in this disease has been reported.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Replacing the liver replaces the capillarized endothelium that carries the lesion.

evidence.snippet: This pathology persists in a Rag2-deficient background in the absence of mature B, T, or NK cells and cannot be adoptively transferred by transplanting gimap5(-/-) bone marrow into wild-type recipients
evidence.explanation: Contradicts the expectation that haematopoietic transplantation addresses the liver disease. The hepatic pathology occurs without mature lymphocytes and is not transferable with marrow.

treatments/3.description: Considered definitive for the immune and haematological disease. The important caveat is mechanistic: because the hepatic lesion is endothelial-intrinsic and lymphocyte-independent, transplanting the haematopoietic system is not expected to reverse established portal hypertension, so the risk-benefit calculation cannot treat it as a cure for the whole disease.

evidence.snippet: Development of NK/NKT cells is restored on transfer of gimap5(-/-) bone marrow into a wild-type environment
evidence.explanation: Shows the lymphoid defect is correctable by changing the haematopoietic environment, which is the principle transplantation relies on.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Replaces the GIMAP5-deficient lymphoid compartment, addressing the immune arm alone.

The prediction is that haematopoietic transplantation will not reverse established portal hypertension. But this has not been tested in patients, and the untested question that matters is whether transplantation performed early, before capillarization is established, changes the hepatic trajectory. Because HSCT carries real mortality and is being weighed for the immune arm anyway, this gap sits directly on a clinical decision rather than beside one.

open_questions/1.rationale: The CK2-ceramide axis was demonstrated in T cells, where inhibiting CK2 or ceramide synthase rescues the cells. This matters because CK2 and ceramide-synthase inhibitors are the leading candidate targeted therapies, and whether they could address the portal hypertension or only the immune disease turns on exactly this question.
