genes/0.notes: RNASEH1 (2p25.3) encodes ribonuclease H1, whose longer isoform carries a mitochondrial targeting sequence. Reported pathogenic variants include the recurrent catalytic-domain missense c.424G>A p.Val142Ile, c.487T>C, the in-frame c.258_260del in the connection domain, the splice variant c.129-3C>G (exon 2 skipping in muscle RNA), and c.86A>G p.Tyr29Cys in the hybrid-binding domain. Most tested variants reduce enzyme activity; p.Tyr29Cys is the documented exception, increasing hybrid-cleaving activity while impairing primer formation.

treatments/0.description: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Management is supportive: ptosis surgery where indicated, assessment and management of dysphagia including enteral feeding when needed, physiotherapy for weakness and ataxia, and surveillance for bulbar involvement.

steps/1.description: DHDDS forms the catalytic subunit of the heterotetrameric cis-prenyltransferase with the NgBR (NUS1) subunit, which condenses isopentenyl diphosphate onto farnesyl diphosphate to build the polyprenyl diphosphate backbone of dolichol. The RP59 K42E substitution destabilizes the active site, raises the Km for farnesyl diphosphate and lowers kcat, leaving substantial residual activity. DHDDS is expressed ubiquitously and is concentrated in rod and cone inner segments in the human retina.

steps/2.description: The mutant enzyme shifts the dolichol pool toward shorter isoprenologues. In patients dolichol-18 replaces dolichol-19 as the dominant species in plasma and urine, and carriers show an intermediate shift; K42E knock-in mice show the same shortening in retina, liver and brain.

evidence.snippet: Our results suggest that the underlying cause of DHDDS K42E variant driven RP59 retinal pathology is defective synaptic transmission from outer to inner retina.
evidence.explanation: Knock-in model conclusion that motivates this hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: We propose that the physiological basis of retinal dysfunction in RP59 involves defective photoreceptor to bipolar cell synaptic transmission with concomitant bipolar/amacrine cell degeneration.
evidence.explanation: Replicated with the second patient allele, T206A.

hypotheses/2.description: In K42E and T206A knock-in mice the earliest and dominant defect is a reduced ERG b-wave with preserved a-wave, inner nuclear layer thinning and loss of bipolar and amacrine cells, suggesting defective transmission from photoreceptors to the inner retina. A corresponding human signature has not been demonstrated, because most patients already have nondetectable ERGs.

evidence.snippet: These results indicate that RPE dysfunction contributes to DHDDS mutation-mediated pathology and suggests a more complicated disease mechanism than simply disruption of glycosylation.
evidence.explanation: RPE-specific Dhdds ablation produces retinal degeneration.

hypotheses/3.description: Loss of DHDDS in the retinal pigment epithelium is sufficient to cause RPE atrophy and secondary photoreceptor loss in mice, and patients show early macular autofluorescence changes; whether RPE involvement is primary in human RP59 is unresolved, and one patient histology showed relative RPE preservation.

evidence.snippet: RT-PCR analysis in 21 human tissues revealed ubiquitous expression of DHDDS.
evidence.explanation: Ubiquitous expression contrasts with retina-restricted disease.

evidence.snippet: Finally, to date, none of the mouse models have shed light on the reason why RP59 is non-syndromic.
evidence.explanation: The question is explicitly open.

open_questions/0.rationale: DHDDS is expressed in every tissue tested and dolichol chain shortening is measurable in blood, urine, liver and brain, yet systemic involvement has been reported only once. Candidate explanations include photoreceptor demand for dolichol in outer-segment membrane renewal, cell-type differences in residual activity, and genetic modifiers such as ALG6.

evidence.snippet: Retinas of DhddsK42E/K42E mice exhibited grossly normal histological organization from 1 to 12 months of age.
evidence.explanation: The knock-in mouse lacks the human photoreceptor degeneration.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, unlike the human or nonhuman primate retina, the mouse retina lacks a cone-rich macula or fovea.
evidence.explanation: Anatomical basis for the species mismatch.

open_questions/1.rationale: The patient allele in mice reproduces the dolichol shortening but not the defining photoreceptor degeneration, while the human disease is a rod-cone dystrophy with early macular involvement. Mice lack a macula, and a b-wave-selective defect has not been sought in early-stage patients, so the synaptic mechanism may be a mouse feature or an early human feature that is masked by the time ERGs are recorded.

evidence.snippet: reports suggest that premature birth leads to the exposure of immature ocular tissues to high levels of exogenous oxygen and hyperoxia, which increase the synthesis of reactive oxygen species and inhibit HIF expression
evidence.explanation: Review documents the mechanism by which supplemental oxygen suppresses HIF expression and arrests retinal vessel development in Phase 1 ROP.

steps/0.description: After premature birth and exposure to supplemental oxygen, retinal oxygen tension rises above normal fetal levels. Elevated oxygen tension downregulates hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1alpha), suppressing transcription of VEGF-A in Muller glia and astrocytes. The resulting lack of VEGF leads to obliteration or arrest of the normally developing retinal vasculature, leaving the peripheral retina avascular. This phase corresponds to the first weeks after birth.

evidence.snippet: the hypoxia-sensitive retina, causing an overproduction of proangiogenic factors and the development of pathological neovascularization
evidence.explanation: Review documents the HIF-1alpha–VEGF axis driving Phase 2 pathological neovascularization in ROP.

evidence.snippet: the oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) mouse model has gained the most popularity and critically contributed to our current understanding of pathological retinal angiogenesis and the discovery of potential anti-angiogenic therapies
evidence.explanation: OIR mouse model evidence supports VEGF-driven pathological angiogenesis as the key mechanism in Phase 2 ROP.

steps/1.description: As the premature infant matures, the incompletely vascularized retina develops increasing metabolic demand. The avascular peripheral retina becomes hypoxic, stabilizing HIF-1alpha and driving strong upregulation of VEGF-A, erythropoietin, IGF-1, and angiopoietin-2. Excess VEGF triggers pathological neovascularization: new vessels grow beyond the inner limiting membrane into the vitreous. These abnormal vessels are fragile and prone to vitreous hemorrhage. Fibrovascular membrane contraction may cause tractional or exudative retinal detachment. The Norrin/FZD4/LRP5 pathway, which normally guides retinal vessel development, is also disrupted in this context.

evidence.snippet: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a proliferative vascular disease of the retina that poses a significant risk to prematurely born children. If untreated, ROP can lead to retinal detachment, severe visual impairment, and even blindness.
evidence.explanation: Review documents retinal detachment as a major downstream consequence of untreated ROP.

steps/2.description: Tractional or exudative retinal detachment occurring in Stage 4 (partial) or Stage 5 (total) ROP. Major cause of blindness in affected infants.

evidence.snippet: If untreated, ROP can lead to retinal detachment, severe visual impairment, and even blindness.
evidence.explanation: Review documents tractional retinal detachment as a direct downstream consequence of untreated ROP pathological neovascularization.

edges/0.description: Fibrovascular membrane contraction exerts tractional forces on the retina, causing partial or total detachment.

evidence.snippet: Treatment includes laser photocoagulation and intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections, both effective options.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review confirms laser photocoagulation as a standard effective treatment for ROP.

treatments/0.description: Peripheral retinal ablation using diode laser to destroy the avascular peripheral retina and eliminate the hypoxic stimulus driving VEGF production. Standard treatment for threshold and Type 1 ROP (Stage 3+ in Zone I, or Stage 2–3 with plus disease in Zone I, or Stage 3+ with plus disease in Zone II posterior). Highly effective but carries risk of peripheral visual field loss and refractive error.

evidence.snippet: anti-VEGF agents showed a higher risk of recurrence compared to laser photocoagulation (RR=2.14, 95% CI: 1.06-4.33, p=0.03)
evidence.explanation: Meta-analysis of 21 studies (6,152 eyes). The quoted result is a trade-off rather than an efficacy measure: it reports a roughly two-fold HIGHER recurrence risk for anti-VEGF than for laser photocoagulation. It therefore establishes that anti-VEGF is an established, studied treatment modality for ROP and characterises its principal drawback, but it does not evidence anti-VEGF efficacy.

evidence.snippet: Treatment preferences shifted from laser coagulation (46.2% in 2015) to anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy (83.7% in 2022)
evidence.explanation: German national registry documents the shift from laser to anti-VEGF as the dominant ROP treatment modality over 2015–2022.

treatments/1.description: Intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF agents (bevacizumab or ranibizumab) to suppress pathological neovascularization. Preferred over laser for Zone I and posterior Zone II ROP due to better structural outcomes and preservation of peripheral retinal function. Bevacizumab is widely used off-label; ranibizumab (RAINBOW trial) has a pediatric indication in some jurisdictions. Risk of reactivation requires careful follow-up.

evidence.snippet: Studies have indicated that vitrectomy produces better outcomes when performed at an earlier stage (stage 4 vs. stage 5 ROP).
evidence.explanation: Systematic review of 10 studies (1,179 eyes) documents vitrectomy as the surgical intervention for Stage 4 and Stage 5 ROP retinal detachment, with better outcomes in earlier (Stage 4) disease.

treatments/2.description: Scleral buckling and/or vitrectomy for Stage 4–5 ROP. Scleral buckling is preferred for Stage 4; vitrectomy (lens-sparing or lensectomy) for Stage 5. Outcomes are poor for total retinal detachment (Stage 5), with fewer than 30% achieving ambulatory vision.

evidence.snippet: The majority were seropositive and had elevated inflammatory markers.
evidence.explanation: This supports seropositive systemic inflammation as a common context in rheumatoid vasculitis cases.

evidence.snippet: Seropositivity, specific HLA variations, and tobacco use are among the genetic and environmental predictors of rheumatoid vasculitis.
evidence.explanation: This review links seropositivity, HLA variation, and smoking to rheumatoid vasculitis risk.

steps/0.description: Rheumatoid vasculitis arises primarily in severe seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, where rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP antibodies, HLA-associated susceptibility, and tobacco exposure mark an immune context that can support extra-articular vascular disease.

evidence.snippet: Rheumatoid vasculitis (RV) is an unusual complication of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, which is characterized by the development of necrotizing or leukocytoclastic vasculitis involving small or medium-sized vessels.
evidence.explanation: This directly defines rheumatoid vasculitis as necrotizing or leukocytoclastic small- or medium-vessel vasculitis.

evidence.snippet: suggests that immune complex disease may be causative
evidence.explanation: This supports immune-complex biology as a proposed pathogenic mechanism.

steps/1.description: Autoantibody-rich rheumatoid inflammation can drive immune-complex disease and inflammatory cell recruitment in small and medium-sized vessel walls, producing necrotizing or leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

evidence.snippet: Pathologic features of rheumatoid vasculitis include mononuclear cells or neutrophilic infiltration of the vessel wall of small and medium vessels.
evidence.explanation: This supports inflammatory cell infiltration of small and medium vessel walls.

evidence.snippet: Features of vessel wall destruction are often found, including necrosis, leukocytoclasis, and disruption of the internal and external elastic lamina.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports destructive histopathologic vessel-wall injury.

steps/2.description: Involved small and medium vessels show inflammatory infiltration of the vessel wall with destructive changes such as necrosis, leukocytoclasis, and elastic-lamina disruption.

evidence.snippet: we define rheumatoid vasculitis as a clinicopathologic manifestation of RA characterized by tissue damage or ischemia verified pathologically by vasculitis.
evidence.explanation: This links rheumatoid vasculitis to tissue damage or ischemia.

evidence.snippet: It has a vast array of clinical manifestations with a predilection for the skin (peripheral gangrene, deep cutaneous ulcers) and the peripheral nervous system (mononeuritis multiplex).
evidence.explanation: This links ischemic tissue injury to the major skin and peripheral nerve manifestations.

steps/3.description: Vascular inflammation and vessel-wall destruction cause tissue damage or ischemia in affected territories, producing skin ulcers, digital ischemia or necrosis, peripheral neuropathy, and less commonly major internal organ ischemia.

edges/0.description: Seropositive systemic rheumatoid autoimmunity provides immune complexes and cellular immune mechanisms that can target vessel walls.

edges/1.description: Vessel-wall inflammation leads to necrosis, leukocytoclasis, and vascular structural damage.

edges/2.description: Destructive vasculitis compromises blood flow and produces tissue ischemia or organ-specific injury.

evidence.snippet: A recent meta-analysis that compiled 14 studies encompassing more than 1500 RA patients revealed a striking relationship between rheumatoid vasculitis and three specific genotypes of the HLA-DRB1 shared epitope: *0401/*0401, *0401/*0404, and *0101/*0401 [5].
evidence.explanation: This supports HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope genotypes as susceptibility associations.

genes/0.notes: HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope genotypes are associated with rheumatoid vasculitis susceptibility in rheumatoid arthritis, but no deterministic monogenic cause is established.

evidence.snippet: Mild rheumatoid vasculitis involving the skin or peripheral nerves can be treated with prednisone and methotrexate or azathioprine.
evidence.explanation: This review supports prednisone plus methotrexate or azathioprine for milder skin or peripheral nerve disease.

treatments/0.description: Limited or milder disease affecting skin or peripheral nerves may be treated with systemic glucocorticoids plus methotrexate or azathioprine, balancing vasculitis control against treatment toxicity.

evidence.snippet: More serious organ system involvement may require treatment with higher-dose steroids and cyclophosphamide or biologic agents (Table 2).
evidence.explanation: This supports escalation for serious organ involvement.

treatments/1.description: Severe systemic or organ-threatening rheumatoid vasculitis may require higher-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide or biologic therapy.

evidence.snippet: RTX was used for induction therapy in 8 patients (47%), relapsing RV in 4 (24%), second-line therapy in 2 (12%), and salvage therapy or in combination with another agent in 3 (18%).
evidence.explanation: This describes real-world indications for rituximab in systemic RV.

evidence.snippet: Systemic RV is difficult to treat effectively. CR of RV was achieved in 62% and PR in 38% of patients within 12 months of RTX use.
evidence.explanation: This supports rituximab response outcomes while preserving the observational evidence context.

treatments/2.description: Rituximab is used for induction, relapsing, second-line, salvage, or combination therapy in systemic rheumatoid vasculitis, with observational evidence of complete and partial responses within 12 months.

evidence.snippet: The confirmation of the diagnosis of CVT relies on the demonstration of thrombi in the cerebral veins and/or sinuses by MR/MR venography or veno CT.
evidence.explanation: This supports venous or sinus thrombus as the defining anatomic lesion in cerebral venous thrombosis.

steps/0.description: Thrombus in a dural venous sinus, including the superior sagittal sinus, obstructs cerebral venous drainage. The lesion involves intraluminal clot formation in the venous sinus and can propagate or impair cortical venous outflow.

evidence.snippet: The pathophysiology of CVST depends on two interconnected events, local signs due to venous infarct, e.g., hemiparesis and global signs due to raised ICP from an obstructed venous system--papilloedema and isolated intracranial hypertension being one of them.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports venous infarction and raised intracranial pressure as linked pathophysiologic consequences of venous sinus thrombosis.

steps/1.description: Venous outflow obstruction produces two linked injury patterns: focal venous infarction that can cause focal deficits, and global intracranial hypertension from an obstructed venous system, which can cause headache, papilledema, encephalopathy, and reduced consciousness.

evidence.snippet: Compared with those with no seizures, significantly more patients with secondary seizures had hemiplegia (37.50 vs. 15.63%; P = 0.020), bleeding (29.40 vs. 10.81%; P = 0.047), lesions involving the frontal (31.25 vs. 10.81%; P = 0.023) and temporal lobe (43.75 vs. 8.11%; P = 0.005)
evidence.explanation: This clinical cohort supports bleeding and focal lobar lesions in CVST patients with secondary seizures, consistent with hemorrhagic parenchymal injury.

steps/2.description: Sagittal sinus thrombosis can be associated with cortical or lobar lesions and hemorrhage when venous congestion and infarction injure brain parenchyma.

edges/0.description: Obstructed venous drainage causes local venous infarction and global intracranial-pressure effects from impaired venous outflow.

edges/1.description: Venous congestion and infarction can be accompanied by bleeding and lobar parenchymal injury.

evidence.snippet: The main intervention in the acute is anticoagulation with either low molecular weight or unfractionated heparin.
evidence.explanation: This review directly supports heparin anticoagulation as the main acute intervention.

evidence.snippet: We found that LMWH and UH are safe and effective for the management of acute CVT and should be considered first line.
evidence.explanation: This recent treatment review supports low-molecular-weight and unfractionated heparin as first-line acute CVT therapy.

treatments/0.description: Acute treatment uses unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin to limit thrombus extension and support recanalization; longer-term anticoagulation is tailored to thrombotic risk after the acute phase.

evidence.snippet: In patients in severe condition on admission or who deteriorate despite anticoagulation, local thrombolysis or thrombectomy is an option.
evidence.explanation: This supports endovascular therapy only for selected severe or deteriorating patients.

evidence.snippet: Cerebral venous thrombosis is generally treated with anticoagulation. However, some patients do not respond to medical therapy and these might benefit from mechanical thrombectomy.
evidence.explanation: This systematic review supports thrombectomy as a possible option after inadequate response to medical therapy.

treatments/1.description: Local thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy may be considered in selected severe cases or when clinical status deteriorates despite anticoagulation, but evidence remains limited and specialist-center selection is important.

evidence.snippet: Decompressive surgery is life-saving in patients with large venous infarcts or haemorrhage.
evidence.explanation: This supports decompressive surgery for selected life-threatening venous infarction or hemorrhage.

evidence.snippet: Decompressive craniectomy may be used to reduce intracranial pressure in life-threatening cases.
evidence.explanation: This recent treatment review supports decompressive craniectomy for selected life-threatening cases.

treatments/2.description: Decompressive craniectomy may be used in life-threatening cases with large venous infarcts, hemorrhage, or severe intracranial pressure elevation.

evidence.snippet: Common relievers involve cooling methods such as local skin cooling or ice water immersion.
evidence.explanation: Documents cooling as the characteristic reliever, the counterpart of the warming trigger.

evidence.snippet: The erythromelalgia was alleviated during busulfan-induced remissions of thrombocythemia and its recurrence coincided with relapsing thrombocythemia.
evidence.explanation: Remission-and-relapse concordance with the underlying thrombocythemia establishes the MPN as the causal upstream driver rather than a coincidental association.

evidence.snippet: Erythromelalgia is a characteristic thrombotic complication in patients with the myeloproliferative disorders, essential thrombocythemia and polycythemia vera.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the two myeloproliferative neoplasms that constitute the principal underlying disorders of this secondary form. Classified OTHER because this is a narrative minireview summarizing the authors' prior work rather than a report of primary data.

evidence.snippet: Erythromelalgia in thrombocythemia already occurred at slightly increased platelet counts above 400 x 10(9)/l.
evidence.explanation: Symptoms arise at only slightly elevated platelet counts, indicating that qualitative platelet hyperreactivity rather than absolute platelet mass drives the mechanism.

steps/1.description: The upstream trigger of MPN-associated erythromelalgia is the clonal thrombocythemia of essential thrombocythemia or polycythemia vera, which supplies a population of qualitatively abnormal, hyperactivatable platelets. The dependence is causal rather than merely associative: erythromelalgia remits during cytoreduction-induced haematological remission and recurs when the thrombocythemia relapses. Notably the threshold is low — symptoms occur at platelet counts only slightly above normal — so absolute platelet mass is not the determinant. The clonal driver biology itself (JAK2 V617F and the haematopoietic consequences) is curated in `Polycythemia_Vera` and `Essential_Thrombocythemia`.

evidence.snippet: Complete relief of pain and restoration of microvascular circulation disturbances was obtained with the cyclo-oxygenase inhibitors aspirin and indomethacin, but not with sodium-salicylate or the platelet inhibitors dipyridamole, sulfinpyrazone, ticlopidine, and dazoxiben.
evidence.explanation: The pharmacological dissection — COX inhibitors work, other antiplatelet agents do not — establishes cyclooxygenase metabolites as mechanistically necessary.

evidence.snippet: Thus, cyclooxygenase metabolites are necessary for erythromelalgia to develop.
evidence.explanation: States the necessity of cyclooxygenase metabolites explicitly.

evidence.snippet: significant higher levels of platelet activation markers beta-thromboglobulin, thrombomoduline and increased urinary thromboxane B2 excretion in thrombocythemia patients suffering from erythromelalgia
evidence.explanation: Quantifies in vivo platelet activation and thromboxane generation specifically in symptomatic patients.

evidence.snippet: Our data suggest that erythromelalgia is caused by the intravascular activation and aggregation of platelets with subsequent sludging or occlusion of the acral arterial microvasculature.
evidence.explanation: Directly states intravascular platelet activation and aggregation as the causal mechanism.

evidence.snippet: The generation of thrombin appears not to be essential for the formation of these platelet thrombi, thereby giving a plausible explanation for the inefficacy of coumadin derivatives and heparin in the prevention and treatment of erythromelalgia in essential thrombocythemia.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the thrombin-independence of the mechanism — the basis for this entry's deliberate non-conformance to the thrombin/fibrin `thrombogenesis` module.

evidence.snippet: The increased platelet consumption in erythromelalgia is attributed to the formation of platelet thrombi in the arterial microvasculature.
evidence.explanation: Radiolabelled platelet-survival kinetics independently confirm ongoing platelet consumption in microvascular thrombi.

steps/2.description: Circulating MPN platelets undergo intravascular activation and aggregation in the acral microcirculation. The process is strictly cyclooxygenase-metabolite dependent: it is abolished by aspirin and indomethacin but not by sodium salicylate or by non-COX platelet inhibitors (dipyridamole, sulfinpyrazone, ticlopidine, dazoxiben). In vivo activation is measurable as elevated beta-thromboglobulin, platelet factor 4, thrombomodulin, and urinary thromboxane B2, together with a markedly shortened platelet survival time that aspirin normalizes. Critically, thrombin generation is NOT required — prothrombin fragment 1+2 and fibrin degradation products are unchanged, and the lesions develop despite heparin or coumarin anticoagulation.

evidence.snippet: Skin punch biopsy samples taken from the affected areas showed typical arteriolar inflammation, fibromuscular intima proliferation, and thrombotic occlusions.
evidence.explanation: Direct histopathological demonstration of the arteriolar inflammatory and intimal-proliferative lesion in affected skin.

evidence.snippet: the demonstration of arteriolar fibromuscular intimal proliferation and occlusions by platelet-rich thrombi in skin biopsies
evidence.explanation: Independently restates the arteriolar intimal-proliferative and platelet-rich occlusive histopathology.

steps/3.description: Skin punch biopsies taken from erythromelalgic areas show a distinctive arteriolar lesion — inflammation of the arteriolar wall with fibromuscular proliferation of the intima — accompanying the thrombotic occlusions. This inflammatory and proliferative wall response, together with the elevated thrombomodulin indicating endothelial injury, distinguishes the lesion from a bland intraluminal clot and is what makes "platelet-mediated arteriolar inflammation" rather than simple thrombosis the accurate description.

evidence.snippet: Histopathologic and immunohistochemical analysis of biopsies derived from erythromelalgic skin areas of 2 ET patients showed that erythromelalgic thrombi stained positively for von Willebrand factor opposed to only a weak fibrin staining.
evidence.explanation: Immunohistochemistry establishes the VWF-rich, fibrin-poor composition of the occluding thrombi, distinguishing them from conventional fibrin-platelet thrombi.

evidence.snippet: platelet-mediated inflammatory and occlusive arteriolar changes play a part in the etiology of erythromelalgia
evidence.explanation: Summarizes occlusive arteriolar change as the operative lesion in the aetiology of the syndrome.

steps/4.description: The convergent lesion is occlusion of acral arterioles by platelet-rich, von Willebrand factor-positive thrombi with only weak fibrin content. The resulting acral perfusion disturbance is the immediate substrate of the erythromelalgic flare and, if unrelieved, of progressive digital ischemia. The VWF-rich, fibrin-poor composition of these thrombi is the histological counterpart of the biochemical finding that thrombin generation is dispensable.

evidence.snippet: Erythromelalgia often progressed to ischemic acrocyanosis or necrosis in toes or fingers.
evidence.explanation: Documents progression from the reversible flare to fixed acral ischemic tissue loss.

evidence.snippet: Untreated erythromelalgia progressed to acrocyanosis or peripheral ischemia with necrosis in a toe or fingertip in 14 cases.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies ischemic progression in 14 of 50 thrombocythemia patients when erythromelalgia was left untreated.

steps/5.description: When the platelet-mediated occlusive process is not interrupted, the reversible erythromelalgic flare progresses to fixed acral ischemia: acrocyanosis and then frank ischemic necrosis or gangrene of toes or fingertips. This ischemic-progression arm is a mechanistically distinct outcome from the self-inflicted cold-immersion tissue injury that dominates complications in the primary form, and it is the reason MPN-associated erythromelalgia is treated as a thrombotic complication rather than purely a pain syndrome.

evidence.snippet: It is often linked to underlying conditions such as myeloproliferative disorders (e.g., essential thrombocythemia, polycythemia vera), autoimmune diseases, infections, tumors, or medication use
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the acquired etiologies named in this node — autoimmune disease, infection, neoplasia and drug exposure alongside the myeloproliferative neoplasms.

evidence.snippet: if the erythromelalgia was thought to be attributable to another cause such as medications, human immunodeficiency virus, or mushroom poisoning
evidence.explanation: A population-based study's own case definition independently names the drug, infection and toxin routes as recognized non-MPN causes of secondary erythromelalgia.

evidence.snippet: secondary, which is associated with myeloproliferative disorders-related thrombocythemia, polycythemia, collagen-vascular diseases, diabetes mellitus, peripheral neuropathy, autoimmune and infectious diseases, and use of certain medicaments
evidence.explanation: Names the acquired associations modeled by this node — collagen-vascular disease, diabetes mellitus, peripheral neuropathy, autoimmune and infectious disease, and drug exposure — alongside the myeloproliferative route curated separately above.

evidence.snippet: secondary erythromelalgia, which is often associated with underlying medical disorders
evidence.explanation: Establishes the defining feature of the secondary form — association with an underlying medical disorder — as distinct from the genetically defined primary form.

evidence.snippet: Primary erythromelalgia is an autosomal dominant inherited disorder, while secondary is associated with myeloproliferative diseases, among others. In its etiopathogenesis, there are neural and vascular abnormalities that can be combined.
evidence.explanation: The review asserts combined neural and vascular contributions to secondary disease without resolving a specific lesion for the non-MPN routes, which is why this node is curated at deliberately low resolution rather than as a mechanism chain.

evidence.snippet: Secondary erythermalgia: Aspirin resistant and associated with different medical conditions.
evidence.explanation: This is item (c) of the Drenth-Michiels three-way classification, which *defines* its "secondary erythermalgia" category by aspirin resistance rather than reporting resistance as an empirical result. Cited as the nomenclature's own statement of the pharmacological split; because the category is defined by the property, the support for the claim is indirect.

evidence.snippet: We describe a female patient in whom thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura was associated with erythromelalgia.
evidence.explanation: A single case report adding thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura to the acquired associations. Recorded as an association only; one patient does not establish a mechanism.

evidence.snippet: We describe, for the first time, a patient in whom chronic myelogenous leukemia was associated with the development of erythromelalgia
evidence.explanation: Extends the myeloid association beyond polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia to chronic myelogenous leukemia, again on a single case.

steps/6.description:
Beyond the myeloproliferative neoplasms, erythromelalgia is reported secondary to small-fiber peripheral neuropathy, autoimmune connective-tissue disease, and drug exposure. These routes are recognised clinically but are far less mechanistically resolved than the MPN arm: combined neural and vascular abnormalities are invoked rather than a single demonstrated lesion, and critically these forms do NOT share the aspirin responsiveness of the platelet-mediated arm, which is why the historical Drenth-Michiels classification separated aspirin-resistant "secondary erythermalgia" from aspirin-responsive thrombocythemic erythromelalgia. Curated here as a deliberately low-resolution node rather than a speculative mechanism chain, with the one downstream lesion that does have a biopsy correlate — the complement/denervation node below — tagged as an emerging hypothesis rather than asserted.
Two further acquired associations are documented as single reports and are named here rather than modeled: thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, whose own mechanism is diffuse platelet aggregation and which is therefore closer to the platelet arm than to this one, and chronic myelogenous leukemia, which extends the myeloid association beyond the classical polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia pair.

evidence.snippet: Biopsies showed superficial vascular ectasia in association with microvascular C5b-9 and variable upregulation of type I interferon expression in endothelial cells.
evidence.explanation: Direct histopathological demonstration of the complement and type-I-interferon endothelial lesion that defines this node.

evidence.snippet: Histology commonly shows capillary proliferation, swelling of endothelial cells, perivascular edema, and chronic inflammation with sparse lymphocytic infiltrate
evidence.explanation: Recorded as NO_EVIDENCE and kept deliberately: an independent statement of the commonly reported secondary-erythromelalgia histology that names neither complement deposition nor autonomic denervation. It does not refute this node — those findings need C5b-9 and CD56 stains that routine histology omits — but it does show that the lesion curated here is not the established histological description of the acquired routes.

steps/7.description:
The endothelial half of the biopsy lesion proposed for the non-platelet acquired routes. In a dermatopathology series of nine patients biopsied from affected acral skin, the findings were superficial vascular ectasia with microvascular C5b-9 (membrane attack complex) deposition and variable type-I interferon upregulation in endothelial cells. The claim here is about the state of the dermal microvascular endothelium, which is why the scale is `CELLULAR`; the denervation finding from the same biopsies is a separate claim at a different scale and is curated as its own node below rather than bundled in here.
Note what this is *not*: it is not the platelet-rich thrombotic occlusion of the MPN arm. Note also that the ectasia is itself a dilation finding, and so is a candidate account of the warm, hyperemic surface in its own right.
Curated as `PROVISIONAL` deliberately. The series is small (n=9), single-centre and retrospective, its cases were selected by clinical concern for erythromelalgia rather than by aetiology, and it is not stratified into MPN versus non-MPN disease — so it cannot by itself establish that this lesion is specific to the acquired non-platelet routes, and the authors themselves frame it as suggesting rather than demonstrating a dysautonomia syndrome. Its edges are recorded in the `immune_dysautonomic_route` hypothesis group rather than asserted.
It is also not the only histology on record for secondary erythromelalgia. A separate case report describes the commonly reported picture as capillary proliferation, endothelial swelling, perivascular edema and sparse chronic lymphocytic inflammation — naming neither complement deposition nor denervation — and reports its own case as unusual again. Those descriptions are not incompatible with this node (the C5b-9 and CD56 findings require stains that routine histology does not perform), but they are the reason this lesion is curated as one candidate account rather than as the histology of the acquired routes.

evidence.snippet: CD56 stain revealed diminished autonomic innervation of the eccrine coil and arteries, mirroring similar autonomic denervation seen in small fiber neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration of the autonomic denervation this node asserts, and of its correspondence with small-fiber neuropathy, one of the acquired routes named upstream.

steps/8.description:
The neural half of the same biopsy lesion, and the half that gives the route its name. CD56 staining in the same nine-patient series showed diminished autonomic innervation of the eccrine coil and of acral arteries, mirroring the denervation pattern seen in small-fiber neuropathy — which is one of the acquired routes named upstream, and the one this finding connects the entity to. The scale is `TISSUE` because the claim is about the innervation of a tissue compartment rather than the state of a cell type.
This is the finding with the most mechanistic reach in the entity, because arteriovenous shunts are under autonomic control: it is therefore a candidate substrate for the shunting hypothesis recorded in `discussions#av_shunting_vs_occlusion_paradox`. It is a candidate only — the study measured innervation, not perfusion, oxygenation or shunt flow.
Curated as `PROVISIONAL` deliberately. The series is small (n=9), single-centre and retrospective, its cases were selected by clinical concern for erythromelalgia rather than by aetiology, and it is not stratified into MPN versus non-MPN disease — so it cannot by itself establish that this lesion is specific to the acquired non-platelet routes, and the authors themselves frame it as suggesting rather than demonstrating a dysautonomia syndrome. Its edges are recorded in the `immune_dysautonomic_route` hypothesis group rather than asserted.

evidence.snippet: The localized painful burning, redness, and warm congestion in the extremities could be accurately documented with thermography.
evidence.explanation: Describes the flare phenotype and its objective thermographic correlate.

evidence.snippet: Erythromelalgia was localized in the forefoot sole and toes in 28, the fingertips in 9, the handpalm in 2.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the acral, foot-predominant anatomical distribution of attacks in a 50-patient thrombocythemia series.

evidence.snippet: Although erythromelalgia is typically bilateral, it can present unilaterally, especially in secondary cases.
evidence.explanation: Supports asymmetric/unilateral presentation as a feature that clinically distinguishes secondary from the characteristically bilateral primary form.

steps/9.description: The clinical expression is the erythromelalgic attack: localized burning pain with redness and warm congestion of the distal extremities, documentable by thermography, most often in the forefoot sole and toes and less often in the fingertips or palm. Unlike the bilaterally symmetric flares of the primary form, secondary attacks are frequently asymmetric or unilateral, and erythromelalgic "hot spots" on the legs can be misread as superficial thrombophlebitis. No `biological_processes` are bound to this node: the obvious candidate (vasodilation) is not measured by any cited study and would sit awkwardly against this entry's occlusive model, in which the red, warm skin accompanies platelet-rich arteriolar obstruction rather than simple vasodilation.

treatments/0.description:
The mechanism-matched treatment of MPN-associated erythromelalgia. Irreversible inhibition of platelet cyclooxygenase-1 abolishes the thromboxane-dependent platelet activation that drives arteriolar occlusion, producing complete relief of pain, restoration of microvascular circulation, normalization of shortened platelet survival, and fall of platelet-activation markers to normal. This dramatic responsiveness is the therapeutic hallmark separating MPN-associated secondary erythromelalgia from the characteristically aspirin-refractory primary (SCN9A/Nav1.7) form. Safety caveat: at very high platelet counts (roughly >1000-2000 x 10^9/L) thrombocythemia converts to a bleeding diathesis, and aspirin — while still preventing the microcirculatory disturbance — further increases the risk of serious haemorrhage.
Two features sharpen the pharmacology and are worth separating from mere efficacy. First, the response is specific to cyclooxygenase inhibition rather than to anticoagulation as such: the same microvascular complications do not respond to coumadin, are relieved immediately by a 500 mg aspirin loading dose, and do not recur on 50 mg daily maintenance or after the platelet count is normalized. Second, holding the flare off appears to require ongoing inhibition rather than being a one-off cure: erythromelalgia emerged within two weeks of aspirin withdrawal in a patient whose myeloproliferative disorder was in remission and who had been taking aspirin for stroke prophylaxis, and remitted on rechallenge. That is a single observation, and it sits against the older series' description of an aspirin effect that is "curative" once the platelet count is controlled; the two are reconcilable only if what is cured is the flare and not the substrate.

hypotheses/0.description:
Proposes that the acquired routes outside the myeloproliferative neoplasms reach the erythromelalgic flare through complement-mediated microvascular injury and autonomic denervation of acral skin, rather than through the platelet-thromboxane pathway that accounts for the MPN arm. If it holds, it explains the entity's most durable clinical puzzle — why the non-thrombocythemic acquired forms are aspirin resistant while the MPN arm is abolished by cyclooxygenase inhibition — and it would make complement- or interferon-directed therapy a rational target in refractory disease.
It rests on a single retrospective nine-patient dermatopathology series and is therefore recorded as EMERGING, not as an alternative model of equal standing to the platelet mechanism. Note the limit precisely: that series was assembled by clinical concern for erythromelalgia and is not stratified primary versus secondary, let alone MPN versus non-MPN, and its own conclusion is pitched at erythromelalgia in general. So the restriction of this route to the non-MPN acquired forms is part of the hypothesis being advanced here, not an observation carried over from the source. What is missing is replication in an independent, larger biopsy cohort with quantitative C5b-9 and type-I interferon scoring and intraepidermal nerve-fibre density, stratified by MPN versus non-MPN aetiology. Until then the edges in this group are hypothesis-tagged rather than asserted.

evidence.snippet: A wide variety of etiological conditions can cause erythromelalgia, all having a single common pathogenetic mechanism - microvascular arteriovenous shunting.

This 2004 review asserts shunting as the SINGLE common mechanism across all erythromelalgia, which the SCN9A/Nav1.7 findings curated in `Primary_Erythermalgia` contradict.

evidence.explanation: Establishes the occlusive half of the paradox — the demonstrated lesion in MPN-associated disease is microvascular occlusion, which is what makes the warm, hyperemic surface appearance require an explanation.

open_questions/0.rationale:
This entry's occlusive model has an unresolved surface paradox. The demonstrated lesion is arteriolar obstruction by platelet-rich thrombi, which should reduce perfusion — yet the defining clinical sign is a red, warm, congested extremity, and the flare node above therefore deliberately binds no `vasodilation` process rather than assert a mechanism it cannot evidence.

The classical reconciliation is microvascular arteriovenous shunting: blood bypasses the nutritive capillary bed through shunts, so the skin is simultaneously hyperemic and warm at the surface while the tissue itself is hypoxic. That model is asserted in the older review literature (PMID:15075045) but, critically, is asserted there as a *single common mechanism for all* erythromelalgia — a claim the later Nav1.7 channelopathy findings contradict, and which the umbrella `erythromelalgia` entry already cites with the same caveat. The deep-research report for this entry describes the same shunting model with a low-transcutaneous-oxygen correlate, but its only source there is a textbook chapter with no PMID and no quotable passage, so it cannot be curated as an evidence-backed pathophysiology node.

Since that gap was first recorded, one half of the question has acquired a candidate answer. The dermatopathology series behind `pathophysiology#Autonomic Denervation of Acral Arteries and Eccrine Glands` reports loss of autonomic innervation of acral *arteries* alongside vascular ectasia — which is a plausible substrate for shunting, since arteriovenous shunts are under autonomic control. It would bear on the second half of the prompt above, the non-platelet routes, *if* that series' patients were in fact non-MPN, which it does not establish: the cases were unstratified by aetiology. It does not close the gap on any reading — no perfusion or oxygenation was measured, and it is a single n=9 study — so this is a lead for the experiment below, not a resolution. Worth noting too that the same series reports superficial vascular *ectasia*, which is itself a dilation finding and may be a more parsimonious reading of the warm, hyperemic surface than shunting.

What would settle it: paired measurements in *aetiologically stratified* patients — laser Doppler skin blood flow and transcutaneous oxygen tension during a flare, in MPN-associated versus non-MPN secondary disease. Until then this entry models only what the histopathology and platelet kinetics directly demonstrate, and records the shunting hypothesis here rather than promoting it to a node.

open_questions/1.rationale:
Two incompatible nomenclatures are in circulation. The historical Drenth-Michiels scheme is three-way and defined by aspirin responsiveness: (a) aspirin-responsive erythromelalgia in thrombocythemia, (b) aspirin-resistant primary erythermalgia, (c) aspirin-resistant "secondary erythermalgia" associated with other medical conditions. Under that scheme, MPN-associated disease is NOT "secondary". Contemporary usage is instead a two-way primary/secondary split that places MPN-associated disease squarely within "secondary" — the Olmsted County population study classified patients as secondary precisely when they had a coexisting myeloproliferative disorder, and a 2025 systematic review lists myeloproliferative disorders first among the conditions secondary EM is linked to. This entry follows that contemporary usage and models the MPN platelet arm as the principal, best-evidenced secondary mechanism, while retaining the non-MPN routes as a separate, deliberately low-resolution node.

THE GAP, stated precisely: which of the two senses MONDO:0035149 itself intends is NOT established here. Its only synonym is "Secondary erythermalgia" EXACT [Orphanet:529864] — i.e. Orphanet's label is the very term the historical narrow scheme used for the aspirin-RESISTANT non-MPN category. No Orphanet definition row was quotable at curation time (the Orphadata bulk XML was not available locally), so this entry's scope decision rests on contemporary clinical/epidemiological usage rather than on a cited ontology definition. Resolving it needs `just structured-rebuild-orphanet --id 529864` and a quoted `ORPHA:529864` definition row. Curators reading the older literature should meanwhile note that "secondary erythermalgia" there means something narrower than this entry's scope, which is also why `synonyms:` carries that string only because MONDO lists it as an exact synonym of MONDO:0035149, and not as an endorsement of the historical narrower reading; "platelet-mediated erythromelalgia" is deliberately NOT listed as a synonym, because it names the MPN arm alone and would make the same mistake in the other direction, and that the aspirin-responsiveness contrast is therefore a contrast between the MPN arm and everything else, not between "secondary" and "primary" as such.

steps/10.description: The unifying upstream lesion of Senior-Loken syndrome is dysfunction of the ciliary base. The nephrocystin proteins encoded by the SLSN genes localize to the transition zone of renal and respiratory cilia and to the photoreceptor connecting cilium, where they gate ciliary membrane composition and bidirectional cargo transport. Loss of these proteins produces a structurally present but functionally incompetent cilium that cannot correctly compartmentalize signaling and phototransduction machinery, biasing the downstream phenotype toward the renal tubule and the photoreceptor. The ten genes bound here are not all transition-zone proteins in the strict sense: they span the transition zone itself, the distal appendages that anchor it (CEP164), and the intraflagellar transport machinery that moves cargo through it (WDR19 in IFT-A, TRAF3IP1 in IFT-B). They are grouped at this one node because each defect produces the same functional outcome - a structurally present cilium that cannot gate its own membrane or cargo - which is what the three biological processes recorded here describe.

evidence.snippet: Nephronophthisis is a recessive disorder of the kidney that is the leading cause of end-stage renal failure in children.

steps/11.description: Renal tubular epithelial cells use the primary cilium as a flow and signaling sensor that maintains tubular architecture. Ciliary dysfunction produces the nephronophthisis phenotype: a chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy with corticomedullary cysts, tubular basement membrane disruption, and interstitial fibrosis that progresses to end-stage renal disease, typically in childhood or adolescence. Nephronophthisis is the leading genetic cause of end-stage renal failure in children.

evidence.snippet: Ten percent of affected individuals have retinitis pigmentosa, constituting the renal-retinal Senior-Loken syndrome (SLSN).

steps/12.description: Photoreceptor outer segments are specialized non-motile sensory cilia connected to the cell body by the connecting cilium, through which all phototransduction cargo is trafficked. In Senior-Loken syndrome, nephrocystin dysfunction at the connecting cilium impairs outer-segment morphogenesis and maintenance, causing progressive photoreceptor death and a retinitis pigmentosa-like retinal dystrophy. Retinal involvement is highly penetrant and is the feature that distinguishes Senior-Loken syndrome from isolated nephronophthisis.

evidence.snippet: Humans are the only natural reservoir and an inoculum of only 10-100 organisms is required for infection
evidence.explanation: Highlights the extraordinary efficiency of Shigella invasion, demonstrating that the T3SS-mediated invasion mechanism is highly optimized for intracellular entry

steps/2.description: Shigella uses a plasmid-encoded Type III secretion system (T3SS/mxi-spa) to deliver bacterial effector proteins directly into host cells. The translocon proteins IpaB and IpaC assemble a funnel-shaped pore in target membranes through which the injectisome docks and delivers effectors. IpaC activates small GTPases and actin nucleation to promote bacterial uptake. IpaB mediates phagosomal membrane disruption and directly activates caspase-1 in macrophages, triggering pyroptotic cell death. This allows bacterial escape from the phagolysosome into the cytosol, where Shigella replicates and spreads.

evidence.snippet: destruction and inflammation of the colonic epithelium accompanied by acute diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain
evidence.explanation: Describes the characteristic tissue damage phenotype resulting from Shigella's actin-based cell-to-cell spread and mucosal invasion

steps/3.description: Within the host cell cytosol, Shigella recruits the host actin polymerization machinery via the polar adhesin IcsA/VirG. The N-WASP (WASL) and Arp2/3 complex are recruited to the bacterial pole, forming actin comet tails that propel the pathogen toward and through the cell membrane into adjacent cells. IcsP regulates IcsA surface distribution; IcsB aids in autophagy evasion. This cell-to-cell spread mechanism drives epithelial fenestration, mucosal ulceration, and the characteristic invasive colitis phenotype without exposure to the lumen.

evidence.snippet: In the colon, they secrete virulence factors that cause severe inflammation and mediate enterotoxic effects, enabling colonization and invasion of the colonic epithelium
evidence.explanation: Establishes inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis and cytokine release as central to Shigella pathogenesis

steps/4.description: Cytosolic detection of Shigella T3SS components (MxiH, MxiI) and other danger signals activates the NAIP/NLRC4 inflammasome complex. Non-canonical inflammasome sensing via caspase-4/5 detects cytosolic lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Both pathways converge on caspase-1 and caspase-4/5 activation, which cleave gasdermin D (GSDMD) to form membrane pores, leading to pyroptotic cell death, cytokine release (IL-1β, IL-18, IL-8), and recruitment of neutrophils. Shigella modulates this response via IpaH family E3 ligases (e.g., IpaH7.8) to favor bacterial survival and dissemination.

steps/5.description: Shigella species, particularly S. dysenteriae, produce Shiga toxins (Stx) which inhibit protein synthesis in host cells via ribosome inactivation. steps/0.description: Sustained antigenic drive selects and expands marginal zone B cells of the splenic white pulp. Two independent lines of evidence point to a specific, non-random antigen rather than a random founding event: strongly biased immunoglobulin heavy-chain variable gene usage, with a large fraction of cases using IGHV1-2, and an epidemiological and therapeutic association with chronic hepatitis C virus infection. A stereotyped receptor repertoire implies that the founding clone is chosen by its antigen-binding specificity, placing SMZL alongside MALT lymphoma in the family of inflammation-associated, antigen-driven B-cell neoplasms.

steps/1.description: SMZL is genetically defined by lesions in the very program that specifies marginal zone B cells and holds them quiescent. NOTCH2 signaling is required for marginal zone B-cell development, and recurrent truncating mutations clustered in the C-terminal PEST degron eliminate the degradation signal, stabilizing the activated protein and producing a sustained differentiation cue. KLF2, a transcription factor that restrains NF-kB and NOTCH output in mature B cells, is recurrently inactivated, removing that brake. Deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7 is the most frequent cytogenetic abnormality in the disease. Mutations in additional NOTCH-pathway members and in other pathways governing marginal zone development affect a majority of cases. This constellation is the mechanistic signature separating SMZL from MALT lymphoma, which reaches a comparable endpoint through BCL10-MALT1 translocations instead.

evidence.snippet: NF-κB, NOTCH, or B-cell receptor (BCR) pathway genes were implicated in samples from 16 of 18 patients (89%).
evidence.explanation: Whole-exome sequencing of marginal zone lymphoma shows the NF-kB, NOTCH, and B-cell receptor pathways are involved in the large majority of cases.

evidence.snippet: given the availability of drugs that can target NOTCH, NF-κB, and other pathways deregulated in this disease
evidence.explanation: Identifies NF-kB as one of the pathways deregulated in SMZL and therapeutically targetable; indirect support since the paper's primary finding concerns NOTCH2.

steps/2.description: Recurrent mutations in regulators of the NF-kB pathway, most notably TNFAIP3 which encodes the negative regulator A20, converge with KLF2 loss and stabilized NOTCH2 to drive constitutive nuclear NF-kB activity. This is the shared effector node across marginal zone lymphomas: MALT lymphoma reaches it through the BCL10-MALT1 translocations, SMZL through mutation of the same pathway's regulators. Sequencing of marginal zone lymphoma treated with a BTK inhibitor found NF-kB, NOTCH, or B-cell receptor pathway genes involved in the large majority of cases, confirming that these three inputs form one convergent signaling module. Constitutive NF-kB output sustains proliferation and suppresses apoptosis without continued antigenic stimulation, which is why advanced disease no longer regresses when the antigenic driver is removed.

evidence.snippet: It presents with marked splenomegaly.
evidence.explanation: Confirms marked splenomegaly as the characteristic presentation produced by splenic infiltration.

evidence.snippet: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma (SMZL), the most common primary lymphoma of spleen, is poorly understood at the genetic level.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the spleen as the defining primary site of disease involvement.

evidence.snippet: SLVL is a chronic B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by splenomegaly and the presence, in peripheral blood, of lymphocytes with "villous' projections.
evidence.explanation: A 100-patient clinical series defines the disease by the pairing of splenomegaly with circulating villous lymphocytes, the two consequences of splenic infiltration and spillover.

steps/3.description: The lymphoma clone expands the splenic white pulp in a characteristic micronodular pattern, effacing normal follicular architecture and spilling into the red pulp. The enlarging spleen sequesters and destroys circulating blood cells, producing cytopenias out of proportion to marrow reserve. Marrow involvement is reported in nodular, interstitial, and intrasinusoidal patterns, and the tumor cells circulate as villous lymphocytes, the feature that gave the disease its older name of splenic lymphoma with villous lymphocytes. Because a substantial share of the cytopenia is mechanical, removing the spleen historically corrected the blood counts without eradicating the lymphoma.

evidence.snippet: immune mediated paraneoplastic phenomena such as autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA), autoimmune thrombocytopenia (ITP) and C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency are relatively common
evidence.explanation: Establishes autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia as common immune-mediated paraneoplastic phenomena in SMZL.

steps/4.description: Anemia and thrombocytopenia in SMZL arise from two superimposed mechanisms: mechanical sequestration by the enlarged spleen, and true autoimmune destruction. The lymphoma clone and the dysregulated B-cell compartment around it generate autoantibodies, so autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia are recognized paraneoplastic complications rather than incidental findings. This dual mechanism matters clinically because it separates patients whose counts respond to splenectomy or to lymphoma-directed therapy from those who require immunosuppression.

edges/3.description: Splenic sequestration combines with lymphoma-associated autoantibody production to produce anemia and thrombocytopenia.

Because NOTCH2 is required for marginal zone B-cell development, this is a lesion in the lineage-identity program itself. NOTCH2 mutation is restricted to SMZL among indolent B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders, giving it diagnostic value.

genes/1.notes: KLF2 is the most frequently mutated gene in SMZL. It is a transcription factor that restrains NF-kB and NOTCH signaling in mature B cells; inactivation removes this brake and promotes nuclear NF-kB accumulation. Note that the mechanistic characterisation rests on murine knockout B cells, so the human mechanism is inferred from a model system even though the mutation frequency itself is human.

evidence.snippet: MYD88, TNFAIP3, and KMT2D mutations correlate with PFS in patients with relapsed/refractory MZL treated with zanubrutinib.
evidence.explanation: Shows TNFAIP3 is prognostically relevant under BTK inhibition; marked PARTIAL because the cohort spans marginal zone lymphoma subtypes rather than SMZL specifically.

genes/2.notes: TNFAIP3 encodes A20, a negative regulator of NF-kB, and is mutated in 7-15% of SMZL. Specificity caveat: the mutation frequency is SMZL-specific, but the mechanistic claim that loss of A20 releases the NF-kB cascade is extrapolated. The source review states the functional consequence was shown "in other NHLs", and the supporting BTK-inhibitor cohort spans marginal zone lymphoma subtypes rather than SMZL alone. The driver role in SMZL specifically should be treated as probable rather than demonstrated.

genes/3.notes: Deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7, most often 7q31-32, is the single most frequent recurrent lesion in SMZL, more common than any individual point-mutated gene. No gene_term is bound because the lesion is a multi-gene chromosomal region rather than a single gene; the minimally deleted region removes both coding genes and microRNAs, and no single driver within it has been established. Together with IGHV1-2*04 usage it is one of the two strongest diagnostic pointers for SMZL.

treatments/0.description: Asymptomatic patients with low-risk disease can be managed expectantly. A prospective study of a risk-adapted strategy found observation to be the best approach for the lowest-risk group, making watchful waiting an evidence-based option rather than merely a default.

treatments/1.description: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, now the preferred first-line therapy for symptomatic SMZL. In a prospective multicenter series, rituximab-containing arms achieved a higher overall response rate than splenectomy.

evidence.snippet: Splenectomy remains one of the first-line options in patients fit for surgery.

It corrects the mechanical cytopenias and relieves mass effect but does not eradicate the lymphoma, and has been largely superseded by rituximab on response-rate grounds.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Splenectomy removes the sequestering organ, correcting the mechanical component of the cytopenias.

evidence.snippet: Interferon and ribavirin based treatment proved to be successful in small case series of hepatitis C virus associated splenic lymphoma with villous lymphocytes, therefore, it is suggested that antiviral treatment could be an alternative to chemo-immunotherapy.
evidence.explanation: Documents lymphoma response to antiviral therapy in hepatitis C virus-associated splenic lymphoma with villous lymphocytes.

evidence.snippet: The association between hepatitis C virus and certain B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas, such as marginal zone lymphomas, is supported by epidemiological studies.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the epidemiological basis for the hepatitis C virus association that makes antiviral therapy rational.

treatments/3.description: In hepatitis C virus-associated SMZL, therapy directed at the virus rather than at the lymphoma can induce hematologic response. This is the splenic counterpart of Helicobacter pylori eradication in gastric MALT lymphoma and is the strongest therapeutic evidence for the antigen-driven model of marginal zone lymphomagenesis.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Clearing the virus removes the chronic antigenic drive sustaining the clone, the same logic as Helicobacter pylori eradication in gastric MALT lymphoma.

evidence.snippet: MYD88, TNFAIP3, and KMT2D mutations correlate with PFS in patients with relapsed/refractory MZL treated with zanubrutinib.
evidence.explanation: Establishes zanubrutinib use in relapsed or refractory marginal zone lymphoma and links NF-kB pathway genotype to progression-free survival.

evidence.snippet: NF-κB, NOTCH, or B-cell receptor (BCR) pathway genes were implicated in samples from 16 of 18 patients (89%).
evidence.explanation: Provides the mechanistic rationale for BTK inhibition by showing B-cell receptor and NF-kB pathway involvement in the large majority of cases.

treatments/4.description: BTK inhibitors block B-cell receptor signal transmission upstream of NF-kB. Zanubrutinib is used for relapsed or refractory marginal zone lymphoma after anti-CD20 therapy, and mutations in NF-kB pathway genes are associated with the response.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: BTK inhibition interrupts B-cell receptor signal transmission into the NF-kB pathway.

evidence.snippet: We tested the hypothesis that a further condition, Spondylo-epiphyseal dysplasia (SED), Maroteaux type (MIM 184095; also known as pseudo-Morquio syndrome type 2), could be caused by TRPV4 mutations.
evidence.explanation: Establishes TRPV4 as the tested and confirmed causal gene for SEDM.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that SED Maroteaux type and parastremmatic dysplasia are part of the TRPV4 dysplasia family and that TRPV4 mutations show considerable variability in phenotypic expression resulting in distinct clinical-radiographic phenotypes.
evidence.explanation: Supports membership in the TRPV4 dysplasia family, but only partially supports a variant-specific mechanism: the authors attribute the distinct phenotypes to variable expression rather than to distinct variant effects.

steps/1.description: Heterozygous missense variants in TRPV4 alter the gating of a calcium-permeable mechanosensitive cation channel in chondrocytes. Several of the variants found in SEDM patients are the same substitutions reported in metatropic dysplasia, so the variant alone does not determine which phenotype in the TRPV4 family results.

evidence.snippet: The known variant phenotypes are spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia Maroteaux type (Pseudo-Morquio type 2), parastremmatic dysplasia, and
evidence.explanation: Places SEDM among the recognized TRPV4 bone dysplasia phenotypes, whose shared substrate is the growth plate. Note this source calls it a variant phenotype that deviates from the general pattern, which the GeneReviews item below reads differently.

evidence.snippet: The five autosomal dominant skeletal dysplasias are (from mildest to most severe) familial digital arthropathy with brachydactyly, brachyolmia, spondylometaphyseal dysplasia (Kozlowski type), spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia (Maroteaux type), and metatropic dysplasia.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews TRPV4 chapter places SEDM as a severity tier between Kozlowski and metatropic dysplasia, rather than as a deviating variant. Graded PARTIAL and OTHER because it is a review chapter's ordering, not an experimental result, and because it conflicts with PMID:22791502 on exactly this point.

evidence.snippet: All TRPV4-related skeletal dysplasias are characterized by brachydactyly; the four most severe forms have short stature that varies from mild to severe with progressive spinal deformity and involvement of the long bones and pelvis.
evidence.explanation: Describes the observed human clinical features shared across the TRPV4 skeletal dysplasias, including the progressive spinal deformity and long-bone involvement seen in SEDM. Graded HUMAN_CLINICAL rather than OTHER: this is a clinical-characteristics statement about patients, and the sibling Kozlowski entry grades the same chapter the same way. The nosology-ordering item above stays OTHER, since that is a classification judgement rather than an observation.

evidence.snippet: skeletal dysplasia associated with TRPV4 pathogenic variants share some clinical features such as short stature with short trunk, spinal and pelvic changes with varying degrees of long bone involvement
evidence.explanation: An independent cohort description of the shared TRPV4 skeletal-dysplasia features, previously cited only in notes prose.

steps/2.description: Disturbed chondrocyte differentiation in the vertebral and epiphyseal growth plates produces the characteristic platyspondyly and epiphyseal dysplasia. The mechanistic detail linking TRPV4 channel dysfunction to the specific Maroteaux-type radiographic pattern — as opposed to the Kozlowski or metatropic patterns — has not been established.

evidence.snippet: Platyspondylysis is present but there are no anterior tongue-like deformities of the vertebral bodies.
evidence.explanation: Documents the platyspondyly and the specific radiographic feature that distinguishes it from Morquio syndrome.

steps/3.description: Generalized platyspondyly without the anterior tongue-like vertebral deformity of Morquio syndrome. A tissue-level structural outcome of the disordered growth plate, kept separate from the organism-level stature deficit it contributes to.

evidence.snippet: All TRPV4-related skeletal dysplasias are characterized by brachydactyly; the four most severe forms have short stature that varies from mild to severe with progressive spinal deformity and involvement of the long bones and pelvis.
evidence.explanation: Graded PARTIAL: this establishes the short stature and names both the spinal and long-bone contributions across the TRPV4 dysplasias as a group, without apportioning them for SEDM specifically.

steps/4.description: Disproportionate short stature with a short trunk, not evident at birth and becoming apparent in childhood. Vertebral flattening supplies the trunk component; GeneReviews records long-bone involvement in the four more severe TRPV4 skeletal dysplasias, so the vertebrae are not the sole contributor.

evidence.snippet: The cases of four patients who had an unusual clinical entity of disproportionately short stature, referred to as spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia of Maroteaux, are described.
evidence.explanation: Short stature is the presenting feature in the original patient series.

steps/5.description: Disproportionate short-trunk short stature, not present at birth and recognized during childhood.

evidence.snippet: Platyspondylysis is present but there are no anterior tongue-like deformities of the vertebral bodies.
evidence.explanation: Directly documents platyspondyly and its distinguishing radiographic form.

steps/6.description: Flattening of the vertebral bodies without anterior tongue-like deformities.

edges/1.description: Altered chondrocyte calcium handling disrupts the ordered proliferation and hypertrophy of growth plate chondrocytes.

edges/2.description: Failure of normal vertebral body growth produces flattened vertebrae.

edges/3.description: The vertebral flattening is what the platyspondyly phenotype records.

edges/4.description: Loss of vertebral height is the trunk-shortening component of the stature deficit.

edges/5.description: This node is what the disproportionate short stature phenotype records.

evidence.snippet: All six patients were found to have heterozygous TRPV4 mutations; three patients had unreported mutations, while three patients had mutations previously described in association with metatropic dysplasia.
evidence.explanation: Establishes TRPV4 as causal in 6/6 tested patients and documents the genotype-phenotype overlap with metatropic dysplasia.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous missense variants in TRPV4 cause SEDM. Notably, some SEDM patients carry substitutions previously reported in metatropic dysplasia, so genotype does not cleanly predict which TRPV4 skeletal phenotype occurs.

evidence.snippet: For skeletal dysplasias, annual evaluation for joint pain and scoliosis; assessment for odontoid hypoplasia before a child reaches school age and before surgical procedures involving general anesthesia; annual hearing assessment; and assessment of weight, height, and weight-for-height at each visit.
evidence.explanation: States the odontoid assessment and its pre-anaesthetic timing.

treatments/0.description: Assessment for odontoid hypoplasia before school age and before any procedure requiring general anaesthesia. This is the clinically actionable item in this entry: undetected odontoid hypoplasia turns routine airway positioning into a cervical-cord risk.

evidence.snippet: For skeletal dysplasias, avoid extreme neck flexion and extension (in those with odontoid hypoplasia); activities that place undue stress on the spine and weight-bearing joints.
evidence.explanation: The agents-and-circumstances-to-avoid recommendation for the skeletal dysplasias.

treatments/1.description: Avoid extreme neck flexion and extension where odontoid hypoplasia is present, and activities loading the spine and weight-bearing joints.

evidence.explanation: States the physical therapy and heel cord stretching recommendation.

treatments/3.description: Surgical intervention when kyphoscoliosis compromises pulmonary function or causes pain, or when upper cervical instability or cervical myelopathy are present.

evidence.snippet: For skeletal dysplasias, annual evaluation for joint pain and scoliosis; assessment for odontoid hypoplasia before a child reaches school age and before surgical procedures involving general anesthesia; annual hearing assessment; and assessment of weight, height, and weight-for-height at each visit.
evidence.explanation: States the surveillance schedule for the skeletal dysplasias.

open_questions/0.rationale: The deep-research report for this entry lists these three alongside the features now curated, but traces every one of them to a single secondary source, the Orphanet clinical description. Orphanet is a citable structured source in this repository, but the Maroteaux-type record is not in references_cache/ and the bulk Orphadata rebuild is currently blocked by a manifest checksum mismatch (dismech#9687), so no quotable row exists. They are recorded here rather than curated so the entry's narrower phenotype list is a stated scoping decision rather than an unexplained omission. The 2004 case report does describe "small and square iliac wings, short femoral necks", which is pelvic and would support the first of the three once a suitable HPO binding is settled.

evidence.snippet: Specific phenotype, age of onset, and disease severity cannot be accurately predicted because of reduced penetrance and highly variable expressivity.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states the unpredictability prospectively for the whole TRPV4 family, which reframes the shared-variant observation in PMID:20503319 as a recognized property of these disorders rather than an artefact of one six-patient series. That is what makes this a genuine open question about mechanism rather than a sampling complaint.

open_questions/1.rationale: PMID:20503319 reports that three of six SEDM patients carried substitutions previously described in metatropic dysplasia. This breaks the usual assumption that a channelopathy's severity tracks the variant's functional effect, and means the pathophysiology node above cannot currently be annotated with a variant-specific gain- or loss-of-function claim. Modifier alleles, mosaicism, and genetic background are all untested explanations.

open_questions/2.rationale: Management is entirely supportive and orthopedic — see treatments:, which carries the GeneReviews physical therapy, surgical, surveillance and agents-to-avoid recommendations. No trial or cohort evidence for a disease-modifying therapy, or for TRPV4 channel modulation altering skeletal outcome, was found for this entity. An earlier version of this rationale opened by saying no treatments section was curated. That was true when the gap was written and false by the time it was read: the same commit that added the five treatments left this sentence untouched.

evidence.snippet: Affected family members were found to have a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in COL9A2, c.843_c.846 + 4del8.
evidence.explanation: The founding COL9A2 allele and its loss-of-function character.

steps/1.description: Biallelic loss-of-function variants — frameshift, splice-disrupting deletion — abolish the alpha-2 chain of collagen IX. Reported alleles include c.843_846+4del8, which removes an exon-intron boundary, and c.1332del.

evidence.snippet: Together the data from the present study and the previous studies suggest that loss-of-function mutations in any of the collagen IX genes can cause autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the disease follows loss of the heterotrimer rather than of a chain-specific function, which is what this node claims.

steps/2.description: Without the alpha-2 chain, functional collagen IX is not formed. Collagen IX is a FACIT collagen that sits on the surface of collagen II fibrils and mediates their interaction with the surrounding matrix, so its absence is felt wherever a collagen II fibril network has to be spaced and stabilised — principally the vitreous gel and hyaline cartilage.

evidence.snippet: All patients were highly myopic with congenital megalophthalmos and abnormal, hypoplastic vitreous gel
evidence.explanation: The vitreous and globe phenotype, present in every patient of the type IX series.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, we demonstrate reduced macular and overall retinal function explaining the reduced visual acuity in patients with Stickler syndrome also without retinal complications.
evidence.explanation: Electrophysiological evidence that retinal function is impaired independently of detachment, which is a claim about the tissue rather than about a complication.

steps/3.description: The vitreous is hypoplastic with abnormal architecture, and the globe is enlarged with high axial myopia. Unlike the dominant forms, which each have a characteristic membranous or beaded vitreous phenotype, the type IX vitreous is described simply as hypoplastic and abnormal. Retinal function is measurably reduced on electroretinography even where the macula looks structurally normal, which is the finding that explains visual acuity loss in these patients without retinal complications.

evidence.snippet: No patients had cleft palate, and 30.8% had midfacial hypoplasia.
evidence.explanation: The craniofacial phenotype quantified in the national cohort, including the negative cleft palate finding.

evidence.snippet: Arthropathy was uncommon but variable in manifestation.
evidence.explanation: The joint phenotype in the same cohort, quoted separately because the two findings are not adjacent sentences in the source.

evidence.snippet: Cleft palate is associated with type XI collagen variants, as well as the non-collagen genes, but is so far unreported with type IX collagen variants.
evidence.explanation: States the gene-specific absence of cleft palate, which is the cleanest single discriminator between the type IX and type XI recessive forms.

steps/4.description: Collagen IX loss in hyaline cartilage produces a markedly milder skeletal and orofacial phenotype than the dominant collagen II and XI Sticklers. Midface hypoplasia is present in a minority, arthropathy is uncommon and variable, and cleft palate — a defining feature of the collagen XI forms — has not been reported in a type IX patient at all. Short stature was described in the founding family.

evidence.snippet: Hearing loss was more prevalent (91.7%) than in dominant SS.
evidence.explanation: The quantified comparison with the dominant forms, from the largest type IX cohort.

evidence.snippet: We suggest that COL9A1, COL9A2, and COL9A3 be added to genetic screening panels for patients with congenital hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: The practical consequence the authors draw from the hearing phenotype.

steps/5.description: Sensorineural hearing loss is near-universal and more severe than in the dominant forms, typically with a down-sloping high-frequency audiogram.
