The step from collagen IX loss to cochlear dysfunction is not mechanistically worked out in humans; what is established is the epidemiology, and it is strong enough that the literature recommends adding COL9A1, COL9A2 and COL9A3 to congenital hearing loss gene panels.

evidence.snippet: High myopia is near-universal, and sensorineural hearing loss is very common in patients with variants in genes for type IX or XI collagen
evidence.explanation: The review's synthesis across all published recessive Stickler patients.

steps/6.description: High myopia is present in essentially every reported patient and is usually the first ocular sign, accompanying congenital enlargement of the globe.

evidence.snippet: Clinical findings included abnormal vitreous architecture and high myopia.
evidence.explanation: The vitreous finding in the national cohort.

steps/7.description: The vitreous gel is hypoplastic with abnormal architecture. In recessive Stickler syndrome it is not assigned to the membranous or beaded categories used to subclassify the dominant forms.

evidence.snippet: Both brothers have severe sensorineural hearing loss with down-sloping audiograms but only subtle midface hypoplasia and no, or mild joint problems.
evidence.explanation: Audiometric characterisation in COL9A2 patients specifically, alongside the mildness of the non-ocular features.

evidence.snippet: Hearing loss was more prevalent (91.7%) than in dominant SS.
evidence.explanation: Frequency in the largest type IX cohort.

steps/8.description: Severe sensorineural hearing loss with a down-sloping audiogram, more prevalent and more severe than in dominant Stickler syndrome. It is the feature most likely to bring a child to attention first.

evidence.snippet: 15.4% of patients developed RD secondary to horseshoe retinal tears, with no cases of bilateral RD or giant retinal tears (GRTs).
evidence.explanation: The rate and the tear morphology together, which is what distinguishes this from the type 1 detachment risk.

evidence.snippet: Retinal detachment has occurred in 18% of all cases, and joint pain in 15%.
evidence.explanation: An independent figure from the review of all recessive Stickler cases, close to the national cohort's 15.4%.

steps/9.description: Retinal detachment occurs but at a much lower rate than in type 1 Stickler syndrome, and with a different mechanism: horseshoe tears rather than giant retinal tears, and no bilateral cases in the national cohort. This is the single most consequential difference between STL5 and the dominant forms, because giant-tear detachment is what prophylactic retinopexy exists to prevent.

evidence.snippet: No patients had cleft palate, and 30.8% had midfacial hypoplasia.
evidence.explanation: Quantified in the national cohort.

steps/10.description: Midfacial hypoplasia is present in a minority and is subtle where it occurs — considerably milder than in the dominant Sticklers.

evidence.snippet: One patient had severe arthropathy.
evidence.explanation: The exception to the mild joint phenotype, recorded so the entry does not assert that arthropathy is always absent.

steps/11.description: Joint pain is uncommon and variable, in contrast with the dominant forms where it reaches 90% by age 40. One type IX patient with severe arthropathy has been reported, so the mild course is not universal.

evidence.snippet: All three collagen IX α chains, α1, α2, and α3, are needed for formation of functional collagen IX molecule.
evidence.explanation: The stoichiometric argument that makes a single-chain null equivalent to loss of the whole molecule, and that explains why three genes give one disease.

edges/1.description: Collagen IX is an obligate heterotrimer of alpha-1, alpha-2 and alpha-3 chains, so losing one chain prevents assembly of the molecule.

evidence.snippet: Affected family members were found to have a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in COL9A2, c.843_c.846 + 4del8.
evidence.explanation: The founding gene-disease observation.

evidence.snippet: Usually inherited in a dominant fashion due to heterozygous pathogenic variants in the collagen genes COL2A1 and COL11A1, it can rarely be inherited in a recessive fashion from variants in COL9A1, COL9A2, and COL9A3, COL11A1, as well as the non-collagen genes LRP2, LOXL3 and GZF1.
evidence.explanation: Places COL9A2 within the full recessive Stickler gene set, which is the differential this entry sits inside.

genes/0.notes:
COL9A2 (1p34.2) encodes the alpha-2 chain of collagen IX. Reported STL5 alleles are loss of function — the founding c.843_846+4del8 removes an exon-intron junction, and c.1332del is a frameshift. Because collagen IX is an obligate heterotrimer, a null in COL9A2 is functionally equivalent to a null in COL9A1 or COL9A3, which is why the three genes produce one clinical entity that the nosology splits into STL4, STL5 and STL6.
Note that heterozygous and other COL9A2 variants have separately been associated with multiple epiphyseal dysplasia and with intervertebral disc disease. Those are different allelic and dosage contexts and are not this disease.

evidence.snippet: Prophylactic retinopexy should only be offered case-by-case for fellow eyes of patients presenting with GRT detachments in their first eye.
evidence.explanation: The cohort's management conclusion, stated as a restriction on a practice established in a different Stickler subtype.

evidence.snippet: Ours results do not point to high RD nor GRT incidence in recessive SS, although given the rarity, our numbers are small.
evidence.explanation: The evidential basis for the restriction, including the authors' own caveat about cohort size.

evidence.snippet: Based on the current body of literature, there is extremely strong evidence from cohort comparison studies demonstrating the efficacy and safety of prophylactic retinopexy to reduce, but not eliminate, the risk of retinal detachment in Stickler syndrome patients.
evidence.explanation: The pro-prophylaxis case for Stickler syndrome as a whole, which is why the type IX restriction is a scoping of an effective intervention rather than a rejection of it.

evidence.snippet: Variable case selection, absence of molecular genetic sub-typing and inconsistent treatment strategies have all contributed to the historic uncertainty regarding the safety and efficacy of prophylactic treatment.
evidence.explanation: Names the absence of molecular sub-typing as a limitation of the historic prophylaxis literature, which is precisely what the type IX cohort supplies.

evidence.snippet: laser therapy for prevention of retinal detachment; education on risks and symptoms of retinal detachment
evidence.explanation: The standard Stickler management recommendation that this entry scopes. It is written for the syndrome as a whole, not for the type IX forms.

treatments/0.description:
Prophylactic cryotherapy or laser retinopexy is standard in type 1 Stickler syndrome, where lifetime retinal detachment risk exceeds 50% and giant retinal tears dominate. The type IX cohort does not support transferring that policy: detachment was less frequent, through horseshoe tears, with no giant tears and no bilateral cases. The authors' conclusion is that prophylaxis should be offered case by case, specifically for the fellow eye of a patient who has already had a giant-tear detachment. This entry records the restriction rather than the intervention, because the restriction is the finding.
The restriction is not a claim that prophylaxis does not work. The pro-prophylaxis evidence base in Stickler syndrome generally is strong, and the review that makes that case names the missing piece itself: the cohort comparisons it rests on were done without molecular genetic sub-typing. The type IX cohort is what sub-typing looks like when it is done, so the two findings are consistent rather than opposed.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Creates a chorioretinal adhesion at the vitreous base to prevent a tear progressing to detachment. It does not address the underlying vitreous abnormality.

evidence.snippet: the need to warn patients and parents of the warning signs of retinal detachment, with regular ophthalmic review
evidence.explanation: The surveillance recommendation from the recessive Stickler review.

evidence.snippet: Annual examination by a vitreoretinal specialist; audiologic evaluations annually
evidence.explanation: Gives the surveillance interval and the specialist, which the recessive review leaves as "regular".

treatments/1.description: Regular ophthalmic review, with patients and parents warned about the warning signs of retinal detachment. This is what replaces routine prophylaxis in the type IX forms.

evidence.snippet: standard treatment of sensorineural and conductive hearing loss
evidence.explanation: The management recommendation for the hearing loss, which in this disease is the near-universal and more severe manifestation.

evidence.snippet: Although recessive SS is rare, early diagnosis would have a high impact for children with potentially dual sensory impairment, as well as identifying risk to future children.
evidence.explanation: Supports the clinical importance of managing the hearing loss. It argues for early diagnosis rather than reporting an amplification outcome, so the support for this specific treatment is one inference step away.

treatments/2.description: Hearing loss is severe and near-universal, so audiological assessment and amplification are central to management. The literature's emphasis is on getting to the diagnosis early, because dual sensory impairment in a child is what the delay costs.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Amplification compensates for the sensorineural deficit downstream of the cochlear matrix lesion. It does not act on the collagen defect, so it is symptomatic rather than disease-modifying.

evidence.snippet: each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being an asymptomatic carrier, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier
evidence.explanation: States the recurrence risks this treatment's description asserts. The previous citation argued for early diagnosis and named no figure.

evidence.snippet: Stickler syndrome caused by pathogenic variants in COL9A1, COL9A2, or COL9A3 is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the inheritance mode the recurrence risks follow from, for the collagen IX genes specifically rather than for Stickler syndrome generally.

evidence.snippet: Carrier testing for at-risk relatives requires prior identification of the pathogenic variants in the family.
evidence.explanation: The precondition for the carrier testing this treatment offers, which is why variant identification in the proband comes first.

treatments/3.description: Recessive inheritance means a 25% recurrence risk for siblings, and most reported families are consanguineous. Identifying the variants allows counselling of the couple and testing of at-risk relatives.

evidence.snippet: Activities such as contact sports that may lead to traumatic retinal detachment.
evidence.explanation: The agents-and-circumstances-to-avoid recommendation, given as the reason for the restriction.

treatments/4.description: Activities carrying a risk of ocular trauma are avoided because trauma can precipitate retinal detachment in an eye whose vitreous is already abnormal. This is the one piece of standard Stickler management that the type IX data does not qualify: the argument rests on the vitreous abnormality, which the type IX cohort confirms, rather than on the giant-tear risk, which it does not.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Removes a mechanical precipitant acting on an already abnormal vitreoretinal interface. It does not alter the interface itself.

evidence.snippet: The proband was operated for retinal detachment and cataract in one eye.
evidence.explanation: Records that both operations were performed in a genotyped COL9A2 patient.

evidence.snippet: Although retinal detachment surgery in the general population has a high success rate, outcomes from surgical repair in Stickler syndrome patients are notoriously poor, providing a strong argument for prophylactic intervention.
evidence.explanation: The outcome caveat that makes repair an unsatisfactory fallback, and the stated basis for preferring prevention.

treatments/5.description: Surgical repair of established detachment, reported in a COL9A2 proband. Outcomes in Stickler syndrome are described as notably worse than detachment repair in the general population, which is the observation the prophylaxis argument is built on — so the poor-outcome figure belongs with the surgery rather than only with the prophylaxis debate.

treatments/5/targets/0.description: Reattaches the retina after detachment has occurred. It is the salvage procedure, not a preventive one.

evidence.snippet: The proband was operated for retinal detachment and cataract in one eye.
evidence.explanation: Records that both operations were performed in a genotyped COL9A2 patient.

treatments/6.description: Cataract extraction, reported in the same COL9A2 proband. Cataract is a curated phenotype here, so the intervention is recorded rather than left implicit.

treatments/6/targets/0.description: Replaces the opacified lens. It addresses the opacity and not the collagen defect.

open_questions/0.rationale: The mechanistic argument says they should be indistinguishable: collagen IX is an obligate heterotrimer, all three chains are required, and a null in any one removes the molecule. Every cohort study to date has accordingly pooled them and reported results for "type IX recessive Stickler syndrome" rather than per gene — the 13-patient national cohort spans all three, and so does the phenotype-expansion series. So there is no published comparison that could detect a difference, and the absence of a reported difference is not evidence of equivalence. A chain-specific effect is not impossible: the three chains differ in their non-collagenous domains, and COL9A2 and COL9A3 have separate associations with multiple epiphyseal dysplasia that COL9A1 does not. The practical stake is whether dismech should carry three entries or one, and whether a clinician seeing a COL9A2 patient can use a COL9A3 cohort's numbers.

open_questions/1.rationale: The epidemiology is solid and the direction is counterintuitive. Collagen IX is a minor, surface-associated FACIT collagen, while collagen II is the bulk fibrillar collagen of the same tissues — so one would expect the collagen II disease to have the more severe cochlear phenotype, and it does not. Candidate explanations include a specific role for collagen IX in the tectorial membrane or in the cochlear extracellular matrix that collagen II does not cover, or a dose difference between a recessive null and a dominant haploinsufficiency that matters more in the ear than in the eye. Nothing published separates them, and no human cochlear tissue from a type IX patient has been examined.

evidence.snippet: A band comigrating with glutamic acid decarboxylase in sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gels appeared to be the only nervous-tissue antigen recognized by cerebrospinal fluid antibodies
evidence.explanation: This landmark paper identified GAD as the target antigen in stiff person syndrome, establishing the autoimmune basis.

evidence.snippet: Very high serum anti-GAD antibody titers are a key diagnostic feature for all GAD-SD, commonly associated with the presence of GAD antibodies in the CSF, a reduced CSF GABA level
evidence.explanation: High GAD antibody titers correlate with reduced GABA levels, supporting the pathophysiological mechanism.

evidence.snippet: caused by impaired GABAergic inhibitory neurotransmission and autoimmunity characterized by very high titers of GAD antibodies and increased GAD-IgG intrathecal synthesis
evidence.explanation: The 2023 review confirms that intrathecal GAD antibody synthesis and impaired GABAergic neurotransmission are central to pathogenesis.

steps/0.description: Anti-GAD65 antibodies target glutamic acid decarboxylase, the enzyme that synthesizes GABA from glutamate. This leads to reduced GABA production and impaired inhibitory neurotransmission, resulting in neuronal hyperexcitability. GAD65 is predominantly localized to synaptic vesicles and provides additional GABA synthesis when there is increased demand for rapid neurotransmitter release during high-frequency neural firing.

evidence.snippet: the phenomenon of reciprocal inhibition as the fundamental mechanism of the patients' muscle stiffness and spasms
evidence.explanation: Directly describes the loss of reciprocal inhibition mechanism.

steps/1.description: Failure of GABAergic interneurons to inhibit antagonist motor neurons during voluntary movement, resulting in co-contraction of opposing muscle groups and the characteristic rigid posture.

evidence.snippet: Very high serum anti-GAD antibody titers are a key diagnostic feature for all GAD-SD, commonly associated with the presence of GAD antibodies in the CSF, a reduced CSF GABA level and increased anti-GAD-specific IgG intrathecal synthesis denoting stimulation of B-cell clones in the CNS
evidence.explanation: Describes the intrathecal B-cell activation and antibody synthesis characteristic of SPS.

evidence.snippet: caused by impaired GABAergic inhibitory neurotransmission and autoimmunity characterized by very high titers of GAD antibodies and increased GAD-IgG intrathecal synthesis
evidence.explanation: Confirms that intrathecal GAD antibody synthesis is central to the autoimmune pathogenesis.

steps/2.description: B-cell-mediated autoimmune inflammation with clonal B-cell activation specifically within the central nervous system. Approximately 67% of patients demonstrate oligoclonal IgG bands in the CSF, and 85% exhibit increased GAD65-specific IgG index values, indicating intrathecal antibody synthesis.

evidence.snippet: Up to 70% of the SPS sera examined, compared with 10% of the controls, immunoprecipitated GABARAP protein
evidence.explanation: Raju et al. (2006, Brain) identified GABARAP as a new autoantigen in SPS with 70% seropositivity, establishing a postsynaptic autoimmune target distinct from GAD.

evidence.snippet: the IgG from GABARAP antibody-positive patients, but not control IgG, significantly inhibited the surface expression of GABA(A)-receptor
evidence.explanation: In vitro experiments demonstrated functional pathogenicity of anti-GABARAP antibodies by showing inhibition of GABA(A)-receptor surface expression.

evidence.snippet: describes the identification of anti-GABARAP antibodies as a new antigenic target in the GABAergic synapse
evidence.explanation: Alexopoulos and Dalakas (2010) confirmed GABARAP as a novel antigenic target in SPS.

steps/3.description: GABA(A)-receptor-associated protein (GABARAP), a 14-kD protein localized at postsynaptic regions of GABAergic synapses, is a distinct autoantigen in SPS. Anti-GABARAP antibodies are found in up to 70% of SPS patients and inhibit the surface expression of GABA(A)-receptors on GABAergic neurons, thereby impairing postsynaptic GABAergic signaling independently of GAD-mediated GABA synthesis deficits.

evidence.snippet: A prominent and significant decrease in GABA level was, however, observed in the sensorimotor cortex and a smaller decrease in the posterior occipital cortex but not in the cingulate cortex or pons
evidence.explanation: Levy et al. (2005) demonstrated region-specific brain GABA reduction using MRS in SPS patients, localizing the deficit to the motor cortex.

evidence.snippet: autoantibodies block the function of GABAergic neurons and interfere with the synthesis of GABA but do not cause structural changes in the brain
evidence.explanation: The study established that SPS pathology is functional rather than structural, with autoantibodies impairing GABA synthesis without neuronal destruction.

evidence.snippet: a reduction in brain levels of GABA, which is prominent in the motor cortex, has been demonstrated with magnetic resonance spectroscopy in patients with the stiff-person syndrome
evidence.explanation: Levy et al. (1999) review confirmed brain GABA reduction by MRS as a key finding in SPS pathophysiology.

steps/4.description: Magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrates a prominent and significant decrease in GABA levels in the sensorimotor cortex of SPS patients, with a smaller decrease in the posterior occipital cortex. The brain structural MRI remains normal, indicating that autoantibodies block GABAergic neuron function and interfere with GABA synthesis without causing structural brain damage.

evidence.snippet: The autoantigens can be either presynaptic such as the smaller isoform of glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65), postsynaptic such as GABA-A receptor-associated protein and gephyrin, or located at the pre- and postsynaptic side such as amphiphysin
evidence.explanation: Holmoy and Geis (2011) mapped the multiple autoantigen targets across the GABAergic synapse in SPS.

evidence.snippet: Most of these autoantigens are intracellular, and antibodies against GAD65 also occur in diabetes mellitus type 1 as well as other neurological diseases. Their pathogenic role has therefore been questioned. We here discuss the role of autoantibodies and T cells in SPS
evidence.explanation: The review discusses both humoral and cell-mediated immunity in SPS, noting that intracellular localization of most autoantigens raises questions about pathogenic mechanisms.

steps/5.description: SPS involves autoantibodies targeting multiple autoantigens at different locations within the GABAergic synapse. Presynaptic targets include GAD65; postsynaptic targets include GABARAP and gephyrin; and amphiphysin is located at both pre- and postsynaptic sides. This multi-target autoimmunity collectively disrupts GABAergic neurotransmission at multiple levels of the inhibitory synapse.

evidence.snippet: the phenomenon of reciprocal inhibition as the fundamental mechanism of the patients' muscle stiffness and spasms
evidence.explanation: The mechanism explicitly describes how reciprocal inhibition failure leads to the characteristic muscle co-contraction.

edges/0.description: Impaired GABAergic signaling disrupts reciprocal inhibition in motor circuits, causing simultaneous contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles.

evidence.snippet: Seventy-two percent carried the DQB1*0201 allele (13 of 18, P = 0.02 vs. 18 of 48 controls), indicating that SMS is associated with this allele.
evidence.explanation: Source of the ~70% DQB1*0201 carriage figure; the original HLA typing study establishing the DQB1*0201 association in stiff-man syndrome.

evidence.snippet: DQB1*02:01 was the only allele found to be significantly more common in patients than in controls
evidence.explanation: Four-digit HLA typing of GAD65-antibody neurological syndromes confirms DQB1*02:01 as the significant association and supports a primary DQ rather than DR effect.

genes/0.notes: Association with HLA class II alleles indicates genetic susceptibility to autoimmunity, though SPS itself is not inherited. The DQB1*0201 allele is carried by approximately 70% of SPS patients and is shared with type 1 diabetes and other organ-specific autoimmune disease. Contemporary four-digit typing of GAD65-antibody neurological syndromes localizes the signal primarily to DQ rather than DR, so this record is keyed to HLA-DQB1 rather than HLA-DRB1.

evidence.snippet: details on symptomatic GABA-enhancing drugs and the currently available immunotherapies in a step-by-step approach
evidence.explanation: Benzodiazepines are established as first-line symptomatic GABA-enhancing therapy.

treatments/0.description: First-line symptomatic therapy. GABA-A receptor agonists that enhance GABAergic inhibition to reduce stiffness and spasms. Diazepam is most commonly used, starting at 5-10mg twice daily.

evidence.snippet: combination therapies with the preferred gamma-aminobutyric acid-enhancing antispasmodic drugs, such as baclofen, tizanidine, benzodiazepines, and gabapentin
evidence.explanation: Baclofen is listed as a preferred GABA-enhancing antispasmodic drug for symptomatic treatment of SPS.

treatments/1.description: GABA-B receptor agonist used for spasticity control. Often used when benzodiazepines are insufficient or poorly tolerated. Can be given orally or intrathecally for refractory cases.

evidence.snippet: Among patients who received immune globulin first, stiffness scores decreased significantly (P=0.02)
evidence.explanation: Randomized controlled trial demonstrated significant efficacy of IVIg.

evidence.snippet: Intravenous immune globulin is a well-tolerated and effective, albeit costly, therapy for patients with stiff-person syndrome and anti-GAD65 antibodies.
evidence.explanation: The trial conclusion establishes IVIg as effective treatment.

evidence.snippet: detailing the application of current immunotherapies with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) plasmapheresis, and rituximab
evidence.explanation: The 2023 review confirms IVIg as a key immunotherapy option in the treatment algorithm.

treatments/2.description: Immunomodulatory therapy that significantly reduces stiffness scores and improves mobility. Administered as 2g/kg divided over 2-5 days with monthly maintenance of 1g/kg. First-line immunotherapy effective in up to 75% of patients.

evidence.snippet: detailing the application of current immunotherapies with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) plasmapheresis, and rituximab
evidence.explanation: Rituximab is included as part of the current immunotherapy options for SPS treatment.

evidence.snippet: focuses on therapies providing details on symptomatic GABA-enhancing drugs and the currently available immunotherapies in a step-by-step approach
evidence.explanation: Rituximab is part of the step-by-step therapeutic approach for refractory cases.

evidence.snippet: Significant clinical improvement occurred in most patients, with a small proportion achieving complete remission.
evidence.explanation: The 2025 systematic review from the deep-research report supports rituximab as a refractory-case option, but evidence remains partial due to small heterogeneous studies.

treatments/3.description: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that depletes B cells. Used as second-line immunotherapy when IVIg fails. Targets peripheral B-cell sources of autoantibodies. Dosing is empirical, typically 1-2g every 6-12 months.

evidence.snippet: Immunomodulatory agents, such as steroids, plasmapheresis, and intravenous immunoglobulin, seem to offer substantial improvement
evidence.explanation: Levy et al. (1999) review lists plasmapheresis alongside steroids and IVIg as immunomodulatory agents offering substantial improvement.

evidence.snippet: detailing the application of current immunotherapies with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) plasmapheresis, and rituximab
evidence.explanation: The 2023 review includes plasmapheresis in the current immunotherapy options for SPS.

treatments/4.description: Plasma exchange removes circulating autoantibodies including anti-GAD65 and anti-GABARAP antibodies. Used as an immunomodulatory therapy, particularly for acute exacerbations or when other immunotherapies are insufficient.

evidence.snippet: Although about one hundred different TWIST1 mutations have been reported in patients with the dominant haploinsufficiency Saethre-Chotzen syndrome (typically associated with craniosynostosis), substitutions uniquely affecting the Glu117 codon were not observed previously.
evidence.explanation: Places Glu117 outside the Saethre-Chotzen loss-of-function mutation spectrum, which is the genetic argument that this codon behaves differently from the rest of the gene.

evidence.snippet: a de novo heterozygous mutation in the basic domain of TWIST1, that is, c.351C>G p.Glu117Asp
evidence.explanation: Documents a third Glu117 allele, extending the substitution series beyond the two index cases.

steps/1.description: A de novo heterozygous missense substitution replaces the conserved glutamic acid at codon 117 of TWIST1. Glu117 lies in the basic region of the bHLH domain — the segment that contacts DNA — so the lesion is positioned to disable DNA recognition while leaving the helix-loop-helix dimerisation surface intact. Three substitutions are reported (p.Glu117Val, p.Glu117Gly, p.Glu117Asp), and this codon is untouched among roughly one hundred loss-of-function TWIST1 alleles catalogued in Saethre-Chotzen syndrome, which is the first indication that it is not simply another way of losing the gene.

evidence.snippet: The genetic analysis favors a predominantly dominant-negative mechanism for the action of amino acid substitutions at this highly conserved glutamic acid residue
evidence.explanation: States the antimorphic mechanism directly, as the conclusion of the C. elegans allelic series.

evidence.snippet: Heterozygous localized TWIST1 and TWIST2 basic domain substitutions exert antimorphic effects to cause Sweeney-Cox syndrome, Barber-Say syndrome, and ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Independently characterises the basic-domain substitutions as antimorphic across the TWIST1 and TWIST2 disorders.

evidence.snippet: proteomic profiling of human TWIST1-expressing cell lines and transcriptome analysis of mouse cranial mesenchyme have revealed that TWIST1 homodimers and heterodimers with TCF3, TCF4, and TCF12 E-proteins are the predominant dimer combinations
evidence.explanation: Identifies the dimer species a Glu117 subunit can be incorporated into, which is what makes an antimorphic effect possible.

evidence.snippet: Disease-causing mutations in TWIST1 can impact dimer formation or shift the balance of different types of TWIST1 dimers in the cell, which may underpin the defective differentiation of the craniofacial mesenchyme.
evidence.explanation: Connects altered TWIST1 dimer behaviour to defective craniofacial mesenchyme differentiation, the downstream node here.

steps/2.description:
TWIST1 acts as homodimers and as heterodimers with the TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12 E-proteins, and it is the basic region of each partner that grips the E-box. Substituting Glu117 alters a DNA-contacting residue while leaving the helix-loop-helix dimerisation surface untouched, so the expected consequence is a subunit that still enters complexes but cannot read their targets. The genetic evidence supports that reading: engineering the five human alleles into the equivalent Glu29 residue of hlh-8, the single Twist homolog in Caenorhabditis elegans, produced a graded severity series rather than a simple null, and the analysis favours a predominantly dominant-negative mechanism.
Two caveats belong on this node. The dimerisation-retained, DNA-binding-lost model is inferred from where the residue sits in the domain — no biochemistry on the human Glu117 protein has been reported, so it is not known directly whether these subunits still dimerise or still occupy chromatin. And "predominantly" is the source's own word: the C. elegans series does not exclude a partial loss-of-function component.
What is established is that this step is where Sweeney-Cox parts from Saethre-Chotzen. Reducing TWIST1 to one functional copy leaves the remaining protein competent; an antimorphic allele does not.

evidence.snippet: mice with neural crest lineage-specific inactivation of Twist1 resulted in dramatic disruption of frontonasal development accompanied by failure of activation of many ectomesenchyme genes, including Alx1, Alx3, and Alx4, in the FNP
evidence.explanation: Establishes that TWIST1 is required to switch on the frontonasal ectomesenchyme programme, the transcriptional output lost here.

evidence.snippet: exhibits high enrichment of Twist1 transcription factor occupancy in mouse embryonic frontonasal tissues and drove Twist1-dependent reporter transgene expression specifically in the developing periocular and frontonasal mesenchyme in transgenic mice
evidence.explanation: Identifies a direct TWIST1-occupied enhancer active in exactly the two tissues affected in this syndrome — periocular and frontonasal mesenchyme.

evidence.snippet: Loss of Twist1 in neural crest cells and their derivatives impairs skeletogenic differentiation and leads to the loss of bones of the snout, upper face and skull vault.
evidence.explanation: Shows the skeletal consequence of losing TWIST1 function in cranial neural crest, matching the frontal-bone and nasal deficiency seen in patients.

evidence.snippet: Coordinator guides cooperative and selective binding between the bHLH family mesenchymal regulator TWIST1 and a collective of HD factors associated with regional identities in the face and limb.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the composite motif through which TWIST1 acts in face mesenchyme, showing that the E-box contact lost by a Glu117 substitution is the one this regulatory system depends on.

evidence.snippet: TWIST1 is required for HD binding and open chromatin at Coordinator sites
evidence.explanation: Shows TWIST1 occupancy is upstream of homeodomain-factor binding and chromatin accessibility in this tissue, so losing TWIST1 DNA contact disables the wider regulatory programme rather than one target.

evidence.snippet: Twist1 suppresses Irf6 and other epithelial genes in CNCCs during the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) process and cell migration. Conversely, a loss of Twist1 leads to a sustained expression of epithelial and cell adhesion markers in migratory CNCCs.
evidence.explanation: Adds a second TWIST1-dependent step upstream of the ectomesenchyme programme: releasing cranial neural crest from its epithelial state. Graded INDIRECT because it is loss-of-function mouse work and no Glu117 allele has been tested for this function, so whether an antimorphic allele impairs the EMT step as well as the later patterning step is unknown.

steps/3.description:
TWIST1 is expressed in migratory cranial neural crest and maintained in the crest-derived mesenchyme of the frontonasal prominence, where it switches on the ectomesenchyme programme. In mouse, neural-crest-specific inactivation of Twist1 disrupts frontonasal development and fails to activate Alx1, Alx3 and Alx4 in the frontonasal prominence; Twist1 occupies a conserved element in a distal Alx1 enhancer and drives Alx1 reporter expression specifically in periocular and frontonasal mesenchyme. Deleting that enhancer alone reproduces frontonasal and ocular defects.
Curated as PROVISIONAL: the enhancer and target-gene work is mouse conditional-knockout and reporter biology, so it establishes what TWIST1 does in this tissue, not that a human Glu117 allele acts through this particular enhancer. The inference from an antimorphic allele to this specific regulatory step has not been made in patient tissue.

evidence.snippet: Sweeney-Cox syndrome characterized by hypertelorism with severe deficiency in frontal bones and hypoplasia of the nose and facial bones
evidence.explanation: States the skeletal phenotype of the syndrome in the terms modelled by this node. Graded OTHER, not HUMAN_CLINICAL: this sentence is background prose in a mouse developmental study summarising the clinical literature, not human data the paper itself reports. It is cited because the primary description of frontal-bone deficiency sits in full text that is not in the reference cache.

steps/4.description: Deficient skeletogenic differentiation of frontonasal ectomesenchyme yields the structural core of the syndrome: severe deficiency of the frontal bones, hypoplasia of the nose and facial bones, and the widened interorbital distance that presents clinically as marked hypertelorism.

evidence.snippet: Sweeney-Cox syndrome, Barber-Say syndrome, and ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome share the facial features of ablepharon, hypertelorism, underdevelopment of the eyelids, and cheek pads adjacent to the corners of the mouth.
evidence.explanation: Establishes ablepharon and eyelid underdevelopment as features of the syndrome and of the paralogous TWIST2 disorders.

steps/5.description:
Eyelid development requires patterned periocular mesenchyme, and the eyelids are the second tissue in which the TWIST1-dependent frontonasal enhancer is active. Clinically this presents as ablepharon or underdevelopment of the eyelids, a feature Sweeney-Cox shares with the TWIST2 Glu75 disorders and which is not part of Saethre-Chotzen syndrome.
PROVISIONAL because the enhancer evidence establishes TWIST1 activity in periocular mesenchyme but no study has traced a Glu117 allele through eyelid morphogenesis; the causal chain from transcriptional lesion to ablepharon is inferred from tissue overlap.

evidence.snippet: The genetic analysis favors a predominantly dominant-negative mechanism for the action of amino acid substitutions at this highly conserved glutamic acid residue
evidence.explanation: Links the Glu117 substitution to antimorphic action on the TWIST1 complex, which is the edge asserted here.

edges/1.description: The substituted basic domain is the direct cause of the mutant protein's failure to transactivate while remaining incorporated into TWIST1 complexes.

evidence.snippet: Disease-causing mutations in TWIST1 can impact dimer formation or shift the balance of different types of TWIST1 dimers in the cell, which may underpin the defective differentiation of the craniofacial mesenchyme.
evidence.explanation: Supports the edge from altered TWIST1 complex behaviour to defective craniofacial mesenchyme differentiation. Graded INDIRECT because the source frames this as a proposed explanation rather than a demonstrated one, and does not test a Glu117 allele.

edges/2.description: Complexes that cannot engage the E-box cannot activate the TWIST1 target genes of the frontonasal prominence.

evidence.snippet: Loss of Twist1 in neural crest cells and their derivatives impairs skeletogenic differentiation and leads to the loss of bones of the snout, upper face and skull vault.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the edge from lost TWIST1 function in cranial neural crest to failed skeletogenic differentiation of the upper face.

edges/3.description: Loss of the ectomesenchyme programme in the frontonasal prominence leads to deficient differentiation of the frontal and nasal skeletal elements.

evidence.snippet: drove Twist1-dependent reporter transgene expression specifically in the developing periocular and frontonasal mesenchyme in transgenic mice
evidence.explanation: Places TWIST1-dependent regulatory activity in periocular mesenchyme. Graded INDIRECT because it establishes the tissue overlap rather than the causal route to ablepharon.

edges/4.description: The same TWIST1-dependent enhancer activity spans periocular mesenchyme, linking the transcriptional lesion to the eyelid phenotype; the intervening steps in eyelid morphogenesis are not established.

evidence.snippet: we describe a new clinical entity, Sweeney-Cox syndrome, associated with distinct de novo amino acid substitutions (p.Glu117Val and p.Glu117Gly) at a highly conserved glutamic acid residue located in the basic DNA binding domain of TWIST1, in two subjects with frontonasal dysplasia and additional malformations.
evidence.explanation: Identifies TWIST1 Glu117 as the causal locus and lists two alleles.

evidence.snippet: This suggests that any amino acid substitutions at Glu117 would likely lead to the Sweeney-Cox syndrome phenotype or lethality.
evidence.explanation: Supports the claim that the pathogenic constraint is on the codon itself rather than on a particular substituting residue.

evidence.snippet: Three rare but clinically defined and distinguishable gene-disease pairs were found to have Limited evidence ranging from 3 to 4 points to support the relationship by the Cranio GCEP: FGFR1-related osteoglophonic dysplasia (OMIM:166250), TWIST1-related Sweeney-Cox syndrome (OMIM:617746)
evidence.explanation: The ClinGen Craniofacial GCEP classifies the TWIST1-Sweeney-Cox gene-disease relationship as Limited. Typed DIRECT because the sentence asserts a curated gene-disease relationship rather than something the claim is inferred from. The Limited grade is a statement of evidence strength, which the schema has no slot for, and it is recorded here: the case count is too small to reach Moderate, this is not a doubt about the mechanism, and the entry should not present the relationship with Definitive-level confidence.

genes/0.notes:
ClinGen's Craniofacial GCEP rates this gene-disease relationship Limited (3-4 points), constrained by the number of reported cases rather than by the quality of the functional evidence. The mechanistic work is strong; the clinical series is three patients.
Nomenclature discrepancy on the third allele: the Takenouchi report states c.351C>G p.Glu117Asp, while ClinVar represents the same protein change as c.351G>T (VCV002572412). Against NM_000474.4 the ClinVar form is the internally consistent one, since GAG to GAT yields Asp whereas the published cDNA change does not. The published string is quoted verbatim in the evidence snippet above and deliberately left uncorrected there, because a snippet belongs to the cited paper; the reconciliation is recorded here instead.

evidence.snippet: After failing lubrication and a moisture chamber, he was fit with a customized scleral contact lens that protected the ocular surface. It was tolerated well, and ocular surface health was maintained for 13 months to permit the growth of eyelid tissue for future oculoplastic surgery.
evidence.explanation: Documents the escalation of corneal protection in a neonate with large upper eyelid coloboma. Graded INDIRECT because it is a single case in isolated eyelid coloboma, not in Sweeney-Cox syndrome; it is cited as phenotype-directed management for a feature this entry curates, not as disease-specific evidence.

treatments/0.description: Ocular surface protection is the management step with the clearest preventable-harm argument in this syndrome, because the curated eyelid phenotypes leave the cornea exposed. Reported practice in large neonatal upper eyelid coloboma escalates from lubrication and a moisture chamber to a customised scleral contact lens, which can maintain ocular surface health long enough for eyelid tissue to grow before oculoplastic reconstruction.

evidence.snippet: Current practice focuses on preventing severe infections with timely administration of vaccinations, antibacterial prophylaxis when indicated, and urgent evaluation and treatment of febrile events.
evidence.explanation: States the standard of care for children with asplenia. Typed INDIRECT because it is a general paediatric asplenia recommendation, not evidence about Sweeney-Cox syndrome; it is cited because asplenia is a curated phenotype of this entry.

treatments/1.description: Asplenia is an annotated feature of this syndrome and carries lifelong risk of fulminant infection with encapsulated organisms. Standard paediatric asplenia care is timely vaccination, antibacterial prophylaxis where indicated, and urgent evaluation of febrile episodes. This matters disproportionately here because asplenia in a child ascertained for a craniofacial phenotype can go unrecognised.

evidence.snippet: Current practice focuses on preventing severe infections with timely administration of vaccinations, antibacterial prophylaxis when indicated, and urgent evaluation and treatment of febrile events.
evidence.explanation: Names timely vaccination first among the preventive measures for children with asplenia. Graded INDIRECT because it is a general paediatric asplenia recommendation and not evidence about Sweeney-Cox syndrome.

treatments/2.description: In asplenia, vaccination against encapsulated organisms is the cornerstone of prevention rather than an adjunct to antibiotics, and the cited recommendation names it first. It is curated separately from antibacterial prophylaxis because the two are different modalities with different schedules, and collapsing them into one treatment would lose that.

evidence.snippet: The present observation suggests that a localized TWIST1 basic domain substitution, that is, p.Glu117Asp, in TWIST1 may exert a mild antimorphic effect similar to that of haploinsufficiency, leading to craniosynostosis and ablepharon.
evidence.explanation: Proposes graded antimorphism explicitly, and is the only clinical observation bearing on it.

evidence.snippet: This allelic series revealed that different substitutions exhibit graded severity, in terms of both gene expression and cellular phenotype, which we incorporate into a model explaining the various human disease phenotypes.
evidence.explanation: Provides the experimental grading of the same allele set that the continuum model rests on.

hypotheses/0.description:
Under this model the substituting residue at Glu117 sets how strongly the mutant subunit interferes with the wild-type pool, and the resulting phenotype moves along a continuum rather than falling into one of two categories. A conservative substitution such as Glu117Asp interferes weakly and behaves closer to haploinsufficiency, which is the reading offered for the one patient who had both the Sweeney-Cox facies and bicoronal craniosynostosis; stronger substitutions produce the non-synostotic frontonasal phenotype, and the C. elegans series ordered all five human alleles by severity rather than separating them into classes.
If correct, the distinction between this entry and Saethre-Chotzen syndrome is quantitative, and the craniosynostosis discriminator is a threshold effect rather than a categorical feature. The competing model is that the two disorders are mechanistically disjoint because the alleles differ in kind, not degree. Three patients, one per allele, cannot separate these.

evidence.snippet: we engineered all five disease-associated alleles into the equivalent Glu29 residue encoded by hlh-8, the single Twist homolog present in Caenorhabditis elegans
evidence.explanation: Documents that the only allele-correct model is an invertebrate with no craniofacial skeleton, which is the mismatch this discussion records.

open_questions/0.rationale: Every mechanistic model of this disorder is currently an allele mismatch. The C. elegans series carries the right substitution but has no craniofacial skeleton; the mouse work has the right tissue but uses conditional nulls, which model haploinsufficiency-like loss rather than the antimorphic allele. The whole clinical point of Sweeney-Cox is that those two lesions give different diseases, so no existing model tests the step that actually distinguishes it from Saethre-Chotzen. Whether the enhancer route is the one a Glu117 allele travels is therefore inference from tissue overlap, not a result.

evidence.snippet: The present observation suggests that a localized TWIST1 basic domain substitution, that is, p.Glu117Asp, in TWIST1 may exert a mild antimorphic effect similar to that of haploinsufficiency, leading to craniosynostosis and ablepharon.
evidence.explanation: States the graded-antimorphism argument that makes the boundary between the two syndromes uncertain.

open_questions/1.rationale: Craniosynostosis is the stated discriminator, but the p.Glu117Asp patient had bilateral coronal synostosis alongside the ablepharon and cheek-pad facies, and that report argued the conservative Glu-to-Asp change exerts only a mild antimorphic effect resembling haploinsufficiency. If severity of antimorphic interference is continuous, the discriminator is quantitative rather than categorical, and the lump/split status of these two entries depends on which it is. With three reported patients there is not enough phenotypic range to settle it.

open_questions/2.rationale: Both curated treatments are phenotype-directed, not disease-directed: they cite sources about eyelid coloboma and about paediatric asplenia in general, because with three reported patients there is no series, no surgical protocol and no ophthalmological guidance for this syndrome. Nothing here tells a clinician whether the timing or escalation of corneal protection should differ in a child whose eyelid defect is part of a TWIST1 developmental lesion. Borrowing the rest of craniofacial management from Saethre-Chotzen would be unsound in the respect that matters: that care is organised around craniosynostosis, which is not a cardinal feature here.

evidence.snippet: This suggests that any amino acid substitutions at Glu117 would likely lead to the Sweeney-Cox syndrome phenotype or lethality.
evidence.explanation: Raises lethality as an outcome of substitution at this codon, which is the ascertainment concern recorded here.

evidence.snippet: This allelic series revealed that different substitutions exhibit graded severity, in terms of both gene expression and cellular phenotype, which we incorporate into a model explaining the various human disease phenotypes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that severity varies by substituting residue, which is what makes a lethal tail plausible.

open_questions/3.rationale: The C. elegans series showed graded severity across substitutions at this residue, and the clinical literature explicitly raises lethality as an alternative outcome of substituting Glu117. If some substitutions are embryonic-lethal or lethal in the neonatal period, the reported phenotype is conditioned on survival and the three living patients are a biased sample. This matters for two curated claims at once: the severity range recorded in the phenotypes section, and the case count recorded under prevalence, which is also the constraint behind ClinGen's Limited gene-disease classification. Prenatal or perinatal-loss sequencing series covering TWIST1 would be the way to test it; nothing of the sort has been reported.

evidence.snippet: The larval stage of the pork tapeworm (Taenia solium) infects the human nervous system, causing neurocysticercosis.
evidence.explanation: The abstract links larval infection to neurocysticercosis.

steps/0.description: Larval Taenia solium infects the human nervous system.

evidence.snippet: either by natural evolution or as a result of antiparasitic treatment, a strong host inflammatory reaction leads to cyst degeneration and death
evidence.explanation: Names the inflammatory reaction and its two triggers, natural evolution and antiparasitic treatment.

steps/1.description: A strong host inflammatory reaction destroys the cyst, producing perilesional inflammation and granuloma formation in the brain parenchyma.

evidence.snippet: calcifications persist in the host brain throughout life, remain as potential seizure foci, and may predispose hosts to a chronic epileptic state
evidence.explanation: Establishes persistence and epileptogenicity of the calcified lesions.

steps/2.description: Calcified granulomas persist in the brain parenchyma for life and act as chronic epileptogenic foci, with perilesional gliosis, oedema and blood-brain barrier disruption reported on human biopsy.

evidence.snippet: Inflammation and mechanical obstruction are the two mechanisms underlying hydrocephalus in NCC. Inflammation within the basal subarachnoid space impairs the normal CSF flow, resulting in the accumulation of CSF in the ventricles
evidence.explanation: States both mechanisms and spells out the inflammatory one.

evidence.snippet: the cysts themselves may obstruct the CSF flow in the narrow spaces of the ventricles and manifest in hydrocephalus even in the absence of inflammation
evidence.explanation: Establishes mechanical obstruction as sufficient on its own, which is why this node carries both mechanisms rather than only the inflammatory one.

steps/3.description: In the ventricles and subarachnoid cisterns, two mechanisms impair CSF flow: inflammation once the immune system recognizes cyst antigens (arachnoiditis, basal fibrosis, ependymitis), and direct mechanical obstruction by the cysts themselves, which can cause hydrocephalus even without inflammation.

evidence.snippet: Seizures were reported in 97.7% of cases
evidence.explanation: Seizures are the predominant manifestation of symptomatic neurocysticercosis, reported in 97.7% of a hospital-based NCC cohort. The band is set to FREQUENT (rather than VERY_FREQUENT) as a conservative whole-disease estimate, since this entry spans taeniasis and cysticercosis and the 97.7% figure derives from a selected symptomatic-NCC population.

evidence.snippet: This disease is one of the main causes of epileptic seizures in many less developed countries
evidence.explanation: Neurocysticercosis is a major cause of seizures in endemic regions.

evidence.snippet: Calcified lesions are the most frequent finding on brain CT in NCC cases from endemic areas (between 10% and 20%), although many infected individuals are presumed to be asymptomatic
evidence.explanation: Establishes calcified lesions as the most frequent brain CT finding in NCC. `frequency` is deliberately left unset: the bracketed 10-20% is attributed to a population-based CT study of an endemic population, not to the fraction of NCC patients, and this cohort was selected for calcified NCC so it cannot supply that fraction either.

evidence.snippet: Patients had a median number of three calcifications (IQR: 1-7), mostly located in the frontal lobes (79%)
evidence.explanation: Describes the radiological distribution of calcified NCC lesions in a 524-patient hospital cohort, supporting the cerebral (rather than extracerebral) localization of the calcification phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Extraparenchymal NCC is commonly accompanied by raised intracranial hypertension due to hydrocephalus, which is an emergency requiring cyst extirpation by surgical intervention to relieve the symptoms
evidence.explanation: Establishes hydrocephalus as a common complication of extraparenchymal neurocysticercosis, distinct from the parenchymal disease captured by the Seizures and Cerebral Calcification phenotypes. No numeric frequency is quantified in this narrative review, so `frequency` is left unset rather than assigning an unsupported band.

evidence.snippet: Inflammation and mechanical obstruction are the two mechanisms underlying hydrocephalus in NCC
evidence.explanation: States the two proposed mechanisms (CSF-flow-impairing inflammation and direct cyst obstruction of the ventricles) underlying the hydrocephalus phenotype in neurocysticercosis. The mechanism itself is modeled in `pathophysiology#Extraparenchymal Cyst Burden with Impaired CSF Flow`.

evidence.snippet: When classified by the type of first symptom, most patients reported headache (273, 52.1%), followed by seizures
evidence.explanation: Headache was the presenting symptom in 52.1% of this 524-patient cohort. `frequency` is left unset for the same reason as Cerebral Calcification: the cohort is hospital-based and selected for calcified NCC, so its symptom shares describe that subpopulation rather than taeniasis/cysticercosis as a whole.

evidence.snippet: Of the 345 patients who reported headache as the first symptom, 126 received medical care, 60 received emergency care, and 18 were hospitalized.
evidence.explanation: Records the care burden of the headache phenotype, establishing it as clinically consequential rather than incidental.

evidence.snippet: Tapeworm larvae establish in the human brain initially as viable brain cysts causing only minimal or no inflammation
evidence.explanation: Establishes the quiescent viable-cyst stage that precedes the inflammatory degeneration node.

edges/0.description: Parenchymal cysts are initially tolerated, then degenerate under a host inflammatory reaction that arises either by natural evolution or after antiparasitic treatment.

evidence.snippet: The evolution of cysts in the CSF compartments (the brain ventricles and the subarachnoid space) is different.
evidence.explanation: Separates the extraparenchymal compartment, whose cysts drive the hydrocephalus arm, from the parenchymal calcification arm.

edges/1.description: Cysts lodged in the ventricles and subarachnoid cisterns follow a different course from parenchymal cysts, remaining hidden from immune surveillance for years.

evidence.snippet: Subsequently, some cysts disappear, whereas other become residual calcifications
evidence.explanation: Establishes residual calcification as the direct outcome of cyst degeneration.

edges/2.description: Degenerating cysts are walled off in a granuloma that finally calcifies, leaving residual calcifications rather than resolving completely.

evidence.snippet: On computed tomography (CT), brain calcifications appear as small hyperdense lesions, with or without enhancement after the administration of contrast material
evidence.explanation: Links the pathological lesion to the radiological phenotype.

edges/3.description: The calcified granulomas are what appears as hyperdense lesions on brain CT.

evidence.snippet: Pathological studies using human biopsies demonstrate perilesional gliosis and edema, abnormal vascular permeability, disruption of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and axonal damage
evidence.explanation: Supplies the tissue-level changes at calcified lesions that underlie their epileptogenicity.

edges/4.description: Calcified lesions act as chronic seizure foci; human biopsy shows perilesional gliosis, oedema and blood-brain barrier disruption at these sites.

evidence.snippet: The association between the presence of calcified NCC and primary headache has also been suggested, likely as a consequence of the remodeling process of calcification and the release of antigen remnants in the brain parenchyma
evidence.explanation: The authors state the proposed mechanism as a suggestion, so this edge records a proposed rather than established causal link.

edges/5.description: Calcified NCC has been associated with headache, proposed to follow remodeling of the calcification and release of antigen remnants into the parenchyma.

evidence.snippet: disturb the CSF flow (either by fibrosis in the subarachnoid cisterns or ependymitis within the ventricles), leading to hydrocephalus
evidence.explanation: Names the CSF-flow disturbance as the immediate cause of hydrocephalus.

edges/6.description: Impaired CSF flow accumulates CSF in the ventricles.

evidence.snippet: Available therapeutic measures include steroids, treatments for symptoms, surgery, and, more controversially, antiparasitic drugs to kill brain parasites.
evidence.explanation: The abstract lists antiparasitic drugs among available treatments.

evidence.snippet: The study demonstrates that the albendazole and praziquantel combination therapy is superior in lesion resolution in pediatric neurocysticercosis
evidence.explanation: Names albendazole and praziquantel as the specific antiparasitic agents used in neurocysticercosis, with a pediatric systematic review and meta-analysis finding the combination superior to albendazole monotherapy.

treatments/0.description: Antiparasitic drugs are used to kill brain parasites in neurocysticercosis.

evidence.snippet: For medical treatment, two anthelmintics have proved effective since the 1980s: albendazole and praziquantel. Their efficacy is similar, both being significantly more active in parenchymal disease than in extraparenchymal disease.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both agents as acting on the cyst burden while recording the reduced activity against the extraparenchymal cysts this node represents.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Albendazole and praziquantel kill the cysts, but both are markedly less active in the extraparenchymal compartment than in parenchymal disease.

evidence.snippet: The anthelminthic treatment may trigger the secretion of various antigens from the cysts, eliciting inflammatory responses that determine the symptoms and can be fatal
evidence.explanation: Records the edge as treatment-induced aggravation of this node rather than suppression of it, which is the reason the same source requires combining anthelminthics with corticosteroids.

treatments/0/targets/1.description: Antiparasitic treatment is itself one of the two triggers of the inflammatory cyst-degeneration node, which is why corticosteroids are co-administered.

evidence.snippet: Of 211 participants diagnosed with taeniasis, 188 provided a follow-up stool sample 30-days after treatment and 141 were cured (treatment effectiveness 75.0%)
evidence.explanation: This study's own FINDINGS for single-dose niclosamide effectiveness against taeniasis, measured by post-treatment stool sampling.

evidence.snippet: MDA with NSM is safe in Taenia solium endemic settings. However, the effectiveness following one dose is lower than expected, which suggests additional treatment may be necessary to enhance the infection control efforts.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own INTERPRETATION. Recorded alongside the effectiveness figure because it qualifies it: niclosamide's safety in this setting is established, but a single dose underperforms prior selective-chemotherapy estimates.

evidence.snippet: 988 (1.5%) reported experiencing at least one AE. Almost all AEs (99.2%) were of mild intensity, with no severe AEs recorded.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the safety profile across 65,551 treated residents, supporting niclosamide's suitability where undiagnosed NCC may be present.

treatments/1.description: Intestinal anthelminthic used to treat adult tapeworm carriage (taeniasis) and interrupt Taenia solium transmission to new intermediate hosts, distinct from the antiparasitic agents used against tissue cysticercosis/neurocysticercosis above.

evidence.snippet: Available therapeutic measures include steroids, treatments for symptoms, surgery, and, more controversially, antiparasitic drugs to kill brain parasites.
evidence.explanation: The abstract includes surgery as a treatment option.

treatments/2.description: Surgical interventions may be used in selected cases.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrate that G12E and the previously described G12V and G60R were gain-of-function variants that increased RAP1B activation, talin recruitment, and integrin activation
evidence.explanation: Functional characterisation of all three recurrent variants together, establishing the direction of effect experimentally rather than by inference from variant position.

evidence.snippet: The residue G12 in the P-loop is required for the RAP1B-GTPase conformational switch.
evidence.explanation: Explains why G12 is a hotspot: it is the residue the conformational switch depends on.

evidence.snippet: monoallelic RAP1B variants that disrupt RAP1B GTPase activity
evidence.explanation: States the effect on GTPase activity specifically, which is the molecular function this node records as decreased.

steps/1.description: RAP1B is a RAS-superfamily small GTPase that cycles between GDP- and GTP-bound states. The recurrent disease variants cluster at two positions controlling that cycle: G12 in the P-loop, the residue the conformational switch depends on, and G60. Substitutions there disrupt GTPase activity, so hydrolysis fails and the protein persists in its active GTP-bound form. The molecular function is therefore recorded as DECREASED while the variant is a gain of function at the level of signalling output — the two are consistent, because losing the off-switch is what makes the switch constitutive.

evidence.snippet: thereby modifying late responses such as platelet activation, T cell proliferation, and migration
evidence.explanation: Names the cellular consequences measured downstream of the integrin change, in both the platelet and the lymphoid compartment.

steps/2.description: Talin recruitment to the integrin cytoplasmic tail converts integrins to their high-affinity conformation. In the disease variants this step is driven constitutively rather than on demand, and the downstream effects are not confined to platelets: T cell proliferation and migration are altered by the same mechanism, which is why the haematological phenotype extends to lymphocytes.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, Rap1a/b-mKO mice displayed a marked macrothrombocytopenia due to impaired proplatelet formation by megakaryocytes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that RAP1 signalling is required for proplatelet formation and that its disturbance produces thrombocytopenia, which is the mechanism this node asserts. The lesion is a double knockout in mouse, not the human variant; see the attached discussion.

evidence.snippet: mice lacking the predominant isoform, RAP1B, display a partial platelet integrin activation defect and have a normal platelet count
evidence.explanation: Deleting Rap1b alone leaves the mouse platelet count normal, so the double knockout above cannot be read as a Rap1b-dose model of this disease. Curated as REFUTE against that reading of the model rather than against the node itself, whose human lesion is activating rather than null.

evidence.snippet: BM biopsy at the age of 3 months (M3) showed megakaryocyte maturation defects and granular hypoplasia, while BM immune phenotype and karyotype were normal.
evidence.explanation: Human marrow megakaryocyte pathology in a RAP1B-variant patient. Does not itself demonstrate a proplatelet-formation defect - a maturation abnormality on biopsy is a different observation - but it establishes that the human megakaryocyte compartment is abnormal, which the node previously rested on mouse data alone.

evidence.snippet: BM smear at M18 showed decreased cellularity for age and only rare, abnormal, hypolobed megakaryocytes (Figure 1A).
evidence.explanation: The morphological detail: megakaryocytes are few, abnormal and hypolobed. Hypolobation is a maturation phenotype, so this constrains what the human lesion looks like without identifying the step.

steps/3.description: Megakaryocytes extend proplatelets to release platelets, and that process depends on RAP1 signalling. Megakaryocyte-specific deletion of both mouse Rap1 isoforms produces marked macrothrombocytopenia through impaired proplatelet formation, establishing production rather than survival as the RAP1-dependent step. Deleting Rap1b alone does not reduce the platelet count, so the mouse shows the pathway matters without modelling the human monoallelic gain-of-function lesion.

evidence.snippet: Both individuals had thrombocytopenia, as well as congenital malformations, and neurological, behavioural, and dysmorphic features, in line with previous reports.
evidence.explanation: Reports thrombocytopenia in both newly identified individuals and states that the pattern matches the earlier cases.

steps/4.description: Present in every reported individual and the feature the entity is named for. Long-standing rather than episodic.

evidence.snippet: We report a boy with neonatal thrombocytopenia, combined immunodeficiency, neutropenia, and monocytopenia caused by a heterozygous de novo single nucleotide substitution, c.35G>A (p.G12E) in RAP1B.
evidence.explanation: The one reported patient with an overt immunodeficiency, with the variant named.

evidence.snippet: While these patients developed mild neutro- and lymphopenia, they had no clinical history suggesting an associated immunodeficiency. However, neither their immune nor platelet function had been investigated.
evidence.explanation: Records both the milder immune findings in the germline cases and the authors' own caveat that those patients were not tested, which is why this phenotype carries no frequency band.

steps/5.description: Mild lymphopenia and neutropenia were reported in the germline cases without clinical immunodeficiency; the somatic-mosaic patient had frank combined immunodeficiency with neutropenia and monocytopenia. The authors note that the earlier patients' immune function had not been investigated, so the difference may be ascertainment rather than biology.

evidence.snippet: hemorrhagic manifestations were more important than expected, given platelet counts requiring repeated platelet transfusions
evidence.explanation: States the disproportion directly. Reported in the somatic-mosaic patient, so it is one case rather than a feature established across the series.

steps/6.description: Bleeding more severe than the platelet count alone predicts, requiring repeated transfusion. Recorded because it is the clinical signal that the platelet defect is qualitative as well as quantitative - a count-only defect would not produce it - and because it is the most direct human correlate of the constitutively activated integrin node.

edges/1.description: Persistently GTP-bound RAP1B recruits talin to the integrin beta tail, which is the committed step of inside-out activation.

edges/2.description: RAP1 signalling is also required for proplatelet formation, so a constitutively active switch disturbs platelet production rather than only platelet function. This edge is the entry's proposed resolution of the gain-of-function-causes-a-deficit paradox and rests on mouse megakaryocyte data; see the attached discussion.

edges/3.description: Altered T cell proliferation and migration is the route from the integrin defect to the immune phenotype.

edges/4.description: Constitutively activated integrin gives platelets that are abnormal in function as well as few, which is the reading the source's own observation supports: bleeding was worse than the platelet count alone predicted. This is an inference from the disproportion rather than a measured platelet function defect, and is curated as such.

edges/5.description: Impaired proplatelet formation reduces the circulating platelet count.

evidence.snippet: Exome sequencing identified two novel de novo heterozygous variants in these patients, c.35G>T p.(Gly12Val) and c.178G>C p.(Gly60Arg), in the RAP1B gene (NM_001010942.2).
evidence.explanation: The founding report, naming both hotspot variants and establishing their de novo heterozygous status.

evidence.snippet: We hypothesize that pathogenic missense variants in the RAP1B gene cause congenital syndromic thrombocytopenia with a spectrum of associated malformations and dysmorphism, possibly through a gain of function mechanism.
evidence.explanation: The gain-of-function direction as originally proposed. Graded INDIRECT because the founding report states it as a hypothesis from variant position; the functional demonstration came later, in PMID:39225097.

genes/0.notes: Monoallelic de novo gain-of-function variants at two hotspots, G12 and G60. Reported substitutions are p.(Gly12Val), p.(Gly12Glu) and p.(Gly60Arg). The gene MIM is 179530 and the phenotype MIM is 620654; some sources cite the gene MIM when they mean the disease, which is worth watching when reconciling records.

treatments/0.description: Reported once, in the patient with somatic-mosaic G12E and combined immunodeficiency, where it restored the haematological and immune phenotype. This is a single-patient outcome in the most severely affected reported case, not an established management standard for the germline syndrome, where the thrombocytopenia is generally mild.

evidence.snippet: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation fully restored the patient's hemato-immunological phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Reports the outcome in the single transplanted patient, and shows the correction was of the hemato-immunological compartment specifically.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replacing the haematopoietic compartment removes the variant-bearing megakaryocyte and lymphoid precursors, which is why the correction is expected to be confined to blood-borne features and not to extend to the congenital malformations.

evidence.snippet: From birth until HSCT, P1 presented platelet counts ranging between 15,000 and 30,000/μL, also when treated with the thrombopoietin receptor agonist romiplostim
evidence.explanation: Records the non-response. Graded REFUTE against the claim that romiplostim is effective in this disease, on the single patient in whom it was tried.

treatments/1.description: A thrombopoietin receptor agonist, tried in the somatic-mosaic patient and recorded as not raising the platelet count: counts stayed between 15,000 and 30,000/uL on treatment, the same range as off it. Curated because a documented non-response is informative here rather than absent evidence - a TPO-receptor agonist acts by driving megakaryocyte production, so failure is consistent with a defect downstream of that signal, which is what the proplatelet-formation node asserts.

evidence.snippet: hemorrhagic manifestations were more important than expected, given platelet counts requiring repeated platelet transfusions
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the transfusion requirement and the disproportion between bleeding and count that motivates it.

treatments/2.description: Required repeatedly in the somatic-mosaic patient, whose bleeding was more severe than the platelet count alone predicted. Supportive care rather than disease-modifying.

open_questions/0.rationale: The direction of effect is experimentally established: G12V, G12E and G60R all increase RAP1B activation, talin recruitment and integrin activation. The phenotype is nonetheless a deficit. The explanation this entry curates is that RAP1 signalling is separately required for megakaryocyte proplatelet formation, so a constitutively active switch disrupts production. That account comes from mouse megakaryocyte knockouts. Human marrow from a variant carrier does show an abnormal megakaryocyte compartment - maturation defects and hypolobed forms - but proplatelet formation itself has not been measured in a human megakaryocyte carrying a hotspot variant. An alternative the literature has not excluded is peripheral consumption or clearance of constitutively activated platelets, which would predict a different marrow picture.

open_questions/1.rationale:
The mouse evidence for this node is a megakaryocyte-specific deletion of both Rap1 isoforms. That lesion is null rather than activating, homozygous rather than monoallelic, and covers both isoforms because they are redundant in mouse. The same paper reports that deleting Rap1b alone leaves the platelet count normal, so the model cannot be read as a Rap1b-dose model of the human disease. What it does establish is that the RAP1 pathway is required for proplatelet formation, which is the premise the node needs; it does not establish that the human variants act through that step.
The human megakaryocyte compartment is not unobserved, and an earlier version of this rationale implied it was. Marrow biopsy and smear in a RAP1B-variant patient show maturation defects, granular hypoplasia and rare hypolobed megakaryocytes, and those findings are now curated on the node. What remains unobserved is narrower: proplatelet formation itself has never been measured in a human megakaryocyte carrying a hotspot variant, so whether the human lesion sits in proplatelet extension or in maturation upstream of it is open. Hypolobation is a maturation phenotype and mildly favours the second reading, which is not what this node asserts.

open_questions/2.rationale: Only the somatic-mosaic patient had overt combined immunodeficiency; the germline patients had mild lymphopenia and neutropenia without clinical immunodeficiency. The authors state directly that neither the immune nor the platelet function of those patients had been investigated, so the contrast may be ascertainment rather than biology. The mosaic patient's variant allele frequency fell over time in the peripheral immune compartment while remaining stable in bone marrow, which is a further reason not to generalise from that case. Immune-function testing of the germline patients would settle it.

evidence.snippet: mice with genetic deletion of Sapap3 exhibit increased anxiety and compulsive grooming behaviour leading to facial hair loss and skin lesions
evidence.explanation: Establishes that loss of a single corticostriatal synaptic protein produces grooming to the point of hair loss.

evidence.snippet: lentiviral-mediated selective expression of Sapap3 in the striatum rescues the synaptic and behavioural defects of Sapap3-mutant mice
evidence.explanation: A rescue experiment localising causation to the striatum rather than leaving the association correlational.

evidence.snippet: Slitrk5(-/-) mice show selective overactivation of the orbitofrontal cortex, abnormalities in striatal anatomy and cell morphology and alterations in glutamate receptor composition, which contribute to deficient corticostriatal neurotransmission
evidence.explanation: An independent gene converging on the same circuit, and the link to glutamate receptor composition.

steps/0.description:
Impaired excitatory neurotransmission at cortico-striatal synapses, the level at which both genetic mouse models of pathological grooming converge. Deleting either SAPAP3 (a postsynaptic scaffolding protein at excitatory synapses, highly expressed in striatum) or SLITRK5 produces defective corticostriatal transmission together with a grooming phenotype severe enough to remove hair.
The direction of causation is established rather than inferred in the SAPAP3 case: restoring the protein selectively in the striatum rescues both the synaptic and the behavioural defect, so the striatal synapse is not merely correlated with the behaviour.

evidence.snippet: N-acetylcysteine, an amino acid, seems to restore the extracellular glutamate concentration in the nucleus accumbens and, therefore, offers promise in the reduction of compulsive behavior
evidence.explanation: States the pharmacological rationale that this node rests on.

steps/1.description:
Altered extracellular glutamate homeostasis in the ventral striatum, curated here principally because a treatment that acts on it works. N-acetylcysteine restores extracellular glutamate concentration in the nucleus accumbens, and in a randomised adult trial it reduced hair-pulling substantially more than placebo.
This is inference from therapeutic response, which is weaker than a measurement. The node is retained because the effect size was large and the mechanism of the drug is specific - but the direction of the underlying abnormality in patients has not been measured, and the paediatric trial of the same drug was negative.

evidence.snippet: Trichotillomania is an impulse control disorder in which individuals fail to resist urges to pull out their own hair and is associated with significant psychiatric comorbidity and functional impairment
evidence.explanation: Defines the disorder as a failure to resist the urge rather than as an absence of insight.

steps/2.description: The behavioural output: an urge to pull that is not successfully resisted, producing repeated pulling despite intact knowledge that it is damaging and repeated attempts to stop. Pulling has been described in two modes - automatic (outside awareness, often during sedentary activity) and focused (in response to an urge or an aversive state) - and treatment trials measure them separately.

evidence.snippet: Trichotillomania, defined as the compulsive pulling out of one's hair, is a psychocutaneous condition associated with functional impairment and decreased quality of life
evidence.explanation: Records the disorder's dual psychiatric-dermatological character.

steps/3.description: The dermatological consequence, and usually the presenting complaint. Because the alopecia is produced by traction rather than by follicular disease, it is mechanically patterned - irregular, incomplete, and distributed where the hands reach - which is what distinguishes it clinically from alopecia areata.
